paragraphs.text: While the Evangelists Luke and Matthew were concerned with the temporal events of the Nativity, John was concerned to bring out the eternal birth of the Lord Christ, because his first concern was to prove the divinity of Christ in the midst of the doubts the Jews raised against the person of Christ. There is no verse stronger than: "and the Word was God." For this reason, we find that a group such as the Jehovah's Witnesses, who deny Christianity and the divinity of Christ, alter in their book the wording of this verse to: "and the Word was a god." What is meant by the Word is the divine Mind, that is, the Second Hypostasis, because the word expresses the mind, proceeds from it, and is equal to it.

The second verse affirms, more clearly, the eternal existence of the Father and the Son. There was no moment, in human language, in which the Father was prior or alone; the eternal birth of the Son is wholly bound up with the existence of the Father, just as we say that the appearing of the disc of the sun is bound up with the going forth of the ray of light from it.

A clear indication affirming the divinity of Christ, since He is the Creator, "and without him was not any thing made" of creation (compare Heb 1:2). The Apostle goes on to a spiritual dimension alongside the theological one, and says: "was life," that is, Christ is not only Creator, but the source of the life and strength of all His children who have believed and been baptized (in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit). St. John points to the rejection of Christ by the Jews, which made him describe them as the darkness that did not comprehend the light sent to the world.

So, beloved, do you thank the Lord Christ that you are the creature of His hands, whom He made and to whom He gave life, and for whom He wanted fellowship with Him in the light? He who truly believes that he is the center of the Lord's concern finds nothing to offer in return except a life of constant thanksgiving.
The talk here is about John the Baptist and his mission, namely, preparing people to receive Christ, and not drawing people to himself and to faith in him.

Preparing people to receive Christ is a shared mission of all the people of His Church. The true Christian does not think of himself as a light, but as a reflector of the light of Christ upon all those around him; his witness is either by word, like the witness of John, or by his works and outward conduct, so that all those around him see the light of Christ through him.
The talk returns here to the person of Christ the Savior. Although the Lord Christ was the hope of the Jews, and they were waiting for Him, they did not know Him and did not receive Him.

This is the condition of Christ today, between those who receive and those who reject, and those who claim to be His children, but by their works do not receive Him, rather they push Him back. For receiving Christ is not a declaration, but the submission of the soul and the will to His will, and the carrying out of His commandments and acting upon them: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Mt 5:16).

"As many as received him ... even to them that believe on his name": there was, and still is, a special gift for everyone who wants Christ, and it is the gift of sonship to God. Physical birth gives lineage and ancestry, and the earthly inheritance ends in death and passing away. But spiritual birth, whose condition is faith and Baptism (Mk 16:16), gives divine sonship and lineage, and a heavenly inheritance that is sure and does not fade away.

We all received this gift freely in the Holy Sacrament of Baptism, which places a great responsibility on the Christian, and a question that keeps presenting itself all the time: is my lineage to the world or to Christ? ... Do I live as one born of the flesh or as one born of the Spirit? Careful attention to this question, and to what we call the daily reckoning of the soul concerning all our deeds, has a great effect on the spiritual life with God.

"The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us": a reference to the mystery of the Incarnation, which is one of the basic doctrines of Christianity, that God the Word became flesh. The meaning of "flesh" here is a perfect man, as the Creed indicates, "became incarnate and became man"; that is, Christ the God took a human body, soul and spirit united with His divinity, so that He became perfect God and perfect man (compare 1 Tim 3:16). And "became" does not mean that the divinity was changed into material flesh, or limited by a material body, but means: He united with it.
We know that the word "flesh," in the language of the Holy Bible, has one of three meanings:
(1) Body: "No man ever yet hated his own flesh" (Eph 5:29).
(2) Evil: "and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Rom 13:14).
(3) A complete human person: "Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh" (Mt 19:6).

The prophet Baruch prophesied of the Incarnation and of dwelling among us when he said: "This is our God, and there shall none other be accounted of in comparison of him ... Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men" (Bar 3:36, 38).

Besides the dimension of faith in these two verses, we can also draw out the following spiritual meanings: "Was made flesh": the Christian became a son of God, because the only begotten Son of God became man.

"Dwelt among us": He lived in our midst as one of us with wonderful humility, experiencing all our pains, feeling for us in all our distress; indeed He is the helper of all who suffer ... for none will feel for you except one who suffered all the suffering for your sake ... this is your Christ (Heb 2:18).

"And we beheld his glory, the glory": how hard it is to speak of the glory of God before the Incarnation. When Moses tried to see the glory of God, the answer came to him: "There shall no man see me, and live" (Ex 33:20). But in the Incarnation of Christ, we saw the glory of God incarnate in His miracles, which none can do but God. And as a man, He became, in His example for us, without a single sin, presenting to us the image of the perfect man in whose image we ought to be, without excusing or justifying our sins by the circumstances of the world around us.

"As of the only begotten of the Father": this distinguishes the sonship of Christ from our own sonship to God, for the sonship of Christ is a sonship of the divine nature, that is, the begetting of the eternal Word from the Father before all ages. But our sonship, we obtained through faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit through the Holy Sacrament of Baptism.
"Full of grace and truth": grace is the free gifts that Christ gives us. And truth is the declaration of the truth of God and faith in Him.
This is a witness of John the Baptist, confirming everything he had previously prophesied about the coming of Christ after him, but that He has the first place, and he also points to His eternity.
In Christ is all the fullness and satisfaction for those who seek Him among those who believe in His name, and from His fullness John and all Christians received.

"Grace for grace": a reference to the difference between the grace of the Old Testament, limited to prophets, promises, hope and commandments, and the grace of the New Testament, in which God spoke through His Son and through His free redemption. The Law gave justification to no one, but was a clarification of the way. But Christ is "the way, the truth, and the life" (ch. 14:6).
God wanted to reveal to us the nature of His essence in a way that can be perceived, and there was no way other than the Incarnation of the Word.

"In the bosom of the Father": a reference to the union and communion between the Father and the Son. It also means that during the Incarnation of Christ on earth, He did not depart from the Father, but He fills every time and place.
"He hath declared him": another affirmation of the eternal unity between the Father and the Son.

There were possibilities about the person of John: either he was a false prophet like some before him, or he was Elijah who precedes the Christ (Mal 3:1; 4:5), or a true prophet of whom Moses prophesied (Deut 18:15), or the awaited Christ. For this reason, a delegation of scribes, Pharisees and Levites, representing the order of ministers, was sent to inquire about this powerful figure whose disciples had multiplied. We notice the cunning of the Jews in their question, for they knew that the Christ is from the tribe of Judah and the seed of David, while John was from the tribe of Levi, the tribe of the priesthood. And when John was asked, he did not, in humility, ascribe to himself any of these attributes, but pointed to his mission of preparing the people with the Baptism of repentance to receive Christ, who alone, by His authority, gives the Baptism of the Holy Spirit. He also testified that Christ was standing in their midst and had become incarnate. And in true humility, he ended his speech by saying that he was nothing before the glory of the One coming after him, whose shoe's latchet he was not worthy to unloose, which was among the services of slaves at that time.
Perhaps we can draw two lessons from this witness of John:
(1) That the mission of every Christian is to bear witness to Christ the God and Savior.
(2) That we learn humility, and do not steal God's glory for ourselves, but it is enough of a boast for us to serve His name while prostrate beneath His feet.
"Bethabara": it is the place where Joshua crossed with the people into the Promised Land.

John reveals to us a new secret from the secrets of the work of the Holy Spirit, for he did not know the person of Christ beforehand, but the work of the Holy Spirit in guidance is what informed John of a clear sign, "like a dove." Through this sign, John became certain that He is the Christ ... Then the Baptist affirms to us, through his witness, that Christ is the Son of God (v. 34), and is the "Lamb of God" given for us as a redemption for the forgiveness of sins (vv. 29, 36), who was at that time coming from the mountain of temptation, to begin His ministry and to offer Himself as a sin offering for the world.
John gave his witness in 3 stages: v. 19 to v. 28; v. 29 to v. 34; vv. 35-36 in the hearing of his two disciples, Andrew and John.

And now, beloved, what you received in the sacrament of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Myron, is able to guide you amid the circumstances and problems of life, so that you live reassured at all times, and even come to know more and more the will of God in your life.

The two disciples of John the Baptist heard his witness to Christ and followed Him. Jesus asked them: "What seek ye?" They answered that they wanted to know where He dwelt, so He welcomed them, and they came with Him to His place, and stayed with Him all day; and thus their discipleship to Him began.

That God asks you, when you follow Him, what you seek, so that your following may be love for His person with faith and surrender, and not for any ulterior purposes such as personal interest, or show and pride, or merely filling spare time.

Andrew was one of the two disciples of John the Baptist who followed Christ, so he called his brother Simon and announced to him the appearing of the Messiah, and took him to Christ, who changed his name to Cephas, that is Peter, which means a rock, a reference to his future ministry in holding fast to the rock of faith and preaching it.

It is known in the Holy Bible that some names were changed, heralding the beginning of a great mission, such as Abram who became Abraham, and Jacob who became Israel; and as is customary now in the ordination of bishops, priests and deacons, each of them receives the name of one of the saints to suit his new mission.

Jesus headed for the region of Galilee in the north, and continued calling His disciples, where He found Philip, who was from the city of Bethsaida, in which also was the home of Andrew and Peter, and He called him and he followed Him. Philip told his friend Nathanael that they had found the awaited Christ, who is the son of Joseph, who is from the city of Nazareth. It appears from Philip's words that the goal of the Law and the prophecies is the awaited Messiah. This Nathanael is the one whose name later became Bartholomew, and he is one of the disciples of Christ.

As for the haste in judgment into which Nathanael fell, and the sweeping condemnation of all the people of Nazareth: we learn from it not to judge anyone, for perhaps, without knowing, we fall into condemning saints, as Nathanael judged Christ Himself.
The Jews knew that the Christ comes from Bethlehem, the city of David (Mic 5:2; Mt 2:5, 6; Jn 7:42), and not from Nazareth of Galilee.

When Christ saw Nathanael, He greeted him by saying that he was an Israelite, that is, not one of the Gentiles scattered in the region of Galilee. Nathanael marveled and asked Him: "Whence knowest thou me?" Jesus continued His words, that He had known him for a long time, when he was under the fig tree. This is a secret story that no one knew except Nathanael and his mother. When Herod ordered the killing of the children in Bethlehem who were less than two years old, Nathanael's mother was afraid and hid her child under a fig tree, and kept watching him from afar. The soldiers searched the whole region and killed the children, but did not find the place of Nathanael, and left. Then she took him and raised him secretly, away from all eyes, so that he would not be killed. And when he grew up, she told him the story of his escape from death, and he kept it as a secret within himself, until Christ revealed it to him when He met him. So Nathanael became certain that Jesus is the awaited Messiah, who knows the unseen, and he declared that He is the Son of God and the King of Israel.
We must not fail to note that the Child Jesus was not in Bethlehem at that time, but on His way to Egypt with His mother St. Mary and Joseph the carpenter.

Jesus added to Nathanael that his faith would increase, not because he had seen Christ who knows the unseen, but for greater things he would see in following Him, namely the accomplishment of redemption on the Cross, by which He reconciles the heavenly beings with the earthly, and the angels ascend with the prayers of the believers to heaven through Christ the Redeemer, and descend from heaven with many blessings through Christ also, the Savior of the world.
The wedding at Cana of Galilee; the cleansing of the temple

entries.section: (1) The wedding at Cana of Galilee

paragraphs.text: The town of Cana lies in the north of Palestine, near the region of Galilee, and is 15 kilometers east of Nazareth. Despite the weariness of fatigue and travel, the Lord Christ did not hesitate to go and attend out of courtesy. For sharing is one of the forms of love, especially that in which effort is expended, and it was also in honor of marriage, which He would make one of the sacraments of the Church.
So three days after the calling of Nathanael, the Virgin Mary was invited, as well as Christ and His disciples, to the wedding feast in the city of Cana.

entries.section: (1) The wedding at Cana of Galilee

paragraphs.text: The love and motherhood of the Virgin appear in her sensing the need of those around her without their asking.

It seems that the number of those who came to the wedding was much greater than expected, so the prepared wine ran out, which was the juice of grapes, naturally fermented, without distillation or the addition of alcohol, that is, by the action of bacteria only, and if it became old, the taste of vinegar appeared in it, but it does not become like the intoxicating wine sold in the markets now, which the Holy Bible forbids.

The Virgin hastened, with love, to ask Christ to rescue the people of the wedding from this embarrassment. It was not in God's plan to begin His miracles and His preaching now, so He said to her: "Woman, what have I to do with thee?" that is, you are a human being, and you do not know the wisdom of God and the time He has appointed. But at the same time He honored her, because she is His mother, the holy Virgin Mary, and He answered her intercession.
The faith of the Virgin appears in that Christ accepts her intercession, in her asking the servants to do whatever He commands them.

My beloved brother, ask God for everything you need, however difficult it may seem, for He loves you ... and seek the intercession of the saints because of their great standing with Him, especially the Virgin Mary.

entries.section: (1) The wedding at Cana of Galilee

paragraphs.text: There were in the house six waterpots, that is, large basins, which they filled with water to wash with in the Jewish purifications according to the Law, and each pot held about 80 liters. Christ told the servants to fill them completely with water, then commanded them to bring it to the ruler of the feast. When he tasted the water that had been turned into wine, he felt that it was of the good kind, so he rebuked the bridegroom for serving the good wine at the end, and the lesser wine at the beginning, and he did not know that the second wine had been changed from water. The servants felt, and indeed all those at the feast afterward, that they were before a great miracle, for it is a miracle of creation, since Christ created grape juice and alcohol that had not existed. This is the first of the miracles of Christ, and the Church counts it as one of the minor Feasts of the Lord, and celebrates it on the third day after the Feast of Theophany.
The Lord Christ took Capernaum as a base for His dwelling and for setting out to minister after Nazareth, and it was an important city lying on the Sea of Galilee in the north.

"His brethren": the Church believes in her doctrine and tradition that the holy Virgin Mary did not bear in the flesh anyone but the person of the Lord Jesus, keeping her virginity, and never knew her betrothed Joseph physically at all, which confirms that Christ, in the flesh, had no brothers from Mary. This is what Ezekiel said in his prophecy: "then he shall go forth; and after his going forth one shall shut the gate" (Ezek 46:12). As for His brethren, they are cousins, since the tradition in the Levant, even to this day, is that cousins are called brothers.

The Passover of the Jews was the most important of their religious feasts. They would come from all over the world to Jerusalem, where the temple of Solomon was, to offer sacrifices and celebrate this great feast. And this is what the Lord Jesus Himself did. And upon His entering the temple, John reveals to us what the Lord saw and what grieved His heart, indeed angered Him, namely that the porches of the temple had been turned into something resembling a marketplace, for there were the tables and the animals and every kind of trade, and the shouting and all the clamor that occurs in markets, which is contrary to the dignity of the house of God and the loss of the purpose of worship. The text here is explicit, and shows the decisiveness of the Lord Christ, and His zeal for His house and the house of His Father, in what He did. There is a difference between feverish, sinful anger, which many justify for themselves and which God condemns, and righteous zeal and holy anger over my sins, or to rescue the oppressed, or for the sake of the house of God and its rights. My beloved brother, how much we also need now to have the same zeal for the Church, which is the house of God and of the angels and the saints. And God is very jealous for His glory and His house ... and perhaps we too, the children of the Church, cause others to stumble by our conduct and our appearance, which do not befit the dignity of the house of God, the heaven on earth, of which David says: "Holiness becometh thine house, O Lord, for ever" (Ps 93:5).
A very frightening question that we ask ourselves: what if the Lord came now and visited His Church, as He visited His temple?!! Would everything He sees please Him? ... Begin with yourself.

However, the Jews, the priests and the merchants did not accept what the Lord had done. For this reason they asked Him: "What sign shewest thou unto us" ... as Moses did to Pharaoh to prove that God had sent him? Its meaning is: by what authority do you do this, for you are not one of the ministers or priests, and you are not a worker of wonders or miracles, that we should listen to you.

This is what is contrary, in our life, to submission to the commandments and works of God. For one of the most important conditions of faith, as we have pointed out, is believing without demands or material confirmations.

We note that the Lord Christ, during the period of His ministry, attended the Passover 4 times: this is the first of them. The second (ch. 5:1), where He healed the sick man of Bethesda. The third (ch. 6:4), where He fed the multitudes. And the fourth (ch. 11:55), where He was crucified.

The Lord cleansed the temple twice: this time at the beginning of His ministry, and the second time at the end of His ministry on earth, four days before the Crucifixion (Mt 21:12, 13; Mk 11:15-17; Lk 19:45, 46).

When the Jews asked for a sign, the Lord Christ surprised them with what they did not expect, that they would destroy the temple and He would raise it up in three days. And because what He said was a prophecy about His death and Resurrection, they did not understand, but scoffed mockingly!! As for the forty and six years, the time of the building of the temple, it has another story ... The temple was first built on the same site, and Solomon built it in 950 B.C. in 7 years, and the Babylonians destroyed it. Then Zerubbabel built it in 515 B.C. Then Herod restored it, beginning in 16 B.C. until 30 A.D., the time of the preaching of Christ, and this is the period meant by the 46 years.
Perhaps the reader will connect what the Lord said here with what is mentioned in (Mt 12:39; Lk 11:

29), when the Jews asked the Lord for a sign (a miracle), and He answered them also that no sign would be given to them but the sign of the prophet Jonah, foretelling also His death and Resurrection after three days ... and of course the saying was hard and not understood by the Jews ... but such are the prophecies, for they are often hard, and when they come to pass, their truth and the truth of their speaker are proved; and this is what the text confirms, that the disciples understood, and their faith was established after the Resurrection of the Lord from the dead.

Despite the faith of many as a result of the miracles the Lord performed, whose number we do not know (compare ch. 21:25), Christ did not commit Himself unto them. This means that He knew what was in the hearts of those around Him ... for He knows that this is not a steadfast faith, but a faith led by amazement, and it is a temporary, shallow faith that does not last. And the expression "for he knew what was in man" is a strong indication of His divinity, which He also confirmed in His ability to raise His body after death.

So I wonder, beloved, which kind of faith do we have of those mentioned in (Mt 3:23; Mk 4:2-20)? Is it a firm faith working in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, or is it a theoretical faith that appears in times of ease and disappears at the Cross?

The Church teaches us not to rejoice and be deceived by abundant and quick fruit, lest it be a faith resembling the faith of the Jews, who quickly turned around crying out: "Crucify him ... crucify him" ... Amen, O Lord, establish us in Your upright faith. Baptism, faith in Christ

The Pharisees were a group of Jews who kept up the appearance of piety and held strictly to carrying out the commandments and the traditions of the elders. The meaning of their title is "the separated ones," and they were distinguished by boasting; they were among the fiercest opponents of Christ during His ministry. Among them was Nicodemus, who held a social and religious standing as "a ruler of the Jews," that is, a member of the Supreme Council of the Jews, which included their great men. He went to Christ by night, for two reasons. First: that he might inquire for himself about the person of Christ and not depend on what he had heard.
Second: that his affair might not be exposed, so he chose the darkness for this visit; he must have feared that the rest of the Pharisees would learn of this visit.

Perhaps we may learn from Nicodemus to go ourselves to the Lord Christ and speak with Him, and to have fellowship with the Holy Bible and the sacraments, instead of being content with hearing about Him only from others.

Nicodemus began his speech by showing respect for the person of Christ, calling Him a teacher, a word with a special significance among the Jews, which is not applied to just anyone. He also offered faith, though his faith needed confirmation. And this was the reason for the visit, as we have already indicated.

Jesus answered without Nicodemus having asked, and from Christ's answer we understand that the question concerned salvation and the condition for entering the Kingdom. Likewise, in Christ's answering without being asked there is a declaration to Nicodemus that the Lord knew what was within him, and it is also a proof of His divinity.

Christ began His answer with an expression He used often: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee (you)," and this expression points to the truthfulness of the speaker, his authority, and the importance of the subject.
The sum of Christ's words and His teaching is that salvation is not limited to the Jews (v. 16), but is available to all; its conditions, however, are:
(1) Birth from above: this means the birth of sonship to God by the Holy Spirit, which makes us children of heaven, and makes us strangers to evil earthly desires.

(2) Birth of water and the Spirit: this is the same heavenly birth as before, but through its visible form in the Holy Sacrament of Baptism. For this reason we see our Church's care in teaching that there is no salvation without the spiritual birth from the waters of holy Baptism, and that the condition of faith alone is not enough.

We find a situation that recurs often, and which St. John highlighted: the inability of the human mind to understand the divine purpose. Nicodemus did not understand the meaning of the second birth, and could imagine nothing except entering a second time into the mother's womb. This also happened when the Lord spoke of the destruction of the temple, "His body" (ch. 2:19), and it will occur again in His dialogue with the Samaritan woman (ch. 4:7-14). Yet despite this, God does not leave man without explaining His purpose to him.
There is a great difference between one who belongs to heaven by his new birth and one who belongs to the flesh.
If we have received the new spiritual nature freely in the sacrament of Baptism, do we walk as spiritual people, or is it the desires and inclinations of the flesh that lead us?

Beloved, the Holy Spirit has given you what others cannot understand; do you value this gift and this responsibility? It is a call to think and to ask: in my affairs and my relationships, do I walk as a heavenly person, or am I ruled, like the others, by the law of the world and its materialism?
It is also noted that the word "must" gave confirmation and obligation to all Christians of the necessity of being born from above (Baptism).

"The wind": the speech here is about the Holy Spirit and His hidden work; you do not see Him materially, but you perceive His action and His effects. If we see a tree shaking with all its leaves and bending, we perceive that it is exposed to the wind and affected by it, without knowing the source of the wind or where it goes ... So it is with the Holy Spirit; we perceive Him by His effects on everyone who has received Him and accepted Him in the anointing of the Myron, or the laying on of the apostolic hands (Acts 19:6). And accordingly, so is everyone who is born of the Spirit: he has received from Him strength, love, wisdom, patience, humility and spiritual insight. Baptism gives us three fundamentals: that we belong to God and not to Satan, that we be stronger than Satan, and that we become inclined to good and not to evil.

entries.section: (2) The importance and loftiness of faith

paragraphs.text: The dialogue continues between Nicodemus' astonishment and Christ's gentle rebuke of him: how is it that you, O teacher and interpreter of the Law, do not grasp the spiritual meanings and the divine purpose? The meaning intended here is that theoretical and literal knowledge is not God's purpose and thought.

Such is the state of many of us now: we read the Holy Bible, and we may even teach from it, yet we do not grasp the spiritual dimensions of the word of God, which are grasped only by man's humility before the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and his submission to Him under the guidance of the Church.

entries.section: (2) The importance and loftiness of faith

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ adds to His words to Nicodemus, who is still unable to understand, an assurance that His words and His testimony are true. The Lord Christ used the plural of Himself, which is unusual among the Jews, saying: "We ... speak ... know ... testify ... our witness." This is a clear indication of His oneness in the Most Holy Trinity; this Trinity alone is the One who knows, teaches, and bears witness to Himself, and not accepting His testimony and teaching is the ignorance of the material world that rejects God Himself.

entries.section: (2) The importance and loftiness of faith

paragraphs.text: The direct meaning here is: if you do not accept simple matters, how will you grasp the more difficult truths of the faith?

"Earthly things": its meaning here is the earthly spiritual matters necessary for life on earth, such as the second spiritual birth, Baptism. It also means that Christ used an earthly comparison to explain the spiritual meaning, when He connected the earthly wind with the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of the believer.

"If I tell you of heavenly things": its meaning is that there is a part that is harder for the mind, yet is at the very heart of the faith, and must be proclaimed and believed, such as His relationship with the Father, "I and My Father are one" (ch. 10:30), and redemption by His death, the resurrection from the dead, the ascension and the sitting at the right hand of the Father, all of which are matters above the level of earthly or material perceptible things.

entries.section: (2) The importance and loftiness of faith

paragraphs.text: When the Lord Christ's conversation with Nicodemus drew near its end, the Lord began to declare three successive truths about His divinity:

The first: that He is God incarnate, who came down from heaven and ascended to heaven and is in heaven at the same time. This means that in the time of Christ's incarnation on earth, He did not leave heaven, in His unlimited divinity, for a single moment; He is in a state of incarnation and ascension continually, as the conjugation of the word "ascended" in the Greek language indicates, for it is not in the past tense as the Arabic language suggests, but in the present perfect tense as in the English language.

The second: the necessity of the Son of Man being lifted up on the wood of the Cross for redemption. The Lord Christ referred to what Moses did in lifting up the bronze serpent by God's command (see Num 21:8-9), to rescue everyone who looked at it from the deadly bite of the serpents of the wilderness; this was nothing but a type of Christ hanging on the wood of the Cross, who, by His death, rescued from death everyone who believes in Him.
The third: the connection of the free salvation offered on the Cross with faith; Christ by His redemption opened the doors of eternal life to all people, but on the condition of faith in Him.

Salvation has become a free gift that does not depend on my worthiness but on the grace of God's love for me. He offered me the Cross and redemption as a rescue, and Baptism as the entrance to it, and gave me life that I might live and enjoy being here with Him, so that I may bear witness to Him and strive for this salvation granted to me, lest I lose it ... Grant me, O Lord, to work out this salvation with fear and trembling (Phil 2:12).

These two verses, in their meaning, repeat what preceded them, that faith in Christ is the basic condition for salvation, but they add a beautiful spiritual dimension, which is that the plan of salvation has no cause other than God's indescribable and unlimited love for man ... a love beyond the grasp of the mind ... that the Father should give His only begotten Son to death for the salvation and life of the world. And this incarnation and redemption did not have as its purpose judgment or the satisfaction of divine justice ... how easy it would have been for God to judge His creation with a single word; the harder thing is the giving and the death for the justification of sinners in the blood of Christ ... But whoever rejected this redemption and this love offered by the Father in giving His only begotten Son deserved judgment.

Beloved ... what distinguishes the saints from us is their practical realization of this indescribable love, for God's love is above the level of changeable human emotions; it is constant and eternal (Jer 31:3), and likewise it is satisfaction for the soul and the spirit. When the saints realized this kind of love, they left everything for its sake, and they are the ones who gained ... Do we realize this wonderful love as they did? And does our conduct express this love? We do not need to know that God loved us, but to enter with Him into the fellowship of infinite love ...
A question we put, beloved, to all of us: what have we left for the sake of the love of Christ, as these did?!

This love and this light were not accepted by many, who deserve judgment. St. John gives us the reason for their rejection of this light, which is that they are evil, and everyone who does evil and sin consequently hates the light that exposes these evil deeds and reproves them.

The secret of the distance of many these days from God and the Church is that they know where the truth is and where Christ is, but they ignore Him because of their love for sin ... This is contrary to the spiritual man who strives in the divine commandment of love; he has no place except Christ, he draws strength from the Church, and his works bear witness to the work of God in his life.
"After these things": a phrase St. John always uses to move the reader from one conversation to another, or from one place to another, or from one time to another.
"The land of Judaea": east of the mountains of Jerusalem on the banks of the Jordan, and it is known that the previous conversation with Nicodemus was in Jerusalem.

"He baptized": its meaning is that His disciples were baptizing and not He Himself (see ch. 4:2), but what His disciples were doing is attributed to their Teacher. St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine agree that the baptism of the disciples was not counted as a sacramental baptism like that which the disciples also practiced after the Holy Spirit came upon them, but the former is considered similar to John's baptism in that it was a preparation for repentance only.

This verse reveals to us the move of John the Baptist from beyond the Jordan to Aenon near Salim, because of the abundance of water in that new place compared with beyond the Jordan. It is implicitly understood that the increase in the numbers of the repentant drove the Baptist to look for a place where the water was more plentiful than the shallow waters of the Jordan, which confirms that baptism was by immersion and not sprinkling. As for Aenon and Salim, they cannot now be identified geographically, but the commentators agree that they lie west of the Jordan River, near the land of Judaea in which Christ stayed with His disciples.

It is understood from this verse that there was a period in which the Baptist ministered during the ministry of the Lord Christ, for the Baptist here had not yet been cast into prison. And we find Nicodemus in (v. 2) testifying to Christ that He performs signs. St. John was careful to mention this, because whoever is content with reading the other three Gospels only believes that Christ's ministry did not begin until after the Baptist's imprisonment, but the truth is that what began after the imprisonment was Christ's ministry in Galilee.

The Jews understood the baptisms of John and of Christ's disciples as one form of purification and repentance, and in this they were not mistaken according to their understanding, which was still bound to the Law of the Old Covenant, which contained ordinances of purification ... But the dispute or argument was a comparison between the baptism of Christ's disciples, which was increasing, with the Jews gathering around Christ, and the baptism of John the Baptist and his followers, which was decreasing on the other hand. In this dispute the Jews provoked John's disciples, who in turn went to John, presenting to him what had stirred them, that everyone was going to Christ instead of him, asking John to defend himself and his baptism, which came before the baptism of Christ's disciples.

The disciples of John the Baptist forgot his first testimony beyond the Jordan to the Lord Christ, when he said that he was not worthy to loose the strap of His sandal (ch. 1:27), and that He is the Son of God (ch. 1:34). Their emotional attachment, and their following of the Baptist with merely human feelings, made them fall into jealousy at the spread of Christ's preaching. We do the same at times: our love for certain persons and our attachment to them may make us fall into a wrong partiality that keeps us from seeing the truth, and we follow them in everything even if we oppose Christ and His commandment ... Do we not then share the error of the Baptist's disciples?!
In these verses the Baptist answers the angry jealousy of his disciples with a kind of calm teaching, clear and frank as well, and the Baptist summarized his teaching in the following points:
(1) That he cannot take anything or claim a right that heaven has not given him (v. 27).

(2) A reminder to his disciples of what he had said before, that he is the forerunner of Christ to prepare the way and the souls, and that he is not the Christ. (3) How great is the difference between the Bridegroom, the Owner of creation and of the wedding, who has the bride (the souls of the believers), and the friend of the bridegroom, for whom it is enough, as a boast and a glory, that he is a friend who contributed to preparing the bride for the bridegroom without claiming that he has any share in her, and for this reason he considers his joy fulfilled (v. 29), because the Church is the Church of Christ.

(4) The Baptist confirms this difference when he declares that the natural order is that "He" (Christ) and His Kingdom must increase because He alone is the Owner of honor, and that he himself must decrease and disappear, so that he may also present all who are with him, his disciples, to Christ the Bridegroom of the true wedding, as if he were saying: when the sun rises, its light [overwhelms] all the lamps. Blessed are you, O Baptist, who were counted worthy to be the greatest prophet born of women. Blessed are you in your humility and the clarity of matters within you, for you did not steal the glory of God for yourself, and you did not take anything that was not given to you. Would that we might learn from you not to think that we are the owners of honor, but merely servants and slaves ... that we attribute all glory and honor to the Lord alone, so that our joy may be fulfilled in Him who saved us, as your joy was fulfilled.

The Baptist continues his speech, clarifying the difference between the Lord Christ and any other created being, even the Baptist himself. Every man is earthly, and however great his knowledge and understanding, it is limited because it is earthly, and heaven with all its mysteries has not been unveiled to him. And however much he speaks, he speaks in the language of the earth, which is limited and deficient in understanding heavenly things and expressing them. This is unlike Christ, who alone is "from above," that is, from the Father, and this is the reason He is "above all," because His source is the Father and not heaven only, otherwise any angel whose source is heaven would also be above all.

What is meant is that Christ testifies to the truth that He knows and declares. As for the use of the expression "seen and heard," it is the Holy Spirit's use of a human expression to bring the meaning near, for the true testimony that man believes is the testimony of an eyewitness, "by sight and hearing," and it is an allusion to the truth of Christ's testimony even if no man accepts it. And the phrase "and no man receiveth His testimony" is a prophecy of the rejection of Christ's teaching and redemption by the scribes and Pharisees, and the many after them, the Council of the Seventy and the priests.

That is, whoever accepted Christ's testimony and believed it has believed and affirmed that God is true, because Christ is God, and because Christ is the Word of God and the One who declares to people the words of His Father, and because He is from God He speaks only the words of His Father ... As for the meaning of "God giveth not the Spirit by measure," it is that the Holy Spirit was given to all the prophets by measure according to what the hearer could bear, and according to the circumstances. But as for Christ, the Holy Spirit is not given by measure, but with the whole fullness of the Spirit, because the measure of Christ's fullness is the measure of God Himself; in other words, because Christ is God, He did not receive a measure of the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit fills Him perfectly just as the Holy Spirit is filled from the wisdom of the Son perfectly, and this is another distinction that the Baptist adds in his testimony about Christ in His difference from the rest of creation, since He is its Creator.
"The Father loveth the Son": a new mystery that St. John reveals to us in the relationship of the three hypostases, for love is the language of the Most Holy Trinity ...

Likewise this verse shows, indirectly, the divinity of the Lord Christ and proves it, for God says: "My glory will I not give to another" (Isa 42:8). Yet that He should give all the glory to the Son, "hath given all things into His hand," is because the Son is equal to the Father in essence, and all that is the Father's is the Son's, and all that is the Son's is the Father's.

St. John concludes this chapter with what he wishes to affirm, and which he spoke of in verses 15, (16, 18): that there is no salvation without faith in the Lord Christ; indeed, this verse is the key and the summary of the Samaritan [woman]

This shows us that the reason the Lord left the land of Judaea was the problems and comparisons that the Pharisees began to stir up between the baptism and followers of John on the one hand, and the baptism and disciples of Christ on the other (ch. 3).
Here the Lord Christ teaches us a spiritual lesson: that a person should avoid fruitless arguments, and even flee from them, lest he waste his time and effort and lose his peace to no benefit ...

"He must needs go through Samaria": this phrase carries two meanings. The first is simple: the geographical meaning, that Samaria lay on His way to Galilee. The deeper meaning is spiritual: that is, God "labored" for the salvation of the Samaritan woman, and for this reason He had to pass through Samaria so that He might meet her and speak with her.
How wonderful is Your plan, O Lord, for the salvation of my soul!

"Sychar": a town near Shechem, which is more famous, and in it was a well dug by Jacob to water his flocks and to affirm his ownership of these lands, since the well bore his name. Jacob had given this place to Joseph in preference to the rest of his brothers (see Gen 48:22), and this also confirms the descent of the Samaritans from their father Jacob.

"Wearied with His journey": all the interpreting Fathers of the Church paused over this verse in contemplation. Here is God who took our flesh and lived our life, and was wearied for our sake in order to offer us salvation ... He experienced pain and weariness as a man, so that we would have no excuse for not also being wearied in serving others. The distance He covered from His departure from Judaea to this town was 40 miles (the mile = 1,609.35 meters), that is, about 64 kilometers, bearing the hardship of walking in the heat for the salvation of one soul!

Among the wonderful parallels between what this story points to and the events of the Cross are what we see of thirst, weariness and the sixth hour, and the goal is salvation, whether for the Samaritan woman or for the whole world, and in both accounts the disciples left Him alone (v. 8).

So, is it a coincidence, or a clear prophetic sign, as a prelude to the events of the Cross? Nor should we overlook that the sixth hour here points to the condition of the Samaritan woman, for, because of her sin and bad reputation, she went out to draw water at a time when it was rare for other women to be present with her, so as to avoid their reproaches and their looks at her ... But Christ loves her and seeks her out!

entries.section: (2) The meeting with the Samaritan woman

paragraphs.text: Since it was in God's prior arrangement and knowledge that He would meet the Samaritan woman, He sent all His disciples to buy food, so that He could meet the Samaritan woman alone. He thereby teaches us that, besides the ministry of teaching and preaching to the crowds, attention to individual work and the single soul is no less important than work with the masses, and also so that He would not shame her as she confessed her sins, as happens now in the sacrament of Confession. Christ asked the Samaritan woman for water to drink although He is "the fountain of living waters" (Jer 2:13, 17:13), and He is "the fountain of the water of life" (Rev 21:6), and He was sitting by the well as though in need of water; all this was so that He might enter her heart by humility.
Humility makes it easy for you to win the hearts of others and to convey the word of God to them.

The Samaritan woman's answer reminds us of the Lord's conversation with Nicodemus (ch. 3): man speaks of tangible material things, while Christ speaks of a deeper spiritual dimension ... What the Samaritan woman said was confined to the enmity existing between the Jews and the Samaritans, and her refusal was in a tone of disapproval so as to hide or forget her sin.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with the Samaritan woman

paragraphs.text: "If thou knewest the gift of God": Christ here addresses the Samaritan woman and every soul; it is He who wills, and He begins the conversation with her in dialogue.

And we, sadly, do not realize the dimensions of this great gift, otherwise this would not be our state. We are still seeking the water of the world and its material things and its desires, although we know that there is no satisfaction or quenching from it, forgetting the source of true riches that fills every material, psychological and spiritual thirst and need; He is the true God who wants to give you everything ... And whoever accepts God's gift rises above the whole world and will never thirst. God's gift does not make a person content with it only, but he becomes a spring that waters the needs of others, like a channel that carries the current of a great river, so that it is first watered itself, and every thirsty person draws from it ... And this is the source of the spiritual richness of man which we have seen in all the saints, the early ones and the contemporary ... And the most wonderful thing is that this divine current that God gives, which is the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in man, never leaves him, even to eternal life.

As for the Samaritan woman, she still does not grasp the Lord's speech; at one time she wonders where He gets this water when He has nothing to draw with (v. 11), and at another she wants this water in its material form, so that she would not have to come back to this well bearing the hardship of the road. Her state even reached the point of mocking Him, for of course He is not better than Jacob and his sons who drank from it, so how could He get better water than this well?!

entries.section: (2) The meeting with the Samaritan woman

paragraphs.text: In this she brings us back again to what we began with, which is the nature of the human being who does not realize God's gift of the indwelling and outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (3) Christ reveals Himself to the Samaritan woman

paragraphs.text: After the Lord Christ spoke of spiritual things in a hidden manner in which He prepared her to ask for the living water, He revealed Himself directly, but only to the extent she could bear. He asked her to bring her husband if she truly desired this living water, and the woman answered with half the truth, that she had no lawful husband, thereby hiding her sin of living with a man without marriage. But the surprise with which Christ astounded her, in declaring that He knew all her past, and even the present she was living, shook her conscience, and so her reply came, which represents the first spark of her faith, as she said, "Sir," after she had at first refused to speak with Him because He was a Jew; then she also testified that He is "a prophet," after she had been mocking and saying, "Art thou greater than our father Jacob?" Dear one ... in the previous conversation we see a glimpse which we may learn from the person of our beloved God, namely His wonderful gentleness in breaking into this sinful soul. He knows her state and her sin, yet look at Him as He praises her twice, once before He declares His knowledge of her sin, and once again after He has declared this knowledge, beginning His speech with the phrase "Thou hast well said," and ending His speech with the phrase "in that saidst thou truly." And with this gentleness, He did not neglect to declare the truth so that this woman might repent of her sin ... Would that we all might learn this manner: God did not smear her over, though He is the Judge, but He exposed the error for the sake of her repentance and not her destruction.

Do we treat sinners with this gentleness, with the difference that we are sinners and under judgment? Let us take this exercise for our lives: to praise the faint ray of light in every person before directing him.

entries.section: (3) Christ reveals Himself to the Samaritan woman

paragraphs.text: When the Samaritan woman realized that the Lord was not an ordinary person but a prophet, her speech turned to another direction, as she was occupied with the religious dispute between the Jews and the Samaritans, and each side's claim to the correctness of its faith, and it was as if, after realizing His distinguished person, she forgot the story of the water and the well and became concerned with the salvation of her soul. And when the Lord saw that the woman had become prepared, He began to speak to her about true worship and its concept, which is not tied to place but to manner, for God does not accept the worship of the body without the spirit.

"In spirit and in truth they must worship": it means worship with contrition and the sense of God's presence. As for bodily and merely numerical worship, God does not accept it, but man is deceived by it in his spiritual practices. And despite this spiritual disclosure about worshiping God in every place, the Lord did not neglect to make clear that the Jewish faith in its essence is the sound faith and not the faith of the Samaritans, and that the awaited salvation has its source in the Jews (v. 22).
"The hour cometh, and now is": a clear indication of the appearance of the awaited Messiah, the end of both the Jewish and the Samaritan worship, and the transition to true spiritual worship.

It is also noted that the Lord Christ corrected the form and manner of worship without abolishing it, for prostration is a duty owed to God; it is an offering of love, respect, contrition, and a feeling of the heart that reflects man's sense of being in the true presence of God. The Church teaches her children prostration, whether in public worship such as the Divine Liturgy, or at the personal and individual level of man in his daily prayers.

entries.section: (3) Christ reveals Himself to the Samaritan woman

paragraphs.text: The woman continued her spiritual conversation, and referred to the coming Christ who knows all things. And when she reached this stage in which she carried her hope of awaiting the Savior, the hope of the Jews and the Samaritans, Christ answered her, declaring Himself and revealing Himself: "I ... am He." The person of Christ is the only One who can dissolve differences, disputes and enmity, and in Him all become one ... For many problems and disagreements, especially marital ones, find no solution because both parties insist on keeping Christ away from their lives. But if He enters, there will be neither Samaria nor Judaea, but humility, contrition, a sense of the Lord's presence, and obedience to His commandment ... Would that You, beloved Lord, were inside every home.

Why did the disciples marvel? Because Jewish teaching forbade a man to speak with a woman in a public place, even if she were his wife, and they did not understand Christ's concern for preaching and salvation. "No man said": a clear indication of the disciples' respect for their Teacher, and it is one of the Christian manners that the Lord mentioned: "The disciple is not above his master" (Mt 10:24); "The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master" (Lk 6:40).
And this spirit our Church received in what is called the life of discipleship ... and it requires true humility of heart before the Church's teachers, priests and servants ...

The Samaritan woman believed, and expressed her faith positively by setting out to her village to preach it, and the word "Is not" here does not carry doubt in her faith, but an incentive to the people to go out and make sure for themselves. "The woman then left her waterpot": it has a beautiful spiritual meaning, which is that the soul that loves Christ cannot but tell others about Him, even if it leaves its various concerns that hinder its progress from serving God, such as the love of money and position ...

A dialogue about food, in which the disciples took the earlier position of the Samaritan woman, for the Lord Christ speaks of spiritual food, "ye know not of," while they thought that someone had brought Him something to eat ... And this does not mean that Christ did not need food, being a perfect man like us, but it is a difference in priorities, for hunger and thirst for the salvation of the human soul have the priority.

Despite the exhaustion after the long journey, and His bodily need for water and food, the Lord Christ considered doing the will of His Father in calling man to salvation, and completing His work of redemption on the wood of the Cross, to be His true food, and indeed the desire of His heart, offering a new proof of His love and longing for the salvation of the human soul.

Then Christ moved to a real scene when He said: "Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields" ... Although the season of harvest was four months away, there was a harvest of another kind, for all the people of Samaria came out from the village of Sychar in their white garments in great groups after the woman's good news, and the fields were filled with them, and the Lord Christ regarded them as a spiritual harvest ready to be reaped with the sickle of faith.

God is not unrighteous to forget a man's labor, so everyone who gathers souls for the Kingdom of God receives an earthly and heavenly reward with joy, and partnership with all who went before him. And Christ, in His faithfulness, remembers the labor of everyone who went before in preparing this seed for harvest, although He is the true Sower who causes His word to grow. Here He points to the prophets of the Old Testament in their labor and their preparing of the people for four thousand years, and this is also a lesson for the disciples, preserving their humility, that whatever fruit they will reap in preaching is the result of the labor of others. And the truth is that in the field of service, the sower cannot be separated from the reaper, for whoever reaps now from the labor of him who sowed before is also sowing for another reaper after him, and this is what the Lord meant in (v. 37) using one of the well-known Jewish proverbs, that it is not necessary for the servant to see the fruits of his service; for Christ Himself, despite the perfection of His labor and redemption, the fruits of Christianity came after His ascension to heaven.

Beloved ... does this not tempt you to share in these joys ... the joys of the labor of service ... the joys of the harvest ... the joys of calling others to the Kingdom of God, so that you may be a sower and a reaper with a heavenly wage? Blessed are you if you do so.

entries.section: (7) The beginning of Christ's ministry in Galilee

paragraphs.text: In continuing the journey to Galilee, after stopping in Samaria, the Lord did not stay in Nazareth, the place of His first upbringing, which did not believe in Him and did not accept His preaching. And because this action of the Lord might raise questions, St. John indicated the reason for Christ's not entering it by His own words about it: "that a prophet hath no honor in his own country." As for the Galileans, they accepted Christ and welcomed Him, for they had seen Him during their visit to Jerusalem at the time of the feast, and they passed on reports about Him ...

entries.section: (7) The beginning of Christ's ministry in Galilee

paragraphs.text: "A certain nobleman" [lit. servant of the king]: the king here is Herod Antipas, who was the ruler responsible for this region (Galilee), and the Jews called him king. The distance this servant covered from Capernaum to Galilee was about 25 kilometers, and this shows the intensity of his attachment to the healing of his son and his knocking on every possible door ... As for the Lord Christ's answer (v. 48), it deserves our thought and contemplation, for He directs our minds to the true faith that does not require miracles to prove it, since it is firm and deeper than the working of miracles or wonders, and does not need material evidence to demonstrate it.

entries.section: (7) The beginning of Christ's ministry in Galilee

paragraphs.text: And yet Christ did not disappoint the man's hope, for He is the One who said: "him that cometh to Me I will in no wise cast out" (ch. 6:37), so His answer carried all the divine authority in healing, and even in raising from the dead, and the man believed in the power of Christ's word, and did not insist on taking Him with him to Capernaum.

entries.section: (7) The beginning of Christ's ministry in Galilee

paragraphs.text: Here the completion of the miracle is announced, and it is highlighted that the hour of the son's healing corresponded to the hour of the man's conversation with Christ.
"The second miracle": an indication that the first sign was at the wedding in Cana of Galilee.

Perhaps, dear reader, we find that faith is the pivot of the preceding miracle, for the man's faith and hope were what first drove him to walk 25 kilometers to meet Christ, and to ask the Lord to heal his son, confident in His power to do so, and so he obtained the healing of his boy.
Chapter five: the sick man of Bethesda; the authority of Christ

"After this": that is, after the miracle of healing the son of the king's servant, Christ went up to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover for the second time. He did not mention the kind of feast, because his focus was on the service of souls and preaching, and the time had not yet come for Him to attend the Passover at which He would offer Himself on the Cross.
"The sheep market" [lit. the sheep gate]: the gate of the city nearest to the temple. It was given this name because the sheep for the sacrifice were brought through it.

"Bethesda": a pool about one hundred meters in length, and its width ranged between 50 and 70 meters, with rows of columns along its sides dividing it into five waiting courts; these porches were built to receive visitors seeking healing. As for the name "Bethesda," its meaning is: house of mercy, and the sick with every kind of chronic disease used to come to it, to obtain healing whenever the still water was stirred by the action of an angel. And the word "withered" means: stiff in the joints.

This miracle shows the difference between the pool of the Old Testament, which is temporary and not permanent, and was for healing bodies by going down into it, and the New Testament, which gives permanent healing of spirit and body, as happens in the sacrament of Baptism.
(2) The healing of the sick man of Bethesda (vv. 5-9):

5- "And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years. 6- When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? 7- The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me. 8- Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk."
9- "And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath."

The purpose of mentioning this miracle is not the healing of the paralytic in itself, but to highlight Christ's surpassing authority. For this reason St. John mentioned the long duration of the illness, and the bitter state of despair through which the sick man was passing, to highlight thereby God's visitation of man with His mercies.
This miracle shows:
(1) That it was Christ who saw him and began the conversation with him, for God is the One who visits and seeks out every soul in weariness or distress, and He forgets no one.

(2) Although Christ is the initiator, and He wants salvation for everyone, the grace of salvation also requires man's will for the salvation of his own soul. For this reason Christ asked him this question, which seems strange to a sick man: "Wilt thou be made whole?"
(3) God's mercy and His unlimited power, which shatters all despair. Although the sick man had been crippled for 38 years, He commanded him to rise and walk, and he was healed at once.

The word "immediately" indicates the power of the miracle and the authority of the Lord Christ over disease. That the man should carry his bed and be able to walk after these long years of lying down is a matter beyond mental conception: that these slackened muscles should suddenly be strengthened, without any supplementary treatments, leaves the observer no room except to say that this is the hand of God.

My beloved God, You sought out the sick man lying there, while I am still bound by my sins ... I want to be healed, but the will is weak ... So come, beloved, and speak a word that strengthens my resolve and makes me rise, casting behind me all the years of laziness and weakness, leaving my despair, holding fast to my hope in You.
The prophet Jeremiah says: "Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not" (Jer 5:21)."

St. Cyril the Great says that this verse applies to the attitude of the Jews toward this miracle ... They forgot the power of the Healer, and the work of mercy offered by God, and held to the letter of the commandment, empty of the Spirit of God. So it is, beloved, with us also in our stubbornness: often we do not see the good will of God. Would that You, my God, open our eyes and our hearts and our understandings, so that we may understand and see Your works and Your wisdom, and leave our evils and our condemnation of others.
It was not the Lord's nature to declare Himself, He who did not receive glory from men.

So may we also learn not to boast of what we do before people, learning humility from our God, and not seeking to receive the praise of people, remembering that our Father who sees in secret will reward us openly.
The man met Christ again in the temple; and in Christ's new conversation with him we find the following meanings:
First: that this illness was the result of a previous sin, for the phrase "sin no more" means "do not sin again," and Christ, by His divinity, knew this sin.
Second: man must always remember God's work with him and His kindness, and thank God. And most important, he must not forget and return again to what he had left.
Third: that the man who ignores God's repeated mercies exposes himself to a greater punishment, "a worse thing" will come upon him.

As for the man's purpose in informing the Jews, it was to clear himself of the charge of carrying the bed, for fear of the Jews and their killing him in carrying out the commandment of the Law. This shows the weakness of this man's faith, for he cared about pleasing the Jews more than holding to Christ's teachings.

St. John shows here the extent of the Jews' hatred of the person of Christ, to the point of seeking to kill Him. He attributed this intense hatred to two reasons. The first: breaking the Sabbath, forgetting the great miracle. The second: the manner in which Christ described the relationship with God as that of His Father, but from another angle, different from God's fatherhood of all; Christ stresses the natural fatherhood of the Father to the Son, which is restricted to Him alone, making Himself equal with the Father in essence, and in that their work is one and continuous. For this reason the Jews sought to kill Him on the charge of blasphemy, because they understood Christ's intention perfectly, yet they rejected Him.

"My Father worketh hitherto, and I work": by this verse Christ makes clear to the Jews that even on the Sabbath the Father works, and does not cease to care for His creation. Consequently the Son, who is one with Him in essence, shares His work. If God is thus, then we also must not cease from serving God and His creation all the days. In this way the Sabbath moves from the letter of the commandment to its spirit and content.

In His answer to the Jews the Lord draws us gradually into the depth of theology, making clear this mysterious relationship between the Father and the Son in the one essence ... proving His divinity through: (1) Unity of will: the Son cannot have a will separate in action from the will of His Father, because they are one in essence. (2) Inseparability: although the Word took flesh, through the divine essence He is in constant communion with the Father, seeing and beholding all that He does, for the two are one.
(3) Unity of power: in that all that the Father does, the Son does likewise, for He is in no way less than the Father in power, because He is one with Him in will and inseparability.

(4) Unity of love: in the Father's opening Himself to the Son with all love, so that the Son knows all the Father's mysteries, works and purposes. This too is evidence of the Son's divinity, who must possess unlimited knowledge and understanding in order to comprehend all God's works and purposes.

"Greater works": Christ here foretells the coming and wonderful miracles, some of which will be shown in the coming verses, or which St. John will mention in the following chapters. We note that the Jews marvel, but they do not believe.

My beloved God and good Savior ... as You, in the fullness of love, were one with Your good Father in will and inseparability ... we too, Your people, long to submit with all our hearts and our will to Your love and Your voice in our lives. Grant us, Lord, to be one with You, as You asked for us, so that we leave everything that hinders us, and turn toward You and follow You with all our hearts.

Another direct proof of Christ's divinity in His heavenly power, equal to the Father's, in raising the dead, which is something no man can do. The phrase "quickeneth whom He will" Christ applied to Himself, distinguishing Himself from some prophets who raised the dead, such as Elijah and Elisha, through their prayers to God. As for the power of Christ, its source is Himself and His divine will alone. And Christ offers another proof of His divinity in that He is the Judge, an attribute restricted to God alone, who knows the deeds of men and the secrets of their hearts.

Another proof of Christ's divinity, as He made honoring the Father and honoring the Son one indivisible thing. If the honor of God and honoring Him has no equal honor, and no man approaches it, at the same time Christ declares that honoring the Son is equal to and bound up with honoring the Father; this is another testimony to the Son's equality with the Father in glorification, worship and Godhead.

Christ affirms once again the unity between the Son and the Father: in hearing the word of the Son and believing in God the Father. The word of the Son is the commandment of the Father Himself; and without faith in God the Father and obedience to the commandment of God the Son, no one will have eternal life, and none will escape judgment. But whoever does this has passed from spiritual death to life in Christ, by faith, repentance and obeying Christ's commandments.
My beloved brother, eternal life has been prepared for you by God out of His great prior love. So come, let us together submit to His commandment, that we may have rest here and eternal life there.

"The hour is coming, and now is": the Lord Christ used the word "now" as a preparation for what He will speak of in verse 28, which He did not mention in it. "Now" here means the spiritual resurrection by repentance, for everyone who hears the word of the Son of God, accepts it and acts on it. But the one who refuses repentance, and ignores the call of the Lord Christ, is dead in his sins to eternal destruction. This verse reminds us of what the divine inspiration said in the Old Testament by the mouth of the prophet Isaiah: "In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in the day of salvation have I helped thee" (Isa 49:8). And in the New Testament, divine inspiration affirms that the time of repentance is now, not tomorrow, and allows no postponement, when it said by the mouth of the Apostle Paul: "In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2).

If God's mercies have opened their arms to receive you by repentance and confession now, why are you not received, and why do you prefer to remain in death rather than life by responding to Christ's call to you?!

This verse is a new proof of Christ's divinity. The attribute of self-existent, uncreated life belongs to God alone, who is its source and giver, and the Son also, because He is God, has this very attribute: First: that He is uncreated.
Second: that He has the very authority of the Father in granting this life to whom He wills, for He is its source, as John said before: "In Him was life" (ch. 1:4).

That is, the divine Being gave the right of judgment to the Son, just as it is the right of the Father (v. 22), and of the Holy Spirit (ch. 16:8). This is because the divine nature is one in essence, but judgment is given to the Son who, by His incarnation, lived our life and suffered, tempted in all things except sin alone. Divine justice and mercy alone made the incarnate Christ, who became man, the judge of all humanity. He is the Judge on the one hand, and the advocate for man on the other, for He pleads for us by His redemption and judges us innocent.

"Marvel not at this": that is, at what He has said before and what He will say after it, for Christ knows the difficulty of accepting what He says for the human mind that is not prepared to deal with divine truths. As for the hour of which the Lord speaks, it is the hour of the Second Coming and judgment, in which all will hear His voice, the righteous and the wicked, going either to eternal life or to eternal destruction ... And we must not miss here, dear reader, the clarity of the verse that recompense and judgment are for the works that man did throughout his life, whether good or evil. And despite the clarity of the verse here, we wonder at those who teach that works have no relation to judgment (compare Mt 25:31-46).
O that I might seize, my God, the opportunity of this life to do good as You did (compare Acts 10:38), and not scatter my times here and there.

My God ... always put the thought of judgment in my heart, so that my longings for eternity are stirred on the one hand, and I feel that for every moment and every work I will give an account, and so my weak soul is strengthened on the other hand.

The Lord Christ here repeats what He said before in (v. 19) about the union of will and work with the Father, so that there can be no separation for a single moment. For this reason, all that He does is the will and the purpose of the Father Himself. This confirms the complete agreement between them, and the meaning of "I can do nothing" here is: "I do not will," as we say: "God cannot lie" ...

And the expression "as I hear" is also similar to what came in (v. 19), that the Son does what the Father does, and it affirms the same previous meaning, which is the unity of communion between the Father and the Son.
(6) The witness to the Son (vv. 31-40):

31- "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. 32- There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true. 33- Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth. 34- But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved. 35- He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light. 36- But I have greater witness than that of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me. 37- And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape. 38- And ye have not his word abiding in you: for whom he hath sent, him ye believe not. 39- Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. 40- And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life."
These verses speak of the witness of the Father to the Son, and of the witness of John the Baptist also.
And Christ declared the purpose of this witness: He is not in need of it, but He mentions it for the salvation of the Jews themselves (v. 34).

Christ begins His speech here knowing what was in the minds of the Jews and in their Law, and in general custom and the Law, that a man's witness to himself is not accepted, as a preparation for presenting the greatest Witness, who is God the Father Himself (the other witness). It is known that the strength and value of a testimony derive from the standing of the witness, so Christ offered the witness of the Father, which allows no room for doubt or refutation, although if He were to bear witness of Himself, His witness is true (ch. 8:14).

Christ moves here to the witness of John, who is a second witness with standing among the Jews, indeed it was they who went to him to question him, and his witness came declaring that Christ is the truth. As for Christ's not receiving the Baptist's witness, this does not mean rejecting it, but is a hidden allusion to His divinity. For despite the greatness of the witness, it is unacceptable that God's truthfulness should depend on the witness of a man. But the Lord adds the Baptist's witness to the Father's witness so that the Jews may believe, for faith in the person of Christ is the first condition of salvation, and Christ wants nothing but the salvation of His people.

A second witness that Christ gives to the Baptist, that he was the shining lamp, after He had described him as the greatest of those born of women, and this is an incidental verse in the context of the speech. But Christ said it for two reasons. The first: that He gives every man his due and forgets no one's labor. The second: that He rebukes the Jews who gathered around the Baptist for a season, a short period of 6 months, and after his imprisonment returned to their former conduct, without the influence of the Baptist's words continuing in their lives.

My God and my Lord, the Baptist was faithful in his mission, a witness and a martyr for the divine truth, and his praise came from Your holy mouth ... Give me, my God, the spirit of the Baptist and some of his strength, so that I too may bear witness to You by my works, as he did by his words and deeds, and so be a shining lamp, a light to the world, that I may fulfill Your good will in my life.

A third witness that the Lord Christ gives, greater than the witness of any man, and more certain, namely those miraculous works, such as the healing of the sick, the opening of the eyes of the blind, and the raising of the dead, works that none before Him had matched in power, greatness, number and variety, so as to bear witness to His divinity. As for the expression "the Father hath given me to finish," its meaning is that the Son carries out the will of the Father, as it came in (ch. 1:18): "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him," and Christ also adds that He is the Father's voice and shape.

The witness of the Father Himself, which He gave to the Son through the prophecies of the Old Testament and the types of the Law, which are the words of the Father that represent His voice and shape. But despite this, the Jews went astray; and instead of accepting eternal life, they rejected it by their rejection of Christ Himself.

If Christ had earlier refused the witness of men to Him, and offered other witnesses not subject to human standards or measures, He also refuses to receive the glory offered to Him by men, but wants to draw them to faith in Him, and consequently to the salvation of their souls.

The first reason for the Jews' not accepting Christ is the absence of the love of God from their hearts, without which man cannot recognize the Son. The proof that they did not love God is that He came in His Father's name, whom they claim to love, and they did not receive Him. But if another came in his own name, and the allusion here is to the false messiahs who appeared from time to time, presenting themselves and seeking honor for themselves, the Jews would receive them; so Christ here wonders at their conduct.

The second reason for not accepting Christ is the Jews' deviation, and their desire for worldly glory instead of the glory that God gives to His children in their humility, for the sin of boasting and seeking vain glory from men turns man's heart away from God so that he does not accept Him, but is content to remain confined within himself. The truth is therefore clear: either man seeks his own glory at the expense of God's glory, or he seeks God's glory at the expense of himself.

My God and Savior ... You humbled Yourself, and did not seek Your own glory, though You are all glory. And I, wretched, am still looking for praise here and there.
