Help me, my God, to rebuke this accursed self that stands in the way of enjoying Your perfect love, and growing in knowing You, and knowing all Your mysteries.

He whom you suppose to be an intercessor and mediator for you, the prophet Moses, is himself the one who accuses you before God. For all that Moses wrote had Christ as its goal. The Jews' unbelief in Christ means rejecting the Law that Moses wrote. If they do not believe the words of the greatest of their prophets, how then will they believe in Christ?!
The feeding of the multitudes; walking on the water; the sacrament of Communion of the Body and Blood of Christ

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: "After these things": that is, after what happened in Jerusalem, the Lord headed to Galilee, and crossed its sea from west to east.
"Tiberias": a city on the Sea of Galilee, built by Herod and named after the Roman emperor "Tiberius" in the year 26 AD.
The crowds followed the Lord Jesus because of the many miracles of healing, so He went up to a high hill with the Twelve, and the crowds began to increase around Him.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: This incidental remark which St. John mentioned, that the Passover was near, cannot be overlooked, for the discussion in this chapter will deal with the bodily feeding of the crowds on the one hand, and the spiritual, saving feeding of the whole world through the bread of life, the body of Christ, on the other. St. John referred to the Passover deliberately, to prepare the mind to link the body of Christ offered to the world with the saving Passover, "for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7).

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: Philip represents the rationalist character, for it was Christ who went to him to call him, and he did not follow Him of himself (ch. 1:43), and he is the one who interrupted Christ in His discourse: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us" (ch. 14:8).

For this reason, Christ directed the question to him in particular, to test his faith on the one hand, and to make him a witness that faith surpasses reason and material and mental resources. And because Philip represents the limited mind in its solutions, he did not offer a solution to the Lord Jesus' question about where to buy bread, but added another complication, namely how much?! ... that is, even if the place were available, where is the money?

The mind, in many cases, is an obstacle that limits God's work in our lives by its limited calculations ... So never let your mind be an obstacle to the life of faith, but make it receptive, thankful for God's works in your life, remembering them and meditating on them.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: "A lad ... barley": St. John draws our attention to something important, which is that God works with the little, so the solution to the problem came through a small boy, and not one of the rich officials. Likewise the barley is the bread of the poor common people, not like wheat, the food of the rich.

Therefore, we must not despise the smallest things, nor boast of the greatest, but boast in the Lord, who with the least of the little does the most of the much. Would that we had this faith, active and working, in offering our weak resources to God, so that He does much with them.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: "Make the men sit down": an organizing action, arranged by the disciples. For this reason it was easy to count the number of the men, and also easy to distribute; order is one of the Christian virtues of conduct to which God alerts us: "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1 Cor 14:40).
However, the total number was greater than this, as St. Matthew indicated: "beside women and children" (Mt 14:21).

We note that the phrase "as much as they would" points to the perfection of the divine work in satisfying them to overflowing. So God always acts toward every creature, and especially His children who rely on Him, for "the blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and He addeth no sorrow with it" (Prov 10:22).

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: Gathering the fragments ... that nothing be lost:

First, the direct meaning: the Lord wanted to make this miracle a memorial that the disciples would not forget, so the number of baskets matched their number, and each one of them carried one as a witness he would not forget, because he had shared in it.

The Lord also wanted to teach us to be prudent in our consumption of food, so that we keep what is left over to come back and eat it, and do not fall into the sin of extravagance, or of making light of the blessings of God which He has given us.

Second: the symbolic meaning in gathering the fragments is that this bread is a sign of His body. First He gave thanks, blessed, and distributed; these are the same steps He took when He instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist (thanksgiving). For this reason it was not acceptable for the fragments of bread to be left to be trodden by feet. Rather He asked the disciples, who represent the priesthood of the New Testament, to gather the remains of what symbolizes His body which He blessed and distributed.

Note, beloved, that in the rite of the Coptic Liturgy nothing of the body of Christ is left over, but the priest does what the disciples did in gathering all the remains of the body of the Lord, and leaving nothing of it ...

May we learn from Christ to pray before we eat our food, and to thank Him, and to bless it by making the sign of the Cross, then distribute the food to those present. And after we finish eating, we gather what is left to eat it, or give it to the needy, for this makes us feel the grace of God that He gives us and that many do not find.

entries.section: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

paragraphs.text: The reaction of the souls to the miracle was limited, for they regarded Christ as the prophet of whom Moses spoke in (Deut 18:15-18), and their minds turned to installing Christ as an earthly king over them, which the Lord did not accept from them, so He departed alone, rejecting the glory of the world for which He had not come.

My beloved God ... make Your body my true satisfaction, and make my weakness and limited resources into strength, for I am less than a loaf of barley, but in Your hand I long to be a source of satisfaction for others, to speak to them about You, and call them to You so that they come to Your Church and have true satisfaction in place of the falseness and emptiness of the world.

entries.section: (2) The miracle of walking on the water

paragraphs.text: On the same day as the feeding of the crowds, at its evening, the disciples, without the Lord, took a boat to cross the Sea of Galilee to Capernaum.

Let us note the expressions which St. John gives with precision (the darkness, Jesus was not [there], the sea arose). It is as though the Evangelist is painting a picture with great precision, for he says that the moments of true weakness (the darkness) in a man's life are the disappearance of Christ from his life, which lets Satan and trials (the great wind) buffet this man, so that his soul is tormented and he falls prey to fear instead of reassurance and safety. And when weariness exhausted them, from the struggle and effort they were in, rowing about 3 or 4 miles, that is, when man runs out of every device and every effort, Christ comes declaring Himself with power, "It is I; be not afraid" ... and peace takes the place of anxiety, and calm the place of tension, as the soul rests in its Savior.

My beloved God ... never leave me, and do not let me, through folly, leave You, for the winds are harsh and the storm is overwhelming, and I have no rescue except Your calm, strong voice: "It is I; be not afraid"; make these words a support for me throughout my life, and let me always pray with Your Church: "O King of peace ... give us Your peace."

Note: the Arabic translation, "they were willing to receive Him," is a very weak translation. In the Greek and English it came with the meaning of "they gladly received Him," which is stronger in meaning and depiction, and an expression of the state the disciples were in when they knew His voice.

entries.section: (2) The miracle of walking on the water

paragraphs.text: In these three verses is the announcement of the miracle, and its perception by the crowds, for they knew that Christ had been at Galilee alone, and that the disciples had taken the only boat. How then did Jesus reach them? They had been standing waiting for Him to come from the mountain, and behold, He was with His disciples in Capernaum. For this reason the crowds also went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

entries.section: (3) The food that perisheth and the food that endureth

paragraphs.text: The Jews, seeking Jesus, begin with a question of wonder about how He reached Capernaum. But Christ answers them as One who knows their inner selves: they seek Him not because of faith in the miracles He did, but only for the material gift, which is free food and satisfaction without toil, so they deserved Christ's rebuke of them, and His counsel to them that there is another kind of food that these do not know, and that none gives except Christ to everyone who follows Him, and it is spiritual food offered as a pledge of eternal life. The discourse here is an introduction to what Christ will take us to in the rest of the chapter, that He Himself is the living spiritual food. As for the expression "Him hath God the Father sealed," it refers to Christ and not the food, for Christ is the One appointed from eternity by the Father to give eternal life. And the Father bore witness to Him from His baptism with an audible voice, and this witness was like a declaration and seal, that is, a confirmation by the Father of the Son's work.

My beloved God ... I still find in myself a concern for the food that perisheth, so I seek material goods and earthly success, forgetting that all this is passing away. Lift my heart, my God, to what is above, so that I seek You, and all my longings become spiritual, centered on You, O food that endureth, O bread of life.

entries.section: (3) The food that perisheth and the food that endureth

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ said in (v. 27): "Labour," so the Jews' inquiry came in this verse:

"What shall we do?" as if their hearts had begun to incline, for a moment, to the spiritual teaching of the Lord Christ in doing the works of God, in order to obtain this food that endureth. Christ's answer to them was that all these works are summed up in faith in Him. And the Church teaches that faith in the Lord Jesus is the first condition of salvation, for spiritual striving and good works are accepted only on the basis of faith in the Redeemer Son whom the Father sent.

entries.section: (3) The food that perisheth and the food that endureth

paragraphs.text: When Christ asked the Jews for faith in Him, they asked Him a direct question: "If the sign God gave to the prophet Moses in the time of our fathers was the coming down of manna from heaven, which is the greatest miracle and gift, because it sustained the whole people for 40 years, then what greater miracle do you work, that we may believe you, as our fathers believed Moses?"

entries.section: (3) The food that perisheth and the food that endureth

paragraphs.text: Once again, as usual, the Lord tries to lift the Jews to what is higher and deeper, to bring them into the divine mysteries hidden from them, so He corrected the error: the manna was not Moses' gift to his people, but the gift of God the Father. And the Father Himself now gives them the greater and true bread, for the manna was a type of the true bread; Christ Himself, who came down from heaven incarnate, and the Giver of life to the world, is the true bread of life.

entries.section: (3) The food that perisheth and the food that endureth

paragraphs.text: The Jews did not understand exactly Christ's intention, but they sensed the greatness of the gift and asked for it, imitating the Samaritan woman who asked for the living water without understanding the deeper meaning that Christ intended. For this reason Christ began, from (v. 35), the detailed explanation of the bread of life, which is above material gifts. We still, my God, ask for material things and are busy with them, while You call us to seek first the Kingdom of Heaven, and You would pour out on us every kind of gift. But we still stumble, and need Your strong arm to raise us and pull us out of what we are in, so that we care for what is above where You are, my God, and the soul is truly satisfied with being always with You, and does not turn back to ask for what is earthly.

The Lord Christ presents Himself as He presented Himself to the Samaritan woman: He is living water and the bread of life, that is, in Him are all of man's needs for life, and without Him there remain only the hunger and thirst which the world with all that is in it cannot make up for. And the phrase "I am" Christ used repeatedly: "I am the light of the world," "I am the door," "I am the way," "I am the truth," "I am the good shepherd," "I am the vine," "I am the resurrection," "I am the life." Likewise it affirms that He is the only One who fills all the needs of the human soul, however its demands or need may differ. Likewise the expression "never" corresponds to the expression "forever" in His discourse with the Samaritan woman. Christ's satisfaction is not limited to the variety of man's needs and his bodily, psychological and spiritual demands, but it is continuous, eternal satisfaction, that is, satisfaction without end.

As for man's responsibility in obtaining this satisfaction, the Lord Christ Himself defined it by His words: "he that cometh to me." So Christ offers and presents His gifts to man without imposing Himself; He stands and knocks at the door without opening it by force, so that man may have the will to choose, and this is a grave responsibility, for whoever does not come to Christ perishes of hunger and thirst, and remains in the torment of need for satisfaction without obtaining it ...

"Ye also have seen me, and believe not": that is, despite Christ's continued revelation of Himself in various ways, the eyes of the Jews remained in a state of spiritual blindness, because they did not seek the person of Christ for Himself, but because they ate of the loaves and were filled bodily (v. 26). So it is with man in all his conditions: if the basis of his relationship with God is only material benefit, God does not regard him as a believer, even if he claims to be.

"All that the Father giveth me": the Lord Christ attributed the act of giving and sending to the Father, and receiving and not rejecting to the Son, for the Son receives everyone who comes to Him, to obtain redemption first through faith in Him. The verse also bears the meaning of the acceptance of the Gentiles in this free redemption, for the Jews saw Him and did not believe. But whoever comes to Him He does not reject, and does not cast out. And how could He, when He is the Lover of mankind, the tender One, who in His love receives the whole world, being incarnate and crucified for us all. What a hope given to all sinners in His ever-open embrace. I thank You, my God, for Your words that encourage our weak souls ... whenever we come acknowledging and confessing our sins, and the priest reads to us the prayer of absolution, we remember Your true promise that whoever comes to You You will not cast out, but You establish him in Your love, and cleanse him that he may bring forth more fruit.

The speech here continues the meaning of the previous verses, for Christ affirms that the reason for His coming down from heaven, that is, His incarnation, is the fulfillment of the one will of God: the Father's will is the salvation of all, and the Son is the fulfiller of this will by His death and redemption. So of all that the Father has given to the Son, nothing is lost from it, but it is kept in the name of Christ for the day of His Second Coming, and the resurrection from the dead.

Christ continues to explain and clarify the will and purpose of the Father, which are, simply, faith in His only begotten Son, apart from whose name there is no other by which we can be saved (Acts 4:12). The following truths of the faith can be drawn out:

(1) That salvation is based on faith in Christ, and this condition was repeated by Christ Himself, and likewise by the Apostles, many times without concession. For this reason the Church believes that salvation is available to the whole world, but its first condition is faith in Christ. And because of this clarity in Christ's words, the Church rejects the heresy of universal salvation (that is, the salvation of people even without their faith in Christ).

(2) That faith, although it is the first condition, nevertheless has other matters without which faith is nullified, and the coming verses of the same chapter will deal with another condition for salvation. For this reason, when the Church interprets the Holy Bible, she does not rely on a single verse, but takes the meaning of the verses as a whole.

Christ's bodily circumstance, according to lineage, stood as a stumbling block before the Jews in accepting His divinity, and they did not accept what the Lord had repeated in 3 earlier verses, that He is the bread that came down from heaven (vv. 33, 35, 38). Their reaction was to murmur at Him, to make light of His words, and not to accept the idea of the Incarnation. "Jesus, the son of Joseph": this is what the Jews knew, in their bodily perception, of the person of Christ. And St. Luke was precise when he referred to this lineage in his Gospel, saying: "as was supposed" (Lk 3:23), that is, the common view and not the true one.

The Lord Christ explains here the inability of the human mind alone to have faith and to follow Christ, for the Father must draw man by the act of the divine gift of faith, and by teaching man through divine inspiration. And the expression the Lord used here: "They shall be all taught of God," is what came on the lips of the prophets (Isa 54:13; Jer 31:33-34), in clear references to the divine role in teaching man the mysteries of the faith, without which man cannot come to Christ.

No man has been able, is able, or will be able to see God, as God Himself said: "for there shall no man see me, and live" (Ex 33:20). But Christ, being "in the bosom of the Father" (ch. 1:18), and one with the Father (ch. 10:30), is the only eternal One who has seen the Father, and who can reveal Him to us. "Verily, verily, I say unto you": an expression the Lord used often to demonstrate the truth of what He teaches, which is that there is no eternal life, and no salvation, for anyone who does not believe in Christ, who is one with the Father in essence.

"I am the bread of life": Christ repeats what He declared in (v. 35), which the Jews did not understand, and they murmured at Him. This verse is regarded as an introduction to the divine mysteries that the Lord will declare concerning this bread. My beloved brother ... let us learn from the Lord Christ here the necessity of holding to the sound faith, for the Lord Christ was long-suffering, and went on explaining, and will complete His explanation, but He never yielded, under the weight of pressures or murmuring, from sound teaching. So has Your Church been throughout the ages, from the days of the pure Apostles, passing through Athanasius and Cyril and others who kept the faith pure and sound, exactly as Christ delivered it, without neglect or alteration ...

If manna was the greatest of the divine gifts in which Israel boasted, Christ makes clear here that it was only food to keep the body alive, whose end in any case is death. This verse is regarded as a comparison, and an introduction to a long discourse to come about the true living bread ...

The Lord Christ reveals to us here the greatest mysteries and gifts of the New Testament: that He is the bread that came down from heaven, in a clear reference to His incarnation, and in His being the source of life, so that whoever eats of it does not die. The manna of the Old Testament was therefore a type that gave life to the body. But Christ, the bread of life, whoever eats Him lives forever, because He is the food of the spirit, contrary to what the Jews wanted or understood. And the phrase "live for ever" means that bodily death cannot harm him. The summary of this is that Christ is the living God and the Giver of life, and He offers His body and blood as the bread of life, so whoever eats of this body and drinks of this blood is united with the One who bestows and gives life. How then shall he die? Rather, the death that is in us becomes life by our union with this heavenly bread. Do you understand now, dear one, the extent of the Church's concern for the sacrament of Holy Communion, and her constant call to all her children to partake of it, because it is eternal life ... it is union with Christ ... it is the forgiveness of sins.

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: "The Jews therefore strove": that is, the Jews were divided between supporting and opposing what Christ had declared, that He is the bread of life, and His body given for the salvation of the world. This lack of understanding reminds us of both Nicodemus (ch. 3) and the Samaritan woman (ch. 4), in their failure to grasp the divine mysteries. And the expression "How can?!" also carries something of mockery at what Christ said.

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: Yet Christ answers them with what is harder, for it is not eating the flesh only, but drinking the blood also, and Christ's use of the expression "Son of man" is a reference to His incarnation and death; and by His death as a sacrifice He gives His body for the life of the world. And as the Passover lamb was a sacrifice whose eating was bound up with the salvation and deliverance of all the people of Israel, so the body of Christ given gives deliverance and salvation. As for the one who abstains from and rejects this living sacrifice, he is spiritually dead in this life, and likewise in the age to come.

So come, beloved, and enjoy the greatest of the divine gifts, and do not deprive yourself of life in Christ and through Christ, for you are the desire of His heart, and the object of His love; do not deprive yourself of Him, and do not make Him wait for you.

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: The sacrifice of Christ, His body and blood and salvation, has been granted to the whole world. But none will enjoy eternal life except one who eats of this sacrifice. Therefore, partaking of the body and blood of the Lord has become a condition for this salvation and eternal inheritance.

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: That is, not a symbol nor an image, but reality. This verse is the most eloquent of the verses answering all who claimed that the sacrifice of Christ in the sacrament of Holy Communion is nothing but a symbol or a remembrance, ignoring Christ's affirmation that His flesh is meat indeed and His blood is drink indeed. And we do not know what more they ask Christ to say than this, that they may believe?!

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: A new gift is given by partaking of the body and blood of Christ, which is the gift and bestowal of abiding. A branch that is cut off has no value and no life in it. But if the branch abides in its source there is fruit, and Christ Himself said: "without me ye can do nothing" (ch. 15:5). As the sap of life flows into the branches of the tree, so the blood of Christ in our bodies gives us abiding, connection and growth ...

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: My Father is the source of life and I am life itself (as if we were to say: the Father is the mind, and the Son is the thought). And I give spiritual eternal life to everyone who eats the sacrifice of My body.

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ concludes His discourse here about His body and blood by returning to the beginning of the discourse (vv. 32, 33) in the comparison between the gift of food for the body, "manna," and the greater gift, namely His body given for the life of the world. This verse comes as a summary of all that was said, and a confirmation of what preceded in verses 33, (50, 51, 54, 57).

My beloved God ... we worship You in thanksgiving for the greatness of the riches of Your gifts which are above our minds and our understanding, and which none understands except one who was born of the Holy Spirit in Baptism, this which St. Gregory chanted in the Divine Liturgy: "You who have given me this service full of mystery ... You have given me the offering up of Your body in bread and wine."
We thank You, our God, because in Your body is eternal life (v. 51), the second resurrection (v. 54), abiding in You (v. 56), and union with You and the Father in respect of life (v. 57).
Grant us never to depart from the table of life, Your holy altar, where is the gift of Your most holy body.

entries.section: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

paragraphs.text: St. John took care to mention that this whole discourse was in the synagogue, and by specifying the place at the end of the discourse he intended to declare that it was not a private discourse to the disciples, but a public proclamation of the truths of the faith, before the priests and all the people.

The disciples here do not mean the Twelve and the other seventy apostles, but the many who followed Him from place to place, considering themselves disciples of His ... And what made them stumble was two things: His saying that He is the bread of life that came down from above, and the emphasis on the necessity of eating His flesh and drinking His blood, for they understood His words literally. Jesus knew by His divinity that His words made them stumble, and He told them so.

If you do not accept what I have said now, how will it be with you when you see Me ascending to heaven, where I was before? For Christ, until now, had not solved for these people their first problem of eating His flesh and drinking His blood, but added to it a new problem, as He speaks of His eternity, referring to His ascension to the bosom of His Father, where He was before His incarnation (Mk 16:19; Lk 24:51; Acts 1:9).

The simple meaning of this verse is that Christ offers those who stumbled at His words the solution, which is that His words must be believed spiritually, apart from limited rational and material understanding: "they are spirit, and they are life." As for the meaning of "the flesh profiteth nothing," St. Augustine and St. Cyril the Great agreed that the meaning Christ intended is: if your conception is of eating My flesh in a material sense, as though you were eating material meat, it profits nothing for eternal life. But what profits is that you eat My true flesh united with My divinity. This is what He explained to His disciples afterward at the Last Supper on Holy Thursday, when He gave them His body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine. And this is the spiritual faith that gives eternal life. See the institution of the sacrament in (Mt 26:26, Mk 14:22, Lk 22:17, 19).

A strong reference to the divinity of the Son, in respect of foreknowledge, which belongs to God alone, for He knows that among those who hear Him are some who do not believe His words. And so that we may know that this was not Christ's inference from reading the faces of the crowd, St. John adds the words "from the beginning," to affirm this divine aspect of Christ's foreknowledge, also indicating that Christ's knowledge is not only of those who do not accept His words, but of the disciple who was about to betray Him as well.

Christ reminds them of what He said earlier in vv. 44, 45, that man cannot come or be received to Christ unless the faith which the Father has put in his heart is the true and only motive. But whoever comes from a utilitarian, or self-interested, or political motive, such as the liberation of the Jews, Christ will be a stumbling block to him; and this is what Simeon the elder said in his prophecy, that He is "set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel" (Lk 2:34).
That is, the people who rejected His saying that His flesh is meat indeed and His blood is drink indeed.

My beloved God, we lift to You a prayer whose subject is those who every day leave You and go back, and no longer walk with You ... They leave the living fountain of life, and leave the embrace of Your love, for what, my God ... for material things and cares, from which man reaps nothing but toil without rest ... My God ... do not allow us, the weak, to be distracted from You by anything, but let us remain with You in Your Church, taking of Your love and Your giving, serving Your holy name all the days of our life ... Amen.

It is not meant that Christ wanted to know their intention, He who knew from the beginning who would leave Him and who would follow Him, but the purpose of this question was to test their faith and their confession of Him. For this reason Peter's answer came fully in agreement with Christ's question, and it was also an expression of what was within the rest of the disciples, and it carries a strong faith. And the phrase "To whom shall we go?" means we have no one but You, and we cannot turn back as the others did. And the phrase "Thou hast the words of eternal life" is an affirmation of all that Christ said in the previous verses about eternal life, and that He is its source and giver, as the bread of life and the gift of His most holy body and blood.

Peter continues his speech, in declaring the disciples' position with Him, that the basis of their following Christ is the faith given to them by the Father, and it is a following that will continue regardless of those who left Him: our faith in You that You are the Christ the Savior, and that You are the Son of the living God, will leave us no other room to leave You, otherwise we would be as though leaving life for death, and eternity for destruction.
The Lord Christ completes the revelation of His divine knowledge by correcting Peter's words, saying to him:

You have spoken, Peter, for all your brother disciples with words of good faith, but this is not the confession of all as you said, for among you is one who does not believe, but Satan has filled his heart, and he is the one who will betray me and deliver me up ... And let us note here the Lord's saying: that despite my choosing you and your discipleship, among you is a devil. And this means that God chooses man and calls him, but man may abide or leave God by his free will. Consequently, the teaching that a believer never perishes is a strange teaching, for God also chose Judas, but Judas did not abide in this choice, so his was destruction.
Christ's discourse about Himself and the Holy Spirit; the faith of the crowd and the rejection of the leaders

"After these things," that is, after the miracle of feeding the crowds and the lengthy discourse about "His body and blood," Christ stayed for a time in Galilee, keeping away from Judaea, the southern region, because of the envy of the Jews and their complaint against Christ who had broken the Sabbath, and they sought to kill Him for this reason.

St. John Chrysostom says: "Christ teaches us here an important principle, which is that keeping away from danger and fleeing from persecutors, wherever necessity requires it, is a kind of wisdom and prudence, for confrontation is in many cases not necessary" ...
And Christ here, God forbid, was not afraid, for He knew that He would give Himself up, but there is a time for everything.

"The feast of tabernacles": one of the three great feasts of the Jews. The duration of the feast was 8 days, and its place was Jerusalem, and it is called the season of harvest, and this feast was imposed on Israel by God (Ex 23:16) for the following spiritual meanings:

(1) A memorial of sojourning: all leave their homes and dwell under booths on the rooftops or on the roads, that God may remind them of the forty years they spent in the wilderness, and then how God gave them this land as an inheritance.

(2) Thanksgiving and joy: the harvest begins with the first of the feasts, the Passover, but is completed at the time of the feast of tabernacles, so there is thanksgiving and joy for the blessings of the whole year.

My beloved God ... make me always remember that I am here in a time of sojourning, wandering, but my true and lasting rest is with You there where the true, abiding inheritance is, so do not let anything distract me from You and from it, and help me to spend my sojourning in peace ...

"His brethren": St. Matthew mentioned them (13:55), and they are James, Joses, Simon and Judas; they are brothers of Christ, but not from the holy Virgin St. Mary, for cousins on the mother's or father's side are called brothers in the region of the Levant, as Abraham and Lot were anciently called brothers, although Abraham was his uncle.

What these brothers said to Christ, in brief, is: you must go where the crowds and the throng are at the feast of tabernacles, to do your miracles there, so that everyone believes in you, instead of doing these wonders here in the small villages where no one knows you. But St. John reveals to us a secret that clarifies the motive for this advice, and this secret is (v. 5): that His brethren did not believe in Him. Consequently, they wanted Christ to go to Jerusalem, so that the priests and scribes might examine Him to know whether He is the Christ or not.

"My time is not yet come": it bears two meanings; the first is what concerns the time of His crucifixion and redemption and offering Himself as a sacrifice for the world. The second: I will go up, but not now. For going up openly amid a state of expectation would stir the envy of the leaders, and they would seek Him to death before the appointed time, which God Himself determined. And this meaning agrees with the context of the events in the same chapter (vv. 10, 14) in His going up to Jerusalem concealing Himself, and then His speaking in the temple.
"Your time is alway ready": that is, you can go to the feast at any time.

The Lord here points to the reason for the Jews' hatred and their not accepting Him, which is that the world as a whole, because of the sin of self-love, does not accept reproof, but is ready even to kill anyone who reproves it, for he who loves darkness hates the light. When Christ exposed their sins to them, they demanded His destruction, instead of listening to Him and repenting of them.

Would that our hearts were humbled and confessed their sins, and that we listened to Your voice, O Savior, so that we reprove ourselves, instead of venturing, in many cases, to throw the blame on You for the discipline that we ourselves deserve.

The Lord Christ completes His discourse to His brethren about their going with the crowds going up to Jerusalem, withdrawing from going with them, presenting what He had said before in (v. 6) about the appointed time for His going; and we may infer from the comparison with (v. 14) that He stayed in Galilee about 4 days, until the middle of the feast, before He appeared in Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ went up secretly to Jerusalem, which was an act of the utmost wisdom. Had He gone up with the crowds, they would have proclaimed Him king, as happened at His last visit to Jerusalem, and this is contrary to the plan He intended, especially since His hour had not yet come.

May we learn in our prayers to wait for God's answer at the time He sees fit, for God has plans for our lives that we cannot reach; rather, let us know that to everything under heaven there is a season.

St. John also depicts the state of the Jews who were watching for Christ's appearing at the first days of the feast, with the question, "Where is he?", which carries in its meaning contempt and malice more than longing expectation. This reveals to us that the waiting had something of lying in ambush, and it confirms Christ's wisdom in choosing the right time to go.

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: Opinions clashed about the person of Christ, for some said "He is a good man," that is, upright and without fault; and the others said that "he deceiveth the people," that is, misleads them. The saints agree that the other group were the envious among the supporters of the scribes and Pharisees, whom Christ had reproved. Yet no one dared to speak of it openly, but most of the talk was in small groups and in secret, because of fear of the leaders and rulers of the Jews (the priests and the Pharisees).

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: That is, after four days, Christ declared Himself, and appeared in the temple with authority, and even began to teach the crowds. St. Matthew describes that His appearing thus took the leaders by surprise, and despite their fury at Him they were afraid to oppose Him, "lest there be an uproar among the people" (Mt 26:5); see also (Mt 21:46).

The reaction of the Jews was astonishment at the loftiness, beauty and precision of the teaching, expressing this astonishment by saying that Christ was not known to be one of the disciples of the Jewish scholars, so how then does He know the Scriptures, that is, the prophecies and the Law, in all their details?

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: This scene is repeated more than once, whether murmuring, or wonder, or whispering, which the Lord Christ read on faces, or knew by His divinity, even without anyone putting a direct question to Him. And as the Lord Christ knew what was in their minds about His origin and His teaching according to their bodily view ... He answered what was perplexing them: that the source of all this is the Father who sent Him into the world. And although the Father and the Son are one, Christ knew well that if He said that He was the source of the teaching, the Jews would not accept it, so He attributed it to the Father, as He had said before: "The Father Himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me" (ch. 5:37).

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: Christ adds in His discourse the means of verifying the truth of the teaching which the Jews hear; the means here is not discipleship under the hands of the Jewish teachers, but the only means here is that man be in accord with God's will, doing it and submitting to it in his life, for this way alone leads man to the knowledge of the truth, and none can discern the voice of God except one who fulfills His will and does it.

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: The Lord adds here and affirms His connection to the Source, for He does not seek glory for Himself as the Pharisees do, and this is a proof of the truth and righteousness of His word.

My beloved God ... You taught us what self-emptying is, You who are the Owner of all glory and honor, and even took the form of a servant, attributing everything to the Father, though You are heavenly to Him ... But I still steal Your glory and boast of everything You gave me, attributing it to myself. How ugly is my sin: God humbles Himself and the creature exalts himself ... Forgive me, and teach me how to walk like You in humility, and acknowledge Your favor.

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ moves the discourse here to the Pharisees, in a confrontation whose purpose is to expose their hypocrisy and the duplicity of their standards in judgment, and He also wants them to be witnesses against themselves in their transgressions of the Law for which they show zeal and for its ordinances. For Christ here lays bare to them that their relation to the Law is outward, while true knowledge and doing of the Law do not exist; for had they truly been subject to the Law by the Spirit of God, their thought would not have gone to killing Christ, and this is what Christ surprised them with, as One who knows the hidden things of their thoughts. But they denied what the Lord Christ exposed, and even added to their denial accusing Him of having a devil, adding to their hypocrisy and their thoughts a new sin, which is blasphemy against God Himself.

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: The work to which Christ refers is the miracle of healing the sick man of Bethesda (ch. 5), a miracle He performed on a Sabbath day, which provoked the anger of the Jews, and they regarded it as a breaking of the Sabbath, and a deed deserving death, and this verse is considered an introduction to (vv. 22-24).

entries.section: (2) Christ's going up to Jerusalem and His teaching in the temple

paragraphs.text: In these verses the Lord Christ raises a logical case, through which He wants man's judgment to be just and logical, and not to go by the appearances of things. What the Lord wanted to offer as proof of this is the subject of circumcision. What Christ said was the following:
(1) Circumcision was a covenant, but from the days of the fathers, Abraham, and before the Law of Moses.
(2) The Law of Moses came forbidding any work on the Sabbath.
(3) But circumcision was on the eighth day after the male's birth, so if the eighth day came on the Sabbath, the Law permitted its performance.

(4) And the last question the Lord puts: if you break the Sabbath for circumcision, which could be postponed a day, and is a sign God asked of man, is the complete healing of a man and giving him the ability to move considered a breaking of the Sabbath? If God permitted breaking the Sabbath for circumcision, He permits breaking the Sabbath also for the life and good of man.

(5) Christ concludes His discourse (v. 24) with advice, not for the Jews only but for all of us, which is that man should not judge superficially and by appearance, but should fully understand the divine purpose.

For this reason, beloved, we find that the saints of the Church never hastened in their judgments, but examined everything in the fear of God and the understanding of the Holy Spirit, and all fled from condemning another ... For which of us knows enough to pass judgments on others?!

entries.section: (3) The Jews' perplexity at Christ's words

paragraphs.text: "Them of Jerusalem": that is, the people of the city, and not the Jews who had come to it. They are more learned and more attached to the leaders, and know what they harbor toward the person of Christ. The people of Jerusalem fell into perplexity for the following reasons:

(1) That Christ speaks and teaches openly, and none of the leaders (the priests and Pharisees) interrupted Him or stopped Him. (2) Perhaps the reason was that the leaders themselves believed that He is the Christ, and for this reason did not oppose or resist Him, though they had decided earlier to kill Him.

(3) But what perplexed them most was a mistaken tradition and teaching that prevailed among the teachers of the Jews, that when the Christ comes, no one will know whence He comes, but He will appear suddenly in the temple; as for this man, despite His works, miracles and teachings, they know His origin, His family and His brethren.

entries.section: (3) The Jews' perplexity at Christ's words

paragraphs.text: "Then cried Jesus": that is, He raised His voice more than He had been teaching with, saying and answering them that what they know of Him is what the prophets testified, that the Christ is born in Bethlehem; and this is what the leaders answered Herod when he asked: "Where should Christ be born?" (Mt 2:4-5). But the Lord was not content with declaring that their bodily knowledge of Him agrees with His being the Christ, but added a theological dimension, which is that the One who sent Him is God the Father, the True One, whom, because of your literalism and your mistaken tradition, you have gone astray in knowing and in knowing His purpose. Consequently, as for my knowledge, I know Him, for I am from Him and from His essence and the same eternal divine nature, and He is the One who sent me (v. 29) as I have said many times before.

entries.section: (3) The Jews' perplexity at Christ's words

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ's words provoked them, that they do not know God, they who regard themselves as His chosen people, so they tried to seize Him, but no one could, because God Himself did not allow them. And this is what St. John indicated: "because His hour was not yet come."
From this we learn two things:
The first: it concerns Christ, who said that He alone has the authority to lay down His life and take it again; and this is a confirmation of His divine power alone.

The second: it is a lesson for us all, that however much the wicked try to touch the children of God, they will be able to do nothing except what God permits ... For this reason we pray, in the Prayer of Thanksgiving and the Creed, calling our God, the protector of His Church, "the Almighty," an attribute that spreads reassurance and stability in the soul of the people, because all things are in the hand of God, the Lover of mankind.

entries.section: (3) The Jews' perplexity at Christ's words

paragraphs.text: "Many of the people believed on Him": that is, the simple folk, and not the rulers of the Jews, and they expressed their faith by a simple rhetorical question, directed to the leaders who rejected the Lord Jesus: "When Christ cometh, will he do more miracles than these which this man hath done?"

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The Pharisees heard of the crowd's faith that He is the Christ, so they sent their servants to seize Him. The difference between this time and the previous one is that the first time it was individuals from the people who wanted to lay hold of Christ; but this time they are servants commissioned, by force of law, by the chief priests and the Pharisees, who together form the "Sanhedrin" council in Jerusalem, which consists of seventy of its elders, the leaders of the Jews, and so it is also called the Council of the Seventy; it is the supreme council to which all the subordinate councils belong. It is also the greatest Jewish authority that takes decisions in the religious affairs of the Jews, and many of the scribes were also members of this council; and it is the highest civil authority of the Jews after the Roman state.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ in His answer refers to the short time remaining for His ministry on earth, about six months, from the feast of tabernacles to the Passover, and after that He will be crucified and die, and rise, and ascend; and they will no longer find Him, for He will be in the bosom of His Father, the place from which He came down (ch. 1:18).

"Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me": this is also what the Lord said in (Lk 17:22): "The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man," and it means that those who reject Him now are the very ones who will regret His going and parting, after He declares the glory of Himself by His resurrection and ascension.

"Where I am": that is, while I am in all My glory, and in the bosom of My Father; no one who rejected the Son of Man and did not believe in Him will be able to enter the Holy of Holies, and enjoy eternal life with Him there, which was given only to everyone who believed in Him and acted on His word. And the speech in all its meaning is that although the servants were commissioned by force of law to seize Christ, He alone has the authority to determine this time, as before in (v. 30).

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: An addition to a scene recurring especially in the Gospel of St. John, which is that what the Lord Christ means, the people understand in another way ... All that came in (vv. 33, 34), some of those present interpreted as meaning that Christ, because of His failure to convince the Jews that He is the Christ, might go to the Greeks and teach the Jews of the Dispersion, that is, the Jews scattered and living in the land of the Greeks, trying to attract them, and make them believe in Him.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: It shows the inner feelings of the Jews, which carry contempt and lack of understanding more than anything else.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: "The last day": it is the eighth day (of the feast of tabernacles) and the greatest of them, because of the number of those celebrating, and because it is a day of retreat on which no work is done. There was a rite accompanying this feast which must be mentioned, because of its relation to what the Lord Christ will say in this verse ... This rite was that the high priest would go for 7 days and fill a golden jar with water from the pool of Siloam, and pour it on the bronze altar, and meanwhile all the people would sing all the prophecies concerning water, in remembrance of the water coming out of the rock in the wilderness, and the salvation of all the people ... throughout the seven days the souls are bound to the rock and to the water as a symbol of life ... And here came Christ's word on the eighth day about spiritual water, describing Himself as the true Rock, in place of the symbol in the wilderness, calling and inviting all to come and drink from Him, that they may have true life. And this is what the Lord also declared in the Book of Revelation, when He said: "And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Rev 22:17).

Yes, beloved ... You are the only source of quenching, for all the allurements of the world are a mirage, but You are the only true spring, as Isaiah said of You: "like a spring of water, whose waters fail not" (Isa 58:11)."

For You are the Creator ... and consequently You are the One who knows the needs of the soul You created, and who is able to satisfy it, and all that is other than You is vanity, and a panting after desires that leave nothing but dryness ... So water me, O spring of love, with the water of Your love, and make me grow in Your grace working in me, renewing the vows of my baptism, O water of life.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The Lord returns and affirms that the source of every gift, grace and bestowal is faith in Him, and this is what St. John was committed to highlighting in his whole Gospel. And the gift of faith this time is the work of Christ by the Holy Spirit in the soul that believes in Him, so that it has the fruit of life, and an abundance of spiritual gifts; for Christ is the spring, and the soul that follows Him takes from Him, so that the spring of Christ in it becomes a current that does not stop ... see ch. 4:14 in His discourse with the Samaritan woman ...

And in (v. 39), St. John links faith in Christ with receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in the name of Christ to all who believe in Him. He also refers here to future events which he himself lived through as well, namely that the Holy Spirit would not come upon the believers until after Christ's death, resurrection and ascension in glory.

It is noted that when the Church speaks of faith, she means practical faith, and not theoretical faith like the faith of the scribes and Pharisees, or even the faith of the demons (Jas 2:19), but as the Lord said: everyone who believes in Me and keeps My commandments ...

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The opinions of the listeners differed into 3 opinions:

The first group: saw that He is the great Prophet of whom Moses foretold (Deut 18:15), but the Jews awaited Him for political salvation from the Romans, after a long period in which the scene was empty of great prophets, and they did not understand that He is the Savior from sin.

And the second group: saw that He is the Christ, through His miracles and His parables and His spiritual discourses, which did not resemble the discourses of all the teachers or the scribes and Pharisees ...

As for the third group: it denied this, and justified its denial on the ground that Jesus was known to them to be from Nazareth, whereas He is supposed to be from Bethlehem as in the Scriptures. Had this group investigated carefully, it would have known that Christ was in fact born in Bethlehem (Mt 2:1-6; see also Mic 5:2), though His upbringing was in Nazareth and Galilee of the Gentiles.

Our great God ... we often slip, and enter into inquiries and mazes which seem outwardly to be all about You, but this slipping takes us far from You, although You are the God of the simple, and Your gifts and bestowals remain as they are. So do not let us be occupied with what takes us away from life with You, for we are all like dry land longing for the spring of Your living water, and the gift of Your Holy Spirit, that our life may flourish in You and grow in Your Spirit.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: As for the people who wanted to arrest Him, they are the servants of the chief priests (v. 32), and they will be spoken of.
(5) The rulers of the Jews reject Christ (vv. 45-53):
45- "Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him?"

46- "The officers answered, Never man spake like this man. 47- Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived? 48- Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? 49- But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed. 50- Nicodemus saith unto them, (he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,) 51- Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?"
52- "They answered and said unto him, Art thou also of Galilee? Search, and look: for out of Galilee ariseth no prophet."
53- "And every man went unto his own house."

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The servants commissioned by the Sanhedrin (see v. 32) returned without arresting Christ, for the following reasons:
(1) Their personal being moved by Christ's teachings, the like of which they had not seen.

(2) The inclination of most of the people to Christ's side, whether regarding Him as the Prophet or the awaited Christ. And the witness these servants brought was a true witness of what they had seen, and its substance was that, were it not for their fear of the authority of the leaders, they would also have said that He is the Christ. We infer this from the sum of their witness: "words not of a man," that is, that He is not a man. And this faithful reply and strong witness provoked the rulers of the Jews, whose fury reached its limit, so that they accused the servants of going astray.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The speech here is on the tongue of the council of priests and Pharisees, the rulers, and it is a scornful rhetorical question, after hearing the servants' shameful and unexpected answer, and its meaning is that nothing remains except that one of us also believes in this deceiver. And as a kind of justification of what happened, they put the blame on this people, that they are an ignorant people, with no knowledge of the Law, a people easily deceived. And St. John reveals to us the hardness of heart of those who claimed to be shepherds and teachers, when they described their people and flock as a cursed people.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: And the speech is to "Nicodemus," whom St. John presented to us before, in (ch. 3), in the night dialogue with Christ about Baptism, who acknowledged in his speech: "we know that thou art a teacher come from God" (ch. 3:2). Nicodemus combined faith in Christ with fear also of the rest of the leaders. For this reason we find him, in (v. 51), trying to defend Christ, and to reduce the spirit of revolt among the rest of the Pharisees and chief priests, by appealing for a lawful right by the force of the Law in favor of Christ, and this right is that the Law decrees that no man be judged without a trial, that is, in the language of law, that Christ is innocent until His guilt is proved.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The Pharisees' answer to Nicodemus was an evasion of the answer they owed to what he said, and, with a kind of mockery of him, departing from the objectivity of the dialogue, for they knew that he was not from Galilee. And this mocking accusation means: why do you favor this man as though you were from his birthplace? in an attempt to silence him, and justify their position, as they said to him: it was never recorded that a prophet came out of Galilee ...
It is noted that even this proof is wrong, for the prophet Jonah was from Galilee, and so were Hosea, Nahum, Elijah and Elisha, by lineage.

entries.section: (4) Christ foretells His ascension and the working of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: The end of the matter and the end of the feast of tabernacles was that each went to his house with feelings of rage and helplessness, because of the people gathering around Christ, and the servants' not obeying in arresting Him. In this way God fulfilled His purpose of His not being arrested, for His hour had not yet come.
She who was caught in adultery; faith in Christ

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: "Jesus went unto the mount of Olives": St. John does not indicate why the Lord went to the Mount of Olives. But it can be inferred from what St. Luke said (Lk 6:12), that He used to go out to the mountain and spend the whole night in prayer. The Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: "Early in the morning": that is, the second day after the end of the feast. And He went to the Temple to complete His teaching of the crowds, and sat down like the great teachers of the Jews, speaking to them about the preaching of the Kingdom.

My beloved brother... do you not notice with me what the manner of life of the Lord Christ was?... There was no time to waste. After arduous service for four days at the feast with the crowds, and then a night spent in prayer, He returned to teaching once more... This is the positive work that all of us lack in our lives, for we squander much of our time on things that are of no use... while the other things, which remain profitable and are necessary for the salvation of our souls, we give nothing but crumbs...
Beloved... would that we remembered that for every moment and every minute we shall give an account...

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: The story of the adulterous woman is one of the famous stories, and St. John took care to record it. Before entering into its events, we note that the key to the whole story is in (v. 6), where it is made clear that the purpose and the motive were one thing: to entrap Jesus and to find a reason to accuse Him, regardless of the woman and her story. What happened can be summarized as follows.

(1) They had no need to ask Christ, for the Law is clear in (Lev 20:10) and (Deut 22:22) that the adulterer and the adulteress both are to be stoned to death, especially since this woman was "in the very act." What need was there, then, to ask Christ?

(2) They presented to Christ the text of what Moses said. Would He contradict the Law, and become a breaker and transgressor of it, exposed before the people? Or would He pass a sentence of stoning upon her, though He had no civil authority, since death sentences were the prerogative of the Roman state, which did not permit the death of an adulteress by stoning under Roman law? Consequently, if Christ declared that she should be stoned, He would become a transgressor against Caesar's authority; and this was the dilemma that the accusers had devised. (3) Cunning prevailed over them, and they wished to entrap the Lord, addressing Him as "Master," a very great title, limited to the class of recognized teachers of the Law (the Rabbis). So their use of the word "Master" did not mean that they respected Him, or that they meant it, but was for the purpose of entrapping Him.

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: "He stooped down, and with His finger wrote on the ground": He stooped down calmly, as though the matter did not concern Him.

This calm is a lesson for us in our conduct from the Lord Christ, for evil is not met with quick, agitated replies. He wanted to absorb their fury and their plot, and to lessen their seething against Him. Would that we learned how to meet plots with calm and prayer, before offering any opinion...
As for what Christ wrote on the ground, John did not mention it, and the Fathers who interpreted it differed over it. The following are some of the opinions:
(1) He may have written "Whoever has erred in one commandment has become a transgressor of all the commandments," as a preparation for what He would tell them, that they had no right to judge anyone.
(2) He may have written some of the commandments which most of them had broken, with the intention of rebuking them for the hardness of their hearts.

(3) He may have written what He had said before in the Sermon on the Mount, "Judge not, that ye be not judged..." (4) He may have written what He spoke, namely: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her."
The Church accepts all these opinions by way of contemplation and inference, and there is no definitive opinion that can be adopted alone.

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: The insistence and the questioning continued, and the Lord broke off what He was writing and straightened up. His answer came as a depth of divine wisdom, against the cunning and malice of devils. For Christ neither acquitted the woman nor condemned her, but added to the Law the depth and spirit of the commandment: one who breaks the Law has no right to condemn another by the Law. So if there is none among you who is a breaker of the Law, let him begin by stoning her...
This is also what St. Paul said: "For wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things" (Rom 2:1).

And so the Lord gives us a beautiful new lesson in how wisdom delivers its possessor from plots. But we must first pray to the Holy Spirit, the Giver of this wisdom, and second be calm and unhurried before answering.

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: The Lord Jesus' stooping down this time was a truce that He gave as an opportunity for the crowd to depart, reflecting on what He had said, without a new confrontation. As for what He was writing, we have referred to it in (v. 6).

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: St. John portrays here how the few words of Christ were effective and at work in hearts and consciences. And how could they not be, since they were the living and powerful Word of God, piercing even to the dividing of soul and joints and bones? The response came first from the elders, because their spiritual perception was higher, then the young followed them, letting the stones fall from their hands, remembering only their own transgressions and sins. And the scene was emptied of everyone, except the Lord alone and the adulterous woman.

entries.section: (1) The woman caught in the very act

paragraphs.text: Here the Lord began to speak with the woman, who was in a state that would never have allowed her to begin to speak, because of her shame and embarrassment...
But is this not the heart of Christ, to whom we pray in the Litany of the Sick: "O hope of those who have no hope, and helper of those who have no helper, comfort of the fainthearted"?
It is a heart of love and forgiveness, and it always stretches out its hand to the brokenhearted.

And He began to ask her about the accusers who had departed, although He knew of their departure, but He wanted to spread reassurance in her. Those who wanted her dead no longer sought her. And when she answered Him, He said to her: even though I am the God who judges, and even though I am the only one who is without sin, I also do not condemn you. But go and sin no more. For God's forgiveness does not mean license and a return to sin, but it means that God's mercies open an opportunity for repentance before the sinner, who must make use of it.

My beloved brother... perhaps we may come out of this story, with all its events, with one important lesson, which is that we should not condemn anyone, placing before our eyes Christ's saying that if any one of us is without sin, let his brother condemn first... So let us cast far away the stones of condemnation that are in our hands, for we are under the very same judgment, and let us pray for our brothers instead of condemning them, that God may have mercy on us also together with them.

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: Here again the Lord connects His words with what He had said before, that He is the living water (ch. 7:38). Just as He cried out about Himself then, so today He cries out, presenting Himself as the light of the world, also using one of the rites and symbols of the feast, the rite of light. In the Temple, in the outer court, there were four very high pillars, and each pillar carried four wicks that were lit at the Feast of Tabernacles, giving a great light. This rite signified God, the light of the world, and was a remembrance of the pillar of fire that God sent in the wilderness to lead His people by night in the wilderness of Sinai. So Christ cries out once more, declaring Himself: "I am the light of the world." Note, dear reader, that when the talk was about the manna, Christ presented Himself as the true bread, the bread of life, and the living bread (ch. 6:32, 35, 48, 51). And now, the talk being about the light of the feast, He presents Himself as the true light of the world. It is as though Christ is saying that all the pale symbols of the past have today become a shining reality in the Son of Man, in His Incarnation, in which all the symbols were fulfilled. And let us note some spiritual meanings in these words:
(1) Because He is the light of the world: everything other than Him, or outside of Him, has become darkness.
(2) Because He is the light of the world: He has become the only source of guidance for the soul lost in sins.
(3) Because He is the light of the world: He has granted His children to have within them a light of life by which they distinguish things, reflecting His light to all who are around them.
(4) Although He is the light of the world: He left man the freedom to follow Him or not to follow Him by his own will.

And the Church, beloved, has taken care to remind her children always of all these meanings in the daily prayer of Prime in the Agpeya, for we read the first chapter of the Gospel of John, which describes Christ as the light that shone in the darkness. We also pray in the Psalms and the morning Midnight Praise: "O true Light, who enlightenest every man that cometh into the world." Would that you always remembered this attribute of your God, so that your soul may shine with His divine light...

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: The Pharisees relied on the fact that the Law of Moses requires two witnesses to establish a case, and does not accept a man's testimony about himself. By this they justified their refusal to accept Christ's thought, and His saying that He is the light of the world.

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: In (ch. 5:31), Christ says: "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true...
There is another that beareth witness of me..." meaning the Father's witness to the Son.

But here, with the days of Christ's Incarnation drawing near and only a little time remaining, He began to declare Himself with power and clarity, and made clear that His witness about Himself is true, because He Himself is the Truth, and it is not for the darkness to judge the light. John the Baptist had already borne witness to me, and the Father likewise bears witness to me, and also my works. But now, I bear witness to myself, and my witness is true, and you will neither accept it nor understand it, because you do not comprehend the mystery of the Incarnation, so you do not know whence I came, and you do not know whither I go afterward, meaning His eternal existence in the bosom of the Father, and then His ascension to heaven.

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: "Ye judge after the flesh": it has two meanings:
The first meaning: you judge according to your fleshly desires and inclinations. This is because they condemned Christ and considered Him a liar when they said, "We do not accept your witness."

The second meaning: they judge according to their fleshly view of the person of Christ, and knowing His lineage and His earthly homeland. This is a limited view according to outward appearance, lacking the spiritual insight that perceives the reality of Christ's divine essence.
"I judge no man": this is because He did not come to judge the world, but to save it (ch. 3:17). And Christ demonstrated this also by not condemning the adulterous woman whom they brought to Him.

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: That is, even if I do not judge now, since the present mission is to offer salvation, judgment belongs to my divine attributes. And His judgment is true, because He is the Truth. And the Lord Christ returns once more to link Himself with the Father in the oneness of the divinity, for judgment is the right of God, and the Father has given it to the Son (ch. 5:22), who will judge everyone who does not accept the work of His salvation, or rejects His commandment and does not act upon it.

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: Christ presents to the Pharisees the answer to their objection about not accepting His witness in (v. 13): that even though His witness about Himself is true, there is One who bears witness and confirms it, namely the heavenly Father who sent Him, and gave Him as salvation for the world (Deut 17:6).

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: The Jews asked maliciously in order to entrap Christ, for when He spoke of His heavenly Father in (ch. 5:18), they sought to kill Him. And here too they wanted to catch Him in a word, but Christ did not answer them as to what they asked, but showed that the reason for their not knowing the Father was their ignorance of His own person, since He is the visible image of the invisible Father; and let us review a saying of Christ in another place: "If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father" (ch. 15:24, 25).

entries.section: (2) Christ the light of the world

paragraphs.text: The treasury is one of the places in the Temple, in the Court of the Women. The Lord used this place because it was the most crowded with people, owing to the offering of vows and the like. And despite the severity of Christ's words to the Jews, no one was able to seize Him, because He alone determines His hour, and not according to the opinion or counsel of any man.

O my God... perhaps the Jews had an excuse for their spiritual blindness and for not recognizing You. But what is my excuse, I who am anointed with the Holy Spirit? How ugly is my offense when I leave You, O true Light, and fall into the darkness of sin. Yes, I am without excuse. But I return and thank You, because You have placed in Your Church those who support me and raise me up, and who read over me the absolution of forgiveness, so that the eyes are opened again to the splendor of Your limitless light... O my God... do not let my knowledge of You be at the level of the mind and theories, but I want the knowledge of complete enlightenment, O true Light, who enlightenest every man that cometh into the world.

entries.section: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: The repeated dialogue returns once more, with Christ meaning one thing and the Jews understanding another. And verse 21 corresponds in its meaning to what came in (ch. 7:33-34), and the meaning is that you will die in the sin of unbelief in the Son, and you will seek and wait for an earthly messiah according to your own desire, and you will not find him. And because of your unbelief, you will not be able to enter the Kingdom of Heaven (v. 22). As for the Jews, with their usual mockery and closed spiritual vision, they did not understand the divine intention, but expressed their spiritual blindness and their hatred of Christ, saying that the only solution for understanding His words is that He is about to kill Himself, and that is the only place to which they cannot go, that is, "Hades."

entries.section: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ makes clear here the cause and the disease, and the difference between the words "I" and "you" in the previous verse, which is the difference between all that is heavenly and spiritual and what is earthly and temporal, tied to the glories of the world which I do not seek. And (v. 23) completes the meaning of (v. 14) of the same chapter: "I know whence I came, and whither I go," and both verses are a clear reference to Christ's Incarnation, His coming down from heaven, and His eternal divine nature. And Christ presents once more the cause of their destruction, which is their unbelief in Him!!!

My beloved Lord... Your conversation with the Jews has raised in me a perplexing and frightening question: am I earthly? Or am I heavenly? Can I be with You where You are, there in Your Father's house, or can I not? You have given me, freely, the grace of the heavenly birth in the sacrament of Baptism. But I still find that what is within me is inclined downward, toward the glories of the world and its falseness, forgetting the greatness of Your calling to me, to be from above as You are... My God, I fear for myself from myself, so do not allow me, my Lord, to slip downward, but draw me upward as You promised: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me," and make all the longing of my heart toward You alone.

entries.section: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: The purpose of the Pharisees in their question, "Who art thou?" was not to seek clarification but to entrap. But Christ answered: "Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning"... that is, I have already declared who I am: "I am the bread which came down from heaven"... "I am the living water"... "I am the light of the world"... "I am He to whom my works bear witness"... "I am He to whom the Father bears witness"... and so on... that is, I am Christ, the Savior of the world. But is there anyone who understands, or accepts, or believes?!

entries.section: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: "I have many things": Christ declares that He alone is the One who knows, and He alone is the Judge. If I speak concerning you of certain things, all of them are true, because I alone know what is in your hearts. And if I judge you, my judgment is true and just. But I also neither judge nor speak of myself, for I say what the Father also says, because I and the Father are one, and He is the One who sent me. And St. John adds in (v. 27) an explanation that Christ was referring to the Father here, without the Jews understanding His meaning.

entries.section: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: Christ denies here any possibility of the Jews' recognizing Him before they lift Him up on the cross. Christ used the word "lifted up" to affirm the responsibility of His own, who rejected Him, for His crucifixion, and some of them would understand at His crucifixion, because of the events and signs that would accompany it, such as "the darkness" and "many coming out of the graves." The word "lifted up" also carries the humiliation of the cross, and the pain, and the glory of the exaltation accomplished through the redemption. And it is a very clear reference to the symbol of the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up on a pole so that everyone who looked at it would not die (Num 21:9). And Christ returns once more to affirm the nature of His unique, close relationship with the Father, in unity of knowledge and communion, and the Lord had pointed to this many times.

entries.section: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: "He that sent me": that is, the Father, is with me and has not left me. And this reveals to us the mystery of the constant communion between the Father and the Son at the level of the one essence. For the Son, in His Incarnation, did not leave the bosom of the Father or depart from it, and likewise the Father also... And Christ concludes by adding a new theological truth, which is the union also at the level of will; for all that the Son does is the will of the Father, and all that the Father wills is done through the Son.

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: "Many believed on Him": but their faith was not sufficient, and is considered mere acceptance, as shown by Christ's urging them in verse 31 to continue in His word. And the coming verses of the same chapter show their swift turning against Christ.

"Ye shall know the truth": you will perceive who I am, for I am "the way, the truth, and the life" (ch. 14:6). And this Truth, that is, I, is the only One who frees from the slavery of lusts and sin, indeed the only Savior from the penalty of sin...

How sweet are Your titles, beloved Savior... for You are the Truth, and all that is besides You is falsehood. And You are Freedom, and all that is apart from You is a prison, even if with golden walls.
