How sweet it is that You free us from ourselves and our worn-out, perishing concerns, and call us to set out and enjoy the freedom of life with You, where all things become small, indeed cease to exist, so that nothing any longer troubles the soul, or imprisons it in its lusts or its base desires, far from You.

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: That is, we are children of Abraham the free man, who was never a slave to anyone, and therefore we are free... We note the following:

First: they did not understand what Christ meant spiritually, but turned to the political meaning of freedom, that they were not slaves to anyone, and their sonship to Abraham was the object of their fleshly boasting before the Gentiles.

Second: that, even on the level of material political understanding, they fell into a historical error, which is that they had in fact been enslaved to many kingdoms, such as Babylon and Assyria and the land of the Greeks, as well as the Roman rule contemporary with Christ. And because of this limited and mistaken understanding, they protested against Christ, how He could call them to freedom... without realizing the call of His salvation?!

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: "Verily, verily": a style of repetition for emphasis, which Christ used often. And the meaning here is: you do not understand what I meant by "the truth shall make you free." Therefore, in a new clarification, Christ confronts the Jews with what He meant, which is that every person who is unrepentant and lives the life of sin is a slave and not free, regardless of his lineage or affiliation or political description; for the measure of Baptism and freedom with God is unlike that of men, since it is either sin or repentance. Consequently, how many saints were imprisoned and exiled, yet the life of righteousness and repentance made them free... "A servant of sin": this word portrays for us the hideousness of the dominion of sin, as an evil master, controlling the will of man, who has no power or strength before this master. And sincere repentance, and the return to the bosom of God, are the way of true freedom from the yoke of this slavery.

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: As for the result, the slave enslaved to this evil master does not abide in the house for as long as sin is his master, for there is no place for slaves among sons. But the Son, that is, Christ, His abiding is a natural thing, for He is the heir of all His Father's house...

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: "If the Son therefore shall make you free": although Christ is the only source of true freedom, He put it in a conditional form: "If He shall make you free." And this condition does not relate to Christ's will in granting freedom, but relates to the Jews in their acceptance of this salvation or not; in other words: you have the true freedom granted by the Son, so will you accept it?

But as for the physical side (v. 37), I know that you are Abraham's seed. But this physical sonship has become very limited, and means nothing to God, as shown by your not accepting my word and believing in me, but instead of this, while I am the One who knows the thought of your hearts, you seek my death; and Christ repeated this saying in (ch. 7:19) regarding their desire to kill Him, and the phrase "my word hath no place in you" corresponds to what He said in (v. 31) "If ye continue in my word," and this means that Christ knew first that they had not continued and would not continue in His word!

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: "I speak that which I have seen with my Father" (see ch. 5:19-20) "and ye do": that is, Christ here denies their sonship to Abraham, and ascribes their sonship to Satan, for their seeking to kill Him is the will of Satan himself, and therefore, they have no right to claim that they are Abraham's children, as long as their work accords with the will of another father, who is the devil.

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ draws our attention here to an important principle, which is that a man is not evaluated by what he claims about himself, but by the works that he does. For example, it is not enough to say: we are a Church that abounds with saints. But do we have the striving and the works of our holy fathers? Therefore, Christ denies to the Jews again their claim of sonship to Abraham, because of their works which contradict this affiliation. And the difference here is that Abraham believed and trusted in the word of God, and followed Him with all his heart. But those who claim to be his children reject the words of truth and life from the mouth of God Himself, and even seek to kill Him.

entries.section: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

paragraphs.text: Since Christ denied to His hearers their sonship to Abraham, which greatly angered them because of their pride in this lineage, their reply came in two points:

The first: we are not born of fornication, that is, our genealogies are preserved back to Abraham, indeed to Adam, and we have not mingled with the Gentiles or intermarried with them; and the Jews always took pride in preserving the records of their genealogies by heart.
The second: they raised their sonship directly to God, who is higher than Abraham, and who is the one Father of us all.

Note: despite this boasting of false sonship, and the denial of the charge of fornication, the history of the Bible tells us that this people often went astray and committed fornication physically with the daughters of the Gentiles and intermarried with them, and also committed spiritual fornication by forsaking God, and worshipping the gods of the Gentiles on the high places and offering sacrifices to them (see Neh 13:23; Jer 3:6-10), which exposed them to the punishments of God, the hardest of which was their captivity and dispersion.

My beloved God... I fear that I may falsely believe of myself that I am called Your son, sharing with the Jews in what they ascribed to themselves. For if my life up to this moment is not free of sins, then do not quench Your Holy Spirit and the gift of life through Baptism within me. And if my sonship to You is deficient, let Your fatherhood to me remain perfect... and never leave me to myself.

entries.section: (5) The children of the devil and their characteristics

paragraphs.text: Just as Christ denied the Jews' sonship to Abraham, He returns and denies their spiritual sonship to God, presenting the proof of this, which is the Jews' rejection of Christ Himself. And Christ presents Himself here, as He had also presented before, as the Word of God incarnate, for He is the One who proceeded forth from God, incarnate, and by the will of the Father for the salvation of mankind. So when the Jews reject the incarnate Christ, they reject God Himself. And Christ adds to His discourse another reason for the Jews' refusal to believe in Him, which is that the Jews heard Christ's words with their fleshly ears, and did not understand His meaning from the beginning, whereas they should have heard His discourse with their hearts, for the word of God is received by faith, and not by the limited mind or the fleshly ear.

entries.section: (5) The children of the devil and their characteristics

paragraphs.text: This verse is considered one of the strongest confrontations in which the Lord Christ faced the Jews. The purpose was not to trample on their feelings, so much as to clear God and Abraham of this hard-hearted people. And by "the lusts of your father the devil" He meant here their desire to kill Him, for the wicked usually come together with Satan in one will, and so become children of his will. And the Lord continues His discourse describing Satan with the following characteristics: 1) "A murderer": that is, since evil entered his heart, Satan's only aim has been to destroy people and to lead them astray, for the perdition of their souls. Indeed, he is the only source of all conflicts and wars, and of inciting many to kill their brothers and their peoples. And Christ used the word "murderer" in the sense of a continual killer, to make clear that the destruction of people is the continuous work of Satan, indeed his only aim in all his works.

2) "Abode not in the truth": when God created Satan, he was a great angel with a rank of leadership, that is, God created him in the light and the truth. But he, by his own will, did not abide in this truth, and sank down to all evil by his separation from God. See the story of the fall of Satan (Isa 14; Ezek 28:12-19).

3) "A liar": one of the most important characteristics of Satan by which he leads people astray, as he led our first parents astray by his lie. And this characteristic passes on, by succession, to his children who bear his characteristics.

And this shows all of us the gravity of the sin of lying, which many do not take seriously, indeed do not consider a great sin, and which has become one of the necessities of daily life... Would that we examined ourselves, and remembered the fearful words of Christ on this subject.

entries.section: (5) The children of the devil and their characteristics

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ returns once more to the reason for the Jews' unbelief in His word: He speaks the truth, but they are the children of the liar, so they neither understand nor believe His words.

And here we take a new lesson from Christ, that the Christian man does not speak anything but the truth, regardless of whether his hearers believe it or not. Was it not so with the prophets whom the Jews killed? Was it not so also with our fathers the martyrs and saints who gave their lives for the sake of the truth?

entries.section: (5) The children of the devil and their characteristics

paragraphs.text: The Lord presents here a strong proof of all that He had said before, and of His coming forth from the Father and His Incarnation. And He presented this proof in the form of a question to the Jews, namely: who of you convicteth me of one transgression, whether of the Law or of any other sin?

And this is evidence of the Lord's walk in righteousness, purity and meekness in His life, and a lesson for us also to walk as He walked, with exactness and continual examination of the soul. For a man is not what he claims for himself, but his conduct that conforms to the truth he proclaims, as was explained before (vv. 39-40).

entries.section: (5) The children of the devil and their characteristics

paragraphs.text: Christ comes here to the end of a part of His dialogue with the Jews, in reply to verse 41: "We have one Father, even God." After He proved to them that they were not Abraham's children because of their works, and that they were children of Satan by their wicked will in attempting to kill Him, and by their lying, He comes to the end of this part, denying completely their sonship to God His Father, and presenting this as the reason for their not hearing His word and believing in Him.

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: The Jews found no charge to bring against Christ more severe than that He was a Samaritan, and the enmity between the two groups was great (see ch. 4). And they added also that He has a devil, as though they were replying to Him regarding what He had accused them of... and that out of their anger at what He had said about them. And they did not support this charge with anything, because they knew well that He was a Jew, and they had not found one sin in Him. Therefore, what the Jews said about Christ is counted as abuse and insult.

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: As for Christ, He was not occupied with defending His Jewish origin and lineage, but was concerned to repel and reject the second accusation, which touches the essence of His divinity and the holiness of His Father, expressing that the Jews' claim that He has a devil is an insult to the dignity of His heavenly Father which cannot be accepted or overlooked, because the One who is in Christ is the Father, so how can they say of the Father that He is a devil?!

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: "I seek not mine own glory": it is not my task to proclaim my glory, which is mine. For I came to bear humiliation and shame, and not to defend myself, for that is the task of my Father, who sees and examines everything, and who is jealous for my glory and seeks it, and who also judges everyone who has dishonored the glory of the only-begotten Son. And what Christ said here is a consolation to all His children who suffer persecution or insult for the sake of His name. For all that a man bears for the sake of Christ is counted as glory laid up for him, and also the just God judges the wicked according to His goodness and His just judgment.

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: Christ affirms a truth of the faith, which is that everyone who hears and keeps His commandment will not be hurt by the second death, but will have eternal life. And He had said the same meaning before in (ch. 5:24).

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: St. John returns and highlights the Jews' continued material, fleshly, literal understanding of Christ's words, instead of the spiritual understanding of them. And by their mistaken understanding they offered proof of the correctness of their previous accusation against Him that He has a devil. And the word "we know" means an assertion, and it resembles the expression of the high priest at the trial: "What further need have we of witnesses?" (Mt 26:65). And they continued to affirm their opinion that Abraham and all the prophets and fathers had died; so who are you that you should be given life and freedom from death? For they did not, of course, realize that He was speaking of release from eternal death, and not bodily death.

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: Verse 54 corresponds in its meaning to what came in (ch. 5:31), and adds that the Jews' claim that God is their Father did not bring them to the true knowledge of God, whom He knows with a personal knowledge, through the unity of nature and essence. And Christ affirms that if He claimed not to know the Father, He would be a liar like the Jews in their claim to know Him. And the proof that Christ offers of His knowledge of the Father is the keeping of His sayings and the obedience of His will, which are the simplest principles of the faith that the Jews did not do toward God Himself, and these are the cause of their judgment, and of their not recognizing the person of Christ.

Note, dear reader, that the Lord Christ still repeats that true faith is not that which is inherited, like the faith of the Jews, or that of which one boasts. But faith in the understanding of God is the keeping of His sayings and commandments and acting upon them in the life that we live... for how many people claim faith, and by their works deny it?!

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: This verse came as a reply to the Jews' insult to Christ in (v. 53) "Art thou greater than our father Abraham?"

As for the meaning: it is that He is truly greater than Abraham, for Abraham, with his standing among the Jews, was no more than a witness to the promises of God... and he, unlike you, believed the promise, and even desired to be a contemporary of the events of the Incarnation and redemption, and he saw them by faith, and believed and rejoiced, and exulted in the Spirit... And this is what St. Paul expressed in (Heb 11:13) when he said: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them."

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: As usual, the Jews did not understand Christ's meaning, but interpreted His words as meaning that He had seen Abraham in the body. Therefore the Jews insulted Him again, saying: you have not reached the age of the elders, which is fifty years among the Jews, so how do you claim to have seen one who died two thousand years ago?! But Christ's answer carried the theological side in the declaration about Himself, and confirms what came in (ch. 1:1) "In the beginning was the Word." And the intended meaning: even if you are astonished and scoff at my being a contemporary of Abraham, the truth, which you also will not accept, is that I am before Abraham was; and this word "I am" is the very word that God used in presenting Himself to His people, when He said in (Ex 3:14) "Ehyeh" as His name, which means: "I am." So Christ here uses the name of God known among the Jews. And His saying "before Abraham was" is a clear reference to His eternal divinity.

entries.section: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

paragraphs.text: The Jews considered what Christ said to be blasphemy, whose penalty is stoning. But because His hour had not yet come, He went out of the Temple, passed through and was hidden from their eyes, without their accomplishing their purpose of stoning Him. And so Christ reminds us again that, in many cases, it is wise to flee from anger, and not to confront it...
The man born blind

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man born blind

paragraphs.text: "Blind from his birth": that is, he had no eyes at all. This makes the coming miracle fall not under the miracles of healing but under the miracles of creation. As for the question that the disciples asked the Lord Christ, inquiring about the cause of this man's blindness, it expresses the belief of the Jews, and their faith in what came in the Law, that God visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, or that illness is a direct result of sin. But God also permits trials and illnesses for His righteous children and saints, to show virtues such as thanksgiving and endurance, and He permits other illnesses for sinners for the purpose of their repentance and return.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man born blind

paragraphs.text: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents": this answer from the Lord Christ to His disciples was to turn them away from searching for causes, and to prepare them to receive the coming work of God. For the blind man here represents a field for the manifestation, not only of a specific work that God the Word performs, but it reveals to us the attributes and the dispensation of the Son toward all His creation; for we find the attribute of tenderness and fatherly love in God who visits His weak creation, for it is Christ who went to the blind man, the Samaritan woman and the paralytic, and they did not come to Him. Likewise the attribute of creation, which is a work in which Christ declares His divinity and His own power to create an eye out of nothing, with all it includes of tissues and nerves and the power of sight. And finally, the Son also declares the relationship between Himself and the Father in will and work in (v. 4). And the last of the purposes of this miracle is the faith in Christ of everyone who saw it, in view of its difficulty.

"While it is day": a reference to His bodily life on earth, and the night is the end of life and death. And this message is directed to all of us, beloved, for Christ is speaking about all of us, because the day is my life and your life. And we are called to use this day, before our life passes, in doing good. It is a great opportunity for us to do in it the works of God, because death comes, and then there is no benefit in us after the opportunity is lost, indeed regret for wasting our life on other things, such as pleasures or preoccupation with the affairs of the world, will profit nothing. So let us make use of this precious opportunity in positive work, and goodness, and the service of the Lord. "I am the light of the world": that is, Christ is the only source of illumination for everyone who lives in the blindness and darkness of sin, and there is no light or savior other than Him. And there has already been discussion in (ch. 8) of Christ as the light of the world. As for enjoying this light, its only entrance is the life of repentance, and fellowship with Christ in His Church.

entries.section: (1) The healing of the man born blind

paragraphs.text: It is wonderful that the Lord should use clay, which damages the eye, in healing and creating the eye.

And St. John Chrysostom says that Christ shows that His power in healing diseases exceeds the powers of nature, and proves that He is not bound to one means in performing His miracles, for sometimes He heals by the word, at other times by touch, and at others by spitting on the dust, and so on...

"Go, wash": that is, the healing begins with washing, and washing is the act of repentance. And in our faith, Baptism is a washing from sin, "that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" (Eph 5:26). Therefore Baptism was the door of Christianity, because it is the entrance of salvation...
Likewise, dealing with the Holy Bible and the word of God is a second source of spiritual washing and purification of the soul.

And the third source is repentance and the sacrament of confession. For repentance and confession are a daily Baptism, in which a person is washed from his sins, and by them receives the gift of healing and the salvation of the soul. As for the word "Go," and the words "went his way and washed," they are a clear reference to the human role; for he was blind. And it would have been easier for Christ to heal him without burdening him with the toil of the way to the pool, while he still could not see, and the return from it seeing. But Christ wants to declare that, although the gifts of healing (Baptism) and salvation are free, there is a role and a responsibility on man in going and returning. And this is what we call "spiritual striving in the life with God." And the blessings of obedience, faith, the washing of Baptism, and man's striving were crowned with sight and enlightenment.
And this is also available to each one of us, if he accepts and does as this man did, and obeys Christ, and holds fast to the means of grace in His Church.

The crowd took the man born blind to the Pharisees, who in the eyes of the Jews were the most learned of people and the teachers of the Law, seeking an explanation for this unique wonder. And St. John mentioned that the miracle took place on a Sabbath, in preparation for what the Pharisees would say in (v. 16) on the one hand, and to confirm Christ's teaching that the Sabbath does not nullify the work of mercy on the other; which Christ had done and taught in all the previous healing miracles.

"Then again the Pharisees also asked him": it means that the Pharisees had heard the story from the crowd. But, for further investigation and clarification, they asked the man concerned himself, and their motive was jealousy and hatred toward the Lord Christ, and an attempt to find a charge against Him, and not to believe the fact and acknowledge it.
And often, beloved, our prejudgments about people lead us to deviate from the truth, despite its clarity, because of the feelings with which our souls are filled toward them that do not please God.

The Pharisees were divided in their opinion, for the majority, who wanted to condemn Christ, closed their eyes to the miracle and its power, and saw nothing but that Christ was a breaker of the commandment to keep the Sabbath. But a few of them could do nothing but declare their rejection of the first opinion; is it reasonable that a sinful man should do what no one can do but God?
And therefore the division occurred, and the council of the Pharisees did not come out with one opinion.

And with this division, they put a question to the blind man himself about his personal opinion of what had happened, hoping they might find in his words a pretext by which to accuse Christ of sorcery, or something that would cast doubt on the occurrence of a miracle.

But the answer of the blind man, who acknowledged the favor of the One who had brought light into his life, came as a disappointment to all their hopes, for he declared his faith that He is a prophet, showing thereby courage and love of the truth, for he bears witness to Christ before a council that he knows is mostly against Christ.

Since the blind man's testimony was not to the Pharisees' liking, they summoned his parents, as a last hope of denying this miracle, and they put their question in a disapproving form, so that they would reject their son's statement. But his parents' answer was brief and decisive, for they acknowledged that the man was their son, and that he was born blind.

But at the same time, they declared that they did not know the events of the miracle, and this for two reasons; the first: that they had not actually seen it. The second, which is the more fitting, is what St. John mentions, that they feared that the Jews would put them out of the synagogue, which would result in their being deprived of religious rights and the practice of worship. And the punishment of expulsion from the synagogue was, in many cases, a prelude to another punishment, which was death. Therefore, they sent him back to the Pharisees to complete his questioning, as a man responsible for his own answer.
"He is of age": it means that he had passed thirty years of his life.

entries.section: (4) The man born blind bears witness to Christ

paragraphs.text: "Give God the praise": it was a legal and religious procedure, like a kind of adjuration, obliging the one addressed to tell the truth. And it is a fearful expression in the soul of every Jew, for it usually preceded the religious trials that ended in the Jew's being banned from the synagogue, or delivered to death... see the story of "Achan the son of Carmi" (Josh 7:19). However, this questioning was not impartial, and its purpose was not to listen to the story in order to arrive at the truth, but the prior and evident condemnation of Christ in their suggestive words to the man, when they said: "We know that this man is a sinner."

But the man's answer came frank and simple: I am not concerned with your judgment of this man, for you see Him as a sinner, but I live a reality that I cannot deny, which is that yesterday I was living in darkness, and today I am in the light.
"I was blind, now I see":

How sweet are these resounding words, whose echo is heard in the suffering soul. For often God opens our eyes and minds and hearts to mistakes we were committing, and had become accustomed to, as the blind man is accustomed to darkness. But after the entry of the divine light, and the illumination of the soul by the love of Christ, a person cannot accept the darkness of sin again. And in proportion as a person grows in life with God, and discovers new dimensions in the divine love, he can only repeat: "I was blind, now I see."

entries.section: (4) The man born blind bears witness to Christ

paragraphs.text: Once more the Pharisees return to a new questioning, hoping they might find something with which to overturn his testimony. But the man was overcome with distress at the attempt to pressure him and have his testimony repeated again and again, and expressed this distress with a certain biting sarcasm, when he said to them: perhaps the purpose of your many questions is to believe in Him, and to become His disciples?! Their answer came as a mixture of sin and arrogance; the sin is that they reviled him, and the arrogance is their vain boasting that they were disciples of Moses, and their considering discipleship to Christ an insult, which they ascribed to the man born blind.

entries.section: (4) The man born blind bears witness to Christ

paragraphs.text: The man marveled, and in this marveling there is a new sarcasm, as though he were saying: how is it that you do not know, when you claim to be the people of knowledge, especially since the event and the miracle are beyond human ability, for God spoke to Moses (v. 29), but he did not perform such works, so is not this One better than Moses, the object of your boasting?!

And the man also presented a new defense against the council of the Pharisees, which is: does God answer sinners?! Or is the one who does these works, and whom God hears, a righteous and godly man, who does the will of God and fulfills it in his life. And the man presents a final proof with which he concludes his speech, which is that it has never been heard in the whole history of mankind, since creation, that eyes were created for a man born blind. Consequently, the One who performed this miracle is not merely a righteous man, but is from God; as though this testimony had been put in his mouth by the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (4) The man born blind bears witness to Christ

paragraphs.text: As for bearing witness to the truth, its reward was reviling and being cast out from before the council of inquiry, without greater condemnation, lest the people who believed in the miracle should rise up.

And we learn from the man born blind that bearing witness to the truth sometimes carries a heavy price, and none is able for it except the man who believes in the power of God and the support of the Holy Spirit for him, like all the martyrs of the Church whom neither pain nor fear deterred from proclaiming the truth, even if they paid their lives as the price for it.

entries.section: (5) The difference between physical blindness and spiritual blindness

paragraphs.text: From our understanding of these verses, we find that Christ, to Him be glory, is the One who sought the man, and "found him." And the man carried the spirit of the glad tidings on the one hand, and the pain of expulsion on the other. But his perception was not complete, for the utmost he reached as a man was that Christ is a prophet. Therefore the Lord had to seek him out, to complete the enlightenment of his heart, as He had enlightened his eyes.

And Christ here uses an expression like the one He used before, for just as He said: "I am the light of the world," "I am the bread of life," which are expressions characterized by the declaration of His divinity, He says here: "It is He," which is the same style by which God described Himself to Moses, when Moses asked Him His name, and God said to him: "I AM THAT I AM," that is, the One who is and who will be. And this declaration from Christ was linked to a direct question to the man: "Dost thou believe on the Son of God?" Therefore the man's answer came, after inquiry, and Christ's declaration of Himself: "Lord, I believe," and he expressed his faith in Christ by worshipping Him. And so his inner sight was opened, and he saw God with his heart after having seen Him with his eyes.

entries.section: (5) The difference between physical blindness and spiritual blindness

paragraphs.text: "For judgment I am come": it means that I came to reveal what is in the hearts of people, and which of them accepts God and is enlightened by the knowledge of Him, or rejects Him and remains in darkness. For the Pharisees were the people most knowledgeable of the Law, but they did not accept the God of redemption and of the promises of whom their Law spoke. So Christ, the true Light, came to uncover their spiritual blindness. But the simple, who had no knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, came by faith to enjoy a spiritual sight higher in rank than any fleshly sight or knowledge. And here we remember what came in (ch. 3:19): "And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil."

entries.section: (5) The difference between physical blindness and spiritual blindness

paragraphs.text: The Pharisees understood the point of Christ's words and His hint, so they asked Him directly: "Are we blind also?" (the scholars of the Law, who examine it and teach it), in an attempt to catch Him in a word. But Christ's answer came stronger and harsher than the Pharisees had expected, which is: if you were blind through ignorance of the Law, and had no ability to distinguish the lawful from the forbidden, or to distinguish the one sent from God from one who is not, you would have an excuse, and sin would not be reckoned against you. But your claim of knowledge is what condemns you, for you have persisted in your obstinacy and have not believed, despite the prophecies fulfilled in me, and the works that none can do but the Creator God. Therefore the judgment for your rejection of me remains on you.

O my God... give me this luminous spiritual sight, for I do not want my mind or my knowledge or my self to be obstacles preventing me from recognizing Your traces and Your works and Your voice in my life... For I do not want to be a Pharisee who claims to see, but a blind man who wants to see, trusting in his God, the only light of the world.
The parable of the good shepherd; the Son's relationship with the Father; the accusation against Christ of blasphemy

entries.section: (1) I am the door of the sheep

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ affirms here that He is the lawful owner and the only shepherd of His people. For the fold here is the Church, the sheep are His people, and the door is Christ, who is charged with the repentance and salvation of the souls of His people; in a comparison between Him and the priests of the Jews and the Pharisees, whom Christ considered thieves who had no compassion on the people but rather harmed them the more, attending to their own interests (see Ezek 34).

And the saying likewise applies to every unfaithful servant in the Church of God, who steals from the people of Christ for his own account, or steals with strange teaching, robbing Christ of His flock.

entries.section: (1) I am the door of the sheep

paragraphs.text: "The porter": a reference to the Holy Spirit, who opens hearts to the word and voice of the shepherd; and it is a continual work of the Holy Spirit. It can also be said that the porter is the faithful servant, who does not claim to be a shepherd but a porter, whose whole work is to open the door for the shepherd, meaning that he strives to bring Christ to people, without claiming for himself a greater role than this. As for the sheep, when they hear the voice of their faithful shepherd, whom they know well through daily companionship and friendship, and trust his leading of their lives, as he calls each one by its own name, as a sign of love, concern and special care... they go out after him to enjoy the sun of spiritual knowledge, and the air of the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

So do you, beloved, have this discernment of the voice of Christ in your life? He is always calling you, and speaking with you, longing for you to go out with Him into His spiritual pastures, that you may have satisfaction and enjoyment. So do not let anything of the voices of this world and its concerns occupy your ears from listening to the voice of your good Shepherd.

entries.section: (1) I am the door of the sheep

paragraphs.text: Since the sheep are reassured by the voice of their shepherd, which they know well, they follow behind him in complete surrender and absolute trust, for he alone knows where the good pastures are for his flock, and his flock looks to his feet, and follows his steps which lead it to the waters of eternal rest, imitating its leader in his humility, meekness, striving and sufferings, captivated by the love of his care for it. As for the stranger, he is the deceiving teacher, like the thief and the robber, for the flock that is aware and instructed within the Church distinguishes teaching foreign to the spirit of its Church and its Christ, and so it shrinks from this misleading teaching.

And therefore, beloved, being present within the atmosphere of the Church provides all of us with spiritual food free of deceit, and protects us from strange teachers who enter houses in the name of Christ, and are thieves and robbers who seek only to tear His body, that is, His Church, so do not listen to them... but flee from them.

entries.section: (1) I am the door of the sheep

paragraphs.text: The Jews did not understand Christ's meaning, especially the last comparison between the true shepherd and the stranger. Therefore, the Lord Christ begins in the coming verses to restate and explain, being long-suffering toward them.

entries.section: (1) I am the door of the sheep

paragraphs.text: "The door of the sheep": that is, I am the only entrance to the way of salvation, and there is no salvation outside my Body and my Blood. And likewise I am the only way out, from tribulation and pain, into the enjoyment of the spacious freedom of fellowship with God.

"All that ever came": of course He did not mean the prophets or the fathers, who were sent according to His choice and calling, but He means everyone who came before Him and claimed that he was the shepherd and teacher. This saying can also be applied to the scribes and Pharisees, but God's flock did not respond to their error. And St. Mark makes clear the difference between the voice of the true shepherd and the robbers, for "He taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes" (Mk 1:22). And Christ Himself described the scribes and Pharisees as robbers when He said of them: "Ye devour widows' houses" (Mt 23:14), that is, they took on the form of shepherds, but they were robbers. Therefore, the true people of God did not respond to their falseness. For just as a child can distinguish the voice of his father, so can the people of Christ with their great Shepherd.

entries.section: (1) I am the door of the sheep

paragraphs.text: "If any man enter in by me": the invitation stands, but God respects man's freedom. Salvation is offered to all people, but man may accept the gift of Christ, or reject it by his stubbornness and pride. For free salvation is conditioned on faith in the Shepherd, following Him, and striving with Him.
"Shall go in and out, and find pasture": the talk is about the fold, which is the Church, which provides its children with: first: union with Christ through Holy Communion.
Second: spiritual satisfaction through sound teaching.
Third: reassurance through the guidance of the fathers.
Fourth: freedom to set out in growth and in the true knowledge of God.
And the meaning of this is that life outside Christ and His Church is death.

My dear friend, Christ granted us life and bought it for us by His death for us all on the cross, and offered it to us and called us to it freely, and He seeks nothing but that we should enjoy all this, and have the better, "For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ" (ch. 1:17). All the revelations and prophets and appearances of the Old Testament become as nothing in comparison with what has been revealed to us in the person of Christ by His Incarnation and His offering of salvation to us. Indeed, the greatest and the best, my friend, is the indwelling of the true Holy Spirit of God within us. For on the day you were anointed with the Holy Myron, God dwelt within you and you became a temple for Him... So do you value this life and this better state, or is it the transient and false life that still allures you and distracts you from your Christ?

"The good shepherd": in (v. 1), we made clear the importance of the attribute of shepherd. But here, what is the goodness of Christ in comparison with shepherds such as Moses and David and others? These shepherds, in their turn, were themselves sheep whom God shepherds; but the goodness of Christ:
First: that He is the only Shepherd of shepherds, the Pantocrator, and the shepherding of no limited man rises to Christ's shepherding of His creation.

Second: the faithful shepherd may defend his flock and fight for it, but he does not risk his life, which is dearer than his flock... But Christ gave Himself for the salvation of all His flock, and it is the work of atoning redemption that no one can undertake except our Christ and good Shepherd...

Third: besides the work of redemption, the expression "the good shepherd" carries deep spiritual meanings... Christ is the One who takes care of preparing all that you need, and He is tender toward you in all your tribulations, and He is the defender of you against evil and danger... So if this is our Shepherd, why then do we worry and why do our daily worldly concerns trouble us?
Trust, beloved, in your loving Shepherd, who lays down His life for you.

A comparison that the Lord Christ presents, whose purpose is to show the extent of love in His shepherding of His flock, which He owns and redeems. For however great the faithfulness of the hireling, it will never rise to the love of the owner of the flock for his flock. The hireling's life is much more important than the sheep, so he flees if he senses the danger threatening his life. But the true owner of the flock takes up his cross and goes up on it by his own will alone, to die himself and give life to his people.

And the words here can be directed to the servants in the Church of Christ. The hireling servant is bound to those he serves by nothing but wages, that is, what he obtains of praise or self-gratification. But the faithful servant is for the sake of Christ, and out of fear for the flock of Christ, spares no effort... even his whole life is cheap for the sake of the Master's flock which was entrusted to him. And the Church is full of the lives of these faithful shepherds who also gave their lives for their people, such as St. Peter the Patriarch, the Seal of the Martyrs, who offered his life willingly, asking Christ that his blood be the end of the age of martyrdom from which the Coptic people suffered at the hands of the Romans.

After the Lord Christ presented the difference between the hireling and the owner of the flock, He returns to affirm the importance of His distinctive pastoral work as the good Shepherd; and He adds a new attribute that this shepherding includes, which is His knowledge of His own. Just as the shepherd knows his flock as a whole and by number, so He knows each one also by name (v. 3), and by his needs and tribulations, and even suffers with his suffering.
And this is a privilege enjoyed by all His children, unlike those who refuse to be within the Church, His fold, to whom the Shepherd says: "I never knew you" (Mt 7:23).

"And am known of mine": the knowledge of love, gratitude and thanksgiving from the sheep to their tender Shepherd, and the knowledge of experience of His strong arm and the work of His grace in our lives. For Christ has no equal or substitute for every soul that has enjoyed His friendship and care; He alone satisfies, and therefore the soul follows Him wherever He goes, and He is the source of its satisfaction and refreshment. Blessed are you, St. Paul, when you declare the depth of this knowledge, and say: "For I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him" (2 Tim 1:12).

Christ here likens His knowledge of His own to the knowledge that exists between Him and the Father. Just as the Father and the Son are in constant openness and communion, so nothing separates Christ from His flock. And as far as the flock is able, it too is in communion with its Master and Shepherd, the source of all its good... and the more a person increases in his love for Christ, the more his communion with Him increases, that is, the more his knowledge of Him increases...

So, beloved, the knowledge of God is available to all, because this is the desire of His heart and His good will. But there is a role for all of us in growing in the knowledge of God that satisfies every soul; and this role is that we give more of our time to spend with God, for whatever the occupations and obligations, they are not acceptable excuses before God. And the time we spend with God in prayer and reading is an investment in our life and our rest and our true peace.

"I lay down my life": since the love of the shepherd for his flock reached its end, self-giving and redemption come as a natural result of this faithful shepherding, and the reference here is to redemption, which is the goal for which Christ became incarnate, for there is no stronger proof than the death that Christ offers in His love for His people (ch. 1:13; ch. 15:13).

As the Lord Christ declares the mystery of redemption to the flock, He makes clear here that this redemption is not only for the people of Israel, for the true flock of Christ is everyone in the whole world who receives Him; He is not limited to the fold of Israel, because redemption and the cross were offered to all, and this is what the high priest prophesied in (ch. 11:52), that Christ would die to gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.
"Them also I must bring":

This phrase lays on all of us an obligation to seek out every soul far from Christ. For the servant and the true Christian man cannot rest while he knows that there are many who are still far from the Church of Christ, and he feels responsible toward these, exactly like his Christ, the great Shepherd. For if the lost sheep come to know the voice of the great Shepherd, they too become part of His flock, following Him wherever He goes.

"Therefore doth my Father love me": the love between the Father and the Son is an eternal love that does not depend on anything, but Christ draws attention here to His giving of Himself as a sacrifice of redemption for the whole world, and this sacrifice the Father accepts with joy and love.

And lest it be thought that the Son's obedience to the Father diminishes His worth, or His equality with the Father, Christ continues His discourse, making clear His authority and absolute will in the process of death and redemption; for the will of the Father and the Son is one and equal in the redemption of man, the Father by planning and the Son by carrying out. Therefore, Christ focuses here on His authority, that it is He who lays down His life of His own will in order to take it again, that is, He is the One going to death to crush it, and death has no authority over Him. And the word "take it again" means the Resurrection, that is, He receives back His spirit that tasted death in the body, and Satan has no authority to seize the human spirit of the Lord Christ, which is subject to the will of the Son alone. "This commandment have I received of my Father": the commandment here refers to the Father's plan in the salvation of man, for Christ accepted this plan by His own will, and not by compulsion or coercion.

Beloved... does the humility of the heavenly Son toward the Father, who is of one essence with Him, not strike you, emptying Himself, and offering Himself, with all love, to buy you with His holy, precious blood? Why then do high self-regard and the pride of the soul still pursue us, and are we deceived by their false appearances? Have we not yet learned from our God?!
As usual (ch. 7:43; ch. 9:16), a division of opinion occurs among the Jews for two reasons:
The first: their not understanding what He said, not perceiving the spiritual dimensions of His words.
The second: their enmity toward Christ as a result of the effect of His words on others, so it was easier for them to accuse Him of blasphemy and of following Satan.

But a group remained who did not agree with the former in their opinion... for they had not yet forgotten the miracle of the man born blind, and brought it forward here as evidence denying Christ any relationship with the kingdom of darkness.

St. John interrupts here the discourse of the Lord Christ about the flock and the good Shepherd, to add for us the dimension of time and place of this discourse, for this Feast of Dedication is a national and spiritual feast, added by Judas Maccabeus as a memorial of the cleansing of the Temple from the Greek occupation, which defiled the Temple and killed more than forty thousand of the Jews. And the time was winter, about the middle of December. And since Solomon's porch was the only roofed porch, the Lord Christ took shelter in it from the cold and the rain.

All the Fathers and interpreters agree that the purpose of the question was not faith in Christ and following Him, but a new attempt to catch Him in a word, so that they might accuse Him of blasphemy, especially what they asked of Him, that He declare this openly, that is, before all the crowds, so that they would have a complaint against Him before the council of the leaders of the Jews on the one hand, and before the Roman state on the other, because the declaration that He is the Christ implicitly includes that He is the King of the Jews, their liberator from the Romans. Therefore, Christ's answer came indirectly, but He did not deny the truth about Himself, but pointed to the miraculous works that He had done, and which no one but He could do. And the Lord used the same reply, that His works bear witness to Him (ch. 5:36; 9:4; 10:

Christ presents here the reason for the Jews' unbelief in Him, whether in His words or His works. And this reason is that they are not of His sheep, or of God; for man's pride prevents him from listening to the voice of God, and this is what the scribes and Pharisees suffered. But the simple and humble people received Christ's word and rejoiced in it. And the phrase "as I said unto you" is a reminder from Christ of what He said in (vv. 4, 14) and also (ch. 8:47).
A repetition of what came in (vv. 4, 14), and the purpose is to affirm the same spiritual meanings in God's knowledge of His own, and their recognition of His voice.

"And I give unto them eternal life": a very special gift enjoyed by the flock of Christ alone, which is the gift of the inheritance of eternal life. But how does He give them this eternal life? The answer is through what He had also spoken of before:
(1) Birth from Baptism and the Holy Spirit, in His discourse with Nicodemus (ch. 3:5).
(2) Faith in the only-begotten Son (ch. 3:16, 36; ch. 6:47).
(3) Partaking of His most holy Body and precious Blood (ch. 6:54).
(4) Continual following of Christ, striving, and acceptance of tribulations (ch. 12:25).
"They shall never perish... neither shall any man pluck them":

How sweet are these words, which spread reassurance in the soul and drive away our doubts about the salvation of our souls... Yes, beloved God, we believe that we have eternal life in You alone, and You are our keeper and protector. And how could we not be saved, when You have granted us free salvation in Baptism, and the forgiveness of sins in the sacrament of the most holy Communion, and the sacrament of repentance and confession? We are reassured, my Lord. But grant us the spirit of striving against sins until we complete the salvation of our souls...

In (v. 28), the Lord says: "Neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand," and here He says: "No man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand," and this is proof and evidence that the hand of the Father and the Son are one in ability, power, and also will. Therefore the important declaration came in (v. 30) "I and my Father are one," which is one of the strongest verses proving the divinity of Christ and the equality of the Son with the Father. As for the expression "My Father, which gave them me," its meaning is that from eternity, before the foundation of the world, all creation was given to the Son, for He is its Creator (ch. 1:3), and He is its Redeemer (ch. 10:15), and He is its protector and ruler (ch. 10:28).
"Is greater than all": whatever the attempts of Satan to snatch and scatter the flock of God, God is stronger, and His protection is unlimited.

So do we trust, my beloved, in the strong hand of God, and His protection of His Church, or do we still worry about this and that? Beloved... you are in the hands of your heavenly Father, enjoying a surpassing protection through which you can be victorious over the power of the wicked adversary. So do not belittle the strong hand of God that crushes all evils, but come, let us sing with Solomon the wise, saying: "The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Prov 18:10).

entries.section: (5) The accusation against Christ of blasphemy

paragraphs.text: The strong declaration that the Lord Christ made of His oneness with the Father angered the Jews, because of their failure to grasp all the previous sayings and wonders, which no man performs. So they tried to stone Him, considering all that He said about His relationship with the Father to be blasphemy. And instead of listening, understanding and taking in the good works that Christ had done, their eyes and hearts were closed to them, and nothing remained but the desire to kill Him. Beloved, do not we too often forget, especially in time of tribulation and trial, all that God has done with us of good and miracles throughout the years of our life, and listen only to the voice of the enemy of good, who casts doubt on God's care for His children?!
Do we not wrong God with us at that time?
O my beloved God... forgive us our boldness and our wronging of You, and do not make us like those whose eyes were blinded to You and to Your goodness.

entries.section: (5) The accusation against Christ of blasphemy

paragraphs.text: A person may endure wrong for the sake of God, and not defend himself. But the charge of blasphemy is the only one that the Christian does not accept against himself, because accepting it would mean denying God. And here, Christ defends Himself against this false charge, using the Law itself. For the Law called Moses a god to his brother Aaron (Ex 4:16), and in (Ps 82:6) it says: "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High," and the Law is true and cannot be broken. So if the Law has called certain men gods, and this was not considered blasphemy, then even if I were only a man... I did not blaspheme when I used the same designation for myself, that is, it is a designation that has a reference among you... And the second objection that the Lord presented is stronger, because He declares about Himself that He is not an ordinary man (v. 36), for He is the Holy One of God, that is, the One appointed from eternity as Christ for the salvation of mankind, and sent by His Incarnation into the world. For all who preceded Him were called gods, because the word of God came to them (v. 35). But He is the Word of God Himself (ch. 1:1), so how can He not be God by nature? Therefore, He is the Son of God, and He is also God, and He and the Father are one.

entries.section: (5) The accusation against Christ of blasphemy

paragraphs.text: As for the third proof that Christ presents against the accusation of blasphemy, it is the works themselves, which were already referred to in (ch. 5:36; 9:3-5; 10:35, 38; 14:

10-12). And it is that the works He does are all divine works, which no man has ever done; from feeding the crowds, and raising the sick man of Bethsaida, to healing the man born blind. And these works alone, even without your listening to my words, are sufficient for you to believe when I said to you: "I and my Father are one," because I am in the Father and the Father in me.

entries.section: (5) The accusation against Christ of blasphemy

paragraphs.text: The events end with all that the Lord said not convincing the Jews, but they sought to seize Him in anger, either to stone Him outside, or to bring Him to the leaders for trial. But Christ, since His hour had not yet come, "no man laid hands on him" (ch. 7:44), and He passed through their midst without their seizing Him (ch. 8:59).

entries.section: (5) The accusation against Christ of blasphemy

paragraphs.text: That is, to the east of the Jordan, where the Lord Jesus was baptized by the Baptist, and this region is known as Perea (Mt 19:1), in which the Lord Christ spent the last 4 months of His Incarnation, that is, from December until the Passover before His crucifixion. And Christ's presence in that place drew to Him many of the crowds who accepted faith in their simplicity; and the comparison these simple people made between the Lord and John the Baptist, who did not perform a single miracle, shows us that Christ performed signs and miracles during the period of His stay there. And these miracles, in addition to John's witness to Him, were a cause of the faith of many. The raising of Lazarus

Lazarus was a person beloved of the Lord, to Him be glory, along with his two sisters. His house served as a station where Christ would rest during His travels. The name "Lazarus" means: "God has helped." And the village of "Bethany" means: "house of affliction," and it is about 3 km from Jerusalem.
And the reference to the illness of Lazarus here is an introduction to the rest of the events of the chapter.
And the story of Mary's anointing Christ with perfume comes in detail in (ch. 12:3-8).

Christ was beyond the Jordan when the two sisters sent to Him, with the familiarity of love and family friendship, hoping for the healing of their brother. Christ did not need anyone to remind Him that He loved Lazarus. But what the two sisters said, and these words, are a kind of intercessory appeal, that Christ might come more quickly. And we learn from Mary and Martha, from what they did in sending a messenger to Christ, to send our prayers to Him on behalf of our sick loved ones, not only those whom we know in particular, but for all the sick in general.

"Not unto death": Christ's answer here is evidence of His divinity, for He answers the bearer of the urgent message, within the hearing of His disciples, that "this sickness is not unto death," and evidence also of His foreknowledge of all the events of this story that were to come. Indeed the Lord repeats what He had said before in (ch. 9:3) before the healing of the man born blind; which is that both illnesses were by a divine arrangement through which the Son's power to create eyes and to raise from the dead would be revealed.
"Jesus loved": it is an example of Christ's love for all His creation, especially these hearts and eyes that are attached to Him.

And St. John mentioned this love here, and affirms it, lest the reader hasten to say: how could the Lord Christ neglect the important message of the messenger about the illness of His beloved Lazarus, and stay for two days away, delaying?! For Christ loves, and this is a fact. And we must learn good spiritual things, which are God's wisdom in ordering the times; for our prayers are raised before Him the moment they are uttered. But the response and its timing depend on God's wisdom in ordering the times: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Eccl 3:1), and the delay sometimes brings more benefits... and may be a test of man's faith and trust in God... We also learn not to condemn people if they are late in asking after us, perhaps they had important matters that kept them from us, but rather to seek excuses for them.

And the loving heart of Christ responded, at the time He saw fit. So after the two days, He set out for Bethany in Judea, leaving Bethabara beyond the Jordan, taking with Him His disciples who would become witnesses of this great event.

entries.section: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

paragraphs.text: The events of the Feast of Dedication, and the Lord's discourse about the flock and the Shepherd, and the Jews' attempt to stone the Lord Jesus or seize Him, were still present before the eyes of the disciples. Therefore came their objecting inquiry about going to Judea, and their fear for Christ, and for themselves, of the violence of the Jews.

entries.section: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

paragraphs.text: What Christ said to the disciples in these two verses is by way of an illustrative parable; for Christ is the light of the day, and the hours of the day are the time of His appointed ministry on earth. Therefore, there is no need for fear, as long as it is day and I am with you. And Christ made this clear when He said: "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light" (ch. 12:35), as though He were saying do not fear, for no one will be able to harm you, because first I am with you, and second no one has authority over me because my hour has not yet come, so make your condition like that of one who travels by day and fears nothing, before the darkness comes.

entries.section: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

paragraphs.text: "Our friend Lazarus": Christ expresses here the relationship of love that binds Him to Lazarus, and He included the disciples in it also.

But the spiritual meaning is that Lazarus alone was not what was meant, for Christ loves you, and loves me also, and loves all His children. Did He not call all of us in the Song of Songs by the name "my love"? You may call God in your prayer "my beloved." But do you also hear Him calling you beloved, and how great is its echo in your soul? Indeed He also calls you beloved before His disciples and all His saints.
"Sleepeth": Christ used this expression to teach us that the death that comes upon His children in the body is not death, but a quiet sleep followed by resurrection and eternal life.

Therefore, the Church in the prayer for the departed says: "It is not death for Your servants, but a departure." But death, for Christ, means perdition resulting from unbelief in Him, or rejection of His commandments, or the pride of man, or rejection of the sacraments of the Church, for this is the true death that is not followed by life, but by judgment.

"That I may awake him": a reference to His divine work in raising Lazarus from the dead. And the disciples did not understand this reference, but they would grasp its meaning after the miracle of the resurrection.

entries.section: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

paragraphs.text: The disciples understood Christ's words literally, without reaching His meaning. And since their heartfelt desire still did not want to go to Judea, they offered his sleep as evidence of the beginning of his recovery... which indeed happens in many illnesses, such as fever, for the beginning of a long sleep precedes recovery... And in the face of this distance from understanding, Christ declared plainly His former meaning, which was the declaration of Lazarus' death in the body.

entries.section: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

paragraphs.text: "I am glad for your sakes": the Lord was not glad at the death of Lazarus, but because of His knowledge of what would happen, for the raising of Lazarus would be a great cause of strengthening the disciples' faith in the face of the events of the cross, which had drawn very near. Also, there are many, besides the disciples, who would believe in Christ after this miracle... And He also makes clear the reason for His gladness... that He was not there at the time of his illness, because the miracle would have been of lesser account, and the disciples had seen repeated examples of it... but the effect would become greater when one who had been dead four days is raised.

entries.section: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

paragraphs.text: The speech here is an aside, in a low voice, from Thomas, who is known for his doubt and anxiety, to the disciples.

As though Thomas were saying that the Teacher did not listen to our advice and our entreaty to Him. Consequently, the inevitable result is that the Jews will seize Him and us, and we shall all die together.

And what Thomas did then, many also do, those whose reason precedes their faith. And instead of believing the news of faith, they cause the simple to doubt their faith, for example by their mockery of miracles, or of the power of God, or of the authority of the saints.
O my God, do not make our minds obstacles and barriers that block the current of faith, but open our hearts, that we may receive and also proclaim Your great works.

entries.section: (3) Christ is the resurrection and the life

paragraphs.text: "Four days": it is the period between Christ's informing His disciples of Lazarus' sleep, and His leaving beyond the Jordan for Judea. And Bethany is about 45 minutes' walk from Jerusalem. And as is the custom of most societies until now, many of the people of the village had gathered to console Mary and Martha in their house.

entries.section: (3) Christ is the resurrection and the life

paragraphs.text: It is understood from the text that Christ did not go to the house of Lazarus, but a messenger told Martha, who went out quickly to meet Christ outside, and left Mary among the mourners, and Mary did not know, or else she would have gone out also with her. Her not knowing is clear from (v. 28), when Martha later told her "The Master is come."

entries.section: (3) Christ is the resurrection and the life

paragraphs.text: With spontaneity and simplicity, Martha spoke what she felt, for she expressed her regret at Christ's absence at the time of her brother's illness, for she knew that His love for the person of Lazarus on the one hand, and His being considered a righteous prophet who had performed many miracles of healing before, and that whatever He asks of God is granted Him on the other hand, would have been enough to heal him and prevent his death. And her saying: "But I know, that even now," meant her expecting something from Christ, which was probably the raising of her brother, but she was not sure of that, as the rest of her speech shows.

And perhaps the most important thing we learn here from Martha is simplicity and frankness of speech, which are important elements that our prayers often lack. We must speak with God of everything we feel, whether distress or a request for help, or thanks for what He has bestowed on us; for sincerity and frankness are the basis of acceptable prayer.

entries.section: (3) Christ is the resurrection and the life

paragraphs.text: A new contrast that St. John presents, as he is accustomed to bring out the great difference between what God intends and what man understands. For Christ makes clear here that Lazarus will truly rise, because the resurrection and the life are among the properties and authority of the only-begotten Son, which He grants to whom He wills of Himself. But Martha had not yet understood this divine dimension in the person of Christ. Therefore her answer, with what is firmly fixed in the minds of all people, was that her brother "shall rise again" also like everyone, "at the last day," that is, the day of the general resurrection of all people.

Christ answers here correcting the concepts, and declaring His divinity in His own power, that He is "the resurrection" and the source of "the life." And the resurrection is possible at any time according to His will and power, and not only on the last day as it is in people's minds, and everyone who dies in the body, like Lazarus, but "believes" in Him, "shall live," that is, will have eternal life. For bodily death does not touch the spirit at all, but the death of the spirit, by sin, is considered unbelief in Christ. Consequently, there will be for him no resurrection of life, but eternal judgment. And this faith makes us realize the secret of our fathers the martyrs' lack of fear of death. For death for the sake of the name of Christ, they considered the beginning of life, and a pledge of the true resurrection.

"I am the resurrection, and the life": an expression full of hope for every soul that still groans from the death of sin. For Christ declares to it that He is the secret of its resurrection and its life, if it wants resurrection from its death.

So come, let us present this Christ who raises up to every soul far from His Church, and we shall enjoy miracles of daily resurrection in His Church through the return of everyone who "was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found" (Lk 15:24, 32).

Faith in Christ adds another advantage for the one who believes in Him, which is not dying eternally, in completion of the meaning of the previous verse. For not only will the one who was dead live, but the one who is alive "shall never die." And this completion makes us realize the difference between the concept of death in the world on the one hand, and with God and His children on the other, as was previously made clear in (v. 25).

"Believest thou this?": the same question Christ asked the man born blind (ch. 9:35). And Christ affirmed, again and again, that faith in the person of the Savior is the basis of salvation, healing and gifts, the most important of which is the resurrection and not dying.
The declaration of Martha's faith comes here as a counterpart to Peter's declaration in (Mt 16:16) that Christ is the incarnate Son, who comes into the world for its salvation.

And St. John Chrysostom comments that Martha, like Peter, could not rise by herself to this level of declaration, but the Holy Spirit declared it through the tongue of Martha, as He declared it through the tongue of Peter. But the certain faith in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, as the Son of God the Savior, was completed after the Resurrection, and was revealed after the descent of the Holy Spirit on the disciples.

"Called Mary her sister secretly": that is, Martha returned to the house and informed her sister of Christ's arrival. And the word "secretly," perhaps she did not want to disturb the mourners. In another opinion, she feared that there might be enemies of Christ among the mourners to whom she did not wish to announce His coming. As for Mary, when she heard, her response was swift. And this is what we all need, that our response be swift to the calls of Christ to us, for we often err by postponing the response, and many opportunities of enjoying the meeting with the person of the beloved Christ are lost.

Christ did not enter the village or the house of Lazarus, for His aim was clear, which was the raising of Lazarus, and not consolation for his death. And Mary's going out with Martha from the house was noticeable to the Jews and the mourners, so they in turn rose up, following them, supposing they were going to the tomb, like the custom of many in weeping at tombs. And perhaps this was a divine arrangement, that the mourners should go out behind them, so that they might witness this unique miracle. And when Mary met Christ, she spoke like what Martha had said before (v. 21). But her worship at His feet is evidence of her great honor to the person of Christ, and also of her being crushed with grief at His not being there before her brother's death.

The sight of Mary's weeping and of the mourners gathered with her was an extremely moving sight, especially as it touched a person close to the heart of Christ. And since Christ was perfect God, able to raise Lazarus, He was also perfect man, bearing within Him all the tender feelings. And the expression "groaned in the spirit" means in Greek that He was not pleased or at ease. And the word "was troubled" also means in Greek a shuddering.

And it is a picture that clarifies the meaning of Christ's feeling for us, for He is tender of heart, He feels the pains of His children, He suffers and is distressed and shares their sorrows (Isa 63:9). And this in itself gives consolation to everyone who is in trial or distress.

And perhaps we also learn from this situation the positive Christian sharing with those who are in distress or deep sorrow, "weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15), and not to belittle or make light of people's feelings when they weep, but our weeping too is not wrong, as long as it does not exceed the limits of our faith and our hope of resurrection after death. For the wrong sorrow, against which God warns us, is the sorrow of those who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13).
"Jesus wept": it came as an expression of all that surged in His heart, and toward His feelings.

And perhaps we remember the words with which the Church prays in the Litany of the Sick: "Hope of those who have no hope, helper of those who have no helper, comfort of the fainthearted, harbor of those in the storm."

St. John continues to describe the scene for us, and relates the comments of the crowd. For some, when they saw the tears of the Lord Jesus, were moved by the degree of the Lord's love for the person of Lazarus. And others, whose words carried doubt about Christ's power, meaning that if what they had heard about His opening the eyes of a blind man was true, was He not able also to rescue and heal His friend, all the more?!

"Jesus therefore again groaning in himself": He felt uneasy, as a result of the surrounding atmosphere in general, and because of His approach to the place of the tomb, and also the talk of the Jews in (vv. 36, 37). And the tomb was a cave in the rock, as was the custom of people in burying their dead, either in natural or hewn caves, and they would close them afterward with a stone.

"Take ye away the stone": could not He who was able to raise the dead by a word also move the stone?! But this is God's way, who allows man to take part in the work. What is within man's power, God does not do. And the involving of man happened also in the filling of the waterpots with water at the wedding in Cana of Galilee (ch. 2:7), and also in the gathering of the baskets in the miracle of feeding the crowds (Mt 15:37; Mk 8:8).

And God's involving of man makes him a witness of God's work and plans. And it is an advantage enjoyed by whoever works in the field of the Lord's service, for he sees His works up close, and takes part in them. We also learn that, although salvation is a divine work in the first place, man also has a role in this salvation by his works, and by sharing with the saving grace of God through his striving.
"He hath been dead four days": that is, the impossibility of resurrection after decomposition and decay. And what is the use of taking away the stone except to stir up needless sorrows?

As for the spiritual meaning, the talk here is about the person who has died in sin, until his will has decomposed before it, and the works of the lusts of the flesh have become stinking; yet even this person, whom everyone supposes has no resurrection, has a resurrection through repentance, which turns the decay and stench of sin into precious perfume.

In (v. 4), the Lord indicates that the illness of Lazarus is not unto death, but for the glory of God. And here, the Lord Christ declares, with power, this glory, or at least one form of the glory of God, in absolute power, and the Son's victory over death, as an introduction to His own resurrection. And as for the expression "if thou wouldest believe," Christ links the beholding of glory to the condition of faith. For without faith, it is impossible to please Him. Therefore St. Matthew says: "And he did not many mighty works there (Nazareth) because of their unbelief" (Mt 13:58).

They took away the stone, with feelings of curiosity overcoming them over what was about to take place; the wavering of feelings here between doubt and certainty among the people is, we might say, natural, with the absence of the final declaration of Christ's divinity, and the presence of believing supporters and opponents in the surrounding crowd. After that Christ turns to speak with God the Father, and the purpose of this prayer, or audible speech, is "that they may believe that thou hast sent me." For Christ wants to use this unique event to declare what has been declared many times in the Gospel of John, that He is from the Father and in the Father, and the will is one between them, and to answer those who said earlier that He performed His miracles by Beelzebub (Mt 12:24; Mk 3:22; Lk 11:15). So here, He declares that the foundation is God and His will working in His Son.

And there is another purpose for us, which is that Christ teaches us the principle of constant prayer, especially before undertaking any work. And Christ also presents in His prayer the element of thanksgiving, with which the Church always teaches us to begin all our prayers.

"Thou hast heard me... thou hearest me always": this saying highlights the constant and continual agreement between the Son's request and the Father's response, for the Son's first work is the petition on behalf of His creation, through His shed blood, and the Father, who is one with the Son in will and essence, always accepts His petition. And Christ affirms this meaning in His discourse with His disciples: "Whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it" (ch. 14:13, 14).

"He cried with a loud voice": Christ's voice came out great and resounding, shaking the foundations of Hades, and commanding it to open its gates for the release of Lazarus' spirit from it, and defeating death that lay upon all mankind. And He commanded Lazarus to rise, and did not command him to rise in the name of the Father, to show that what the Father does, the Son also does with the same power and authority.

How great, one wonders, must have been the astonishment and bewilderment of those present before this dead man rising, after decay and decomposition lasting "four days"?! Yet Christ intervenes with His voice once more to rouse the crowd from its bewilderment, and commands some of them to loose him and let him go.

And as Christ had given man a role in taking away the stone, so here He also entrusts the soul raised from the death of sin to the care of the Church, priests and servants. For He has done His atoning work with it, and granted it forgiveness of sins and resurrection, but He left part of the work to the Church, which continues in its shepherding the completion of the work of the healing Physician. For when He raised the girl, He commanded that something be given her to eat (Lk 8:55). And Christ has deposited all His spiritual food in His Church, so whoever repents and does not partake continually of the food of life dies forever (ch. 6:53).

The situation remains as it is between those who accept the work of God and believe in it, and those who watch and deny. And this is what Christ said in the Gospel of our teacher Luke: "Neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead" (Lk 16:31). For the first group, the resurrection of Lazarus ran like a current through their bodies, and their faith in Christ grew great. But the others, their earthly attachment and their fear for their interests stood as a barrier that prevented their believing in this great event.
O my God, open my sight and my heart to see Your works, and do not let my mind or the desires of my heart be an obstacle that lessens my faith in all Your works.

The aim of the priests and Pharisees was clear, to be rid of the person of the Lord Jesus, who drew everyone to Him, and because of whom their fame and their power over the people had receded. Therefore, and because of the power of this miracle, they gathered a council with the intention already set to be rid of Christ (see ch. 5:18; 7:1, 25, 30, 44; 8:40, 59; 10:31-33, 39).

And they had nothing before them but to formulate the reasons that would support their decision, and justify it before themselves and before the people.
