So their minds hit upon a very flimsy political reason, which was that the crowds' following Christ would provoke the Romans and stir up disturbances, and the end would be the extermination of the Jewish nation. However, what condemns them most is their own admission that the Lord was performing many signs. And instead of this leading them to believe in Him, they sought to kill Him. And perhaps the sin of justifying judgments and actions is one we also fall into, as the priests and Pharisees did, and we care about what numbs our consciences and improves our image before people, forgetting God the true Judge, who searches the hearts and thoughts of all mankind... Blessed are those who cared to justify their conscience before God alone... "Blessed is he whom his conscience hath not condemned, and who is not fallen from his hope" (Sir 14:2).
Caiaphas was high priest, and was a relative by blood of Annas, the former high priest.
And the length of Caiaphas' tenure as high priest was 11 years, in which he was contemporary with all the events of the Lord Christ, and he was known in Jewish history as ignorant and hard of heart.

"Ye know nothing at all": thus Caiaphas began his speech, sheltering in his high office in the eyes of the rest, and as a suggestive introduction that what he would say was God's opinion, because the Law is sought from the mouth of the priest. So he came forward, as a man of religion and politics, offering what would set consciences at ease: "that it is expedient that one man (even if he is righteous) should die for the people." And what Caiaphas offered here was the formula that everyone was looking for in order to set their consciences at ease.

Caiaphas was not truly a prophet, but God put on his tongue what points to God's purpose and prior appointment, for God used him here to announce the course of events. As for what came in (v. 52), which is dying for the rest of the world to gather the children of God, this is outside Caiaphas' speech, and is a digression by St. John, by which he completes the declaration of God's purpose that Christ's death was not for the redemption of the Jewish nation only, but for the redemption of the whole world; and this is what came on the tongue of Christ Himself in (ch. 10:16) "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring."
This was the end of the session of the priests and Pharisees, for the decision had become clear, and what remained was to consult on how to carry it out and seize Christ.

The session ended, the news spread, and many learned of the decision of the secret council. And since Christ's hour had not yet come, and He is the only One who knows its time, the Lord preferred wisdom to declaring Himself, so He went away from the place of the inflamed events, and went to the city of Ephraim, a city now known as "al-Taybeh," about 20 km east of Jerusalem and the regions of the wilderness of the Jordan.

St. John begins here to bring us to the last section of his Gospel, for he prepares the reader for the first scene of the last Passover, with the Jews streaming from all parts of Judea to Jerusalem, days before the Passover itself, so that they might prepare for the Passover by offering purification sacrifices, because the Law forbade the defiled to touch the Passover lamb or eat it, so purification was necessary, especially for everyone who had become defiled.

My beloved brother... the Jews were careful to obey God by the necessity of purification before approaching the Passover lamb, which is a symbol of the true sacrifice of Christ... So what of people among us who approach the Body of our true God, and partake of it, without also being purified by true spiritual repentance, and by the practice of the sacrament of confession, in which they receive absolution, forgiveness and purification, not by water or by the sprinkling of an animal's blood, but by the Holy Spirit, God the Life-giver and Purifier?!

In these two verses there are two groups seeking the Lord Jesus, although their intentions and purposes differ; the first group: the simple people, who yearned to see this righteous One who had done all these signs, especially the sign of the raising of Lazarus from the dead. The second group: its motive was to lie in wait in order to seize Him, as a prelude to trying Him and killing Him. And this verse clarifies the verdict on which the council settled in (v. 53). The pouring of the perfume; Christ's entry into Jerusalem; Christ's discourse about His redemption and His judgment

The celebration of the Jewish Passover was on the 14th of Nisan (April), and therefore Christ's arrival at Bethany (house of affliction) was on the Friday after sunset, which is reckoned as the Sabbath. The supper feast was in the house of Simon the leper, whom the Lord Jesus had healed (Mt 26:6; Mk 14:3). And St. John mentioned the presence of Lazarus at this feast, as an affirmation of his resurrection, and also his sister Martha, who came to help and serve at this supper.

As for Mary, the sister of Martha, she brought a flask of perfume of a mina, which is the Roman pound, and is equivalent to about a third of a kilogram or a third of a liter. Spikenard is among the costly perfumes mentioned in the Song of Songs, and it was a source of pride for whoever owned it because of its quality and high price. It was common in honoring the great to pour a little perfume on the head. But what Mary did surpassed many, for she used the most costly perfume of all, and was not content with the head only, but also the feet of the Lord, which shows her love and her gratitude for what the Lord Jesus had done in raising her brother, and she also showed humility by wiping His feet with her hair. And the house's being filled with the fragrance is evidence of the quality of this kind of perfume, and also of the abundance of the quantity Mary used.

Beloved, what Mary offered was not perfume, but a loving and humble heart; and God does not accept an offering from a person if it is empty of love and humility (1 Cor 13). Therefore, He rejected the prayer of the Pharisee, and accepted the prayer of the tax collector. For God, in His riches, does not need our offerings at all. But in His love for us, He also rejoices in our love. So take care, beloved, before you offer time or anything to God, that you offer a loving heart and a humble mind, so that God may accept what you offer.

In (Mt 26:8, 9; Mk 14:4, 5), the Evangelists mentioned that some objection occurred to Mary's action. But John makes clear that the instigator of this objection was Judas, and makes clear the cause of his objection, revealing the real reason, which is that he was the thief of the money box and a betrayer of trust, and although he claimed otherwise, pretexting the service of the poor, he revealed nothing but his anger at the loss of this sum from under his hands. And on the other hand, St. John reveals to us that the value of this perfume was 300 denarii, and it was known that a laborer's wage for a day was one denarius (Mt 20:10), that is, what Mary offered was the wage of a man for about a year.

Christ did not intend any diminishing of the service of the poor (v. 8), but He said this to answer the objector, whose intentions He knew well on the one hand, and so as not to belittle the value of the work of love offered by Mary to His person on the other. Therefore, we find that the Lord began His words by saying "Let her alone," in the plural form, that is, the objection that Judas expressed was agreed with by most of those sitting. And the phrase "against the day of my burying" was a prophetic reference to the coming events, although those present did not understand it. And some see that Christ is pointing out that the journey of death had actually begun with His visit to Bethany, and His last ascent to Jerusalem.

Lazarus, raised from the dead, became the strongest evidence that the Lord Jesus is the expected Christ. Therefore, St. John points out that this living evidence was the reason for many Jews coming to Bethany, to see and behold this one raised from the dead. And John also makes clear the extent of the evil to which the chief priests had come in that they wanted to kill an innocent man, Lazarus, to be rid of this conclusive proof, instead of believing and having faith in the person of Christ the Savior.

O my God, can the evil heart to this extent overturn the truths, and be led along behind its hatreds?! I beg You, Lord, keep far from us and from all Your people all the wars of the evil one, which toy with minds and hearts, making us blind unjust judges.
(2) The entry of Christ into Jerusalem (vv. 12-19):

12- On the next day much people that were come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, 13- Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, "Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord."

14- And Jesus, when he had found a young ass, sat thereon; as it is written, 15- "Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt." 16- These things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things unto him. 17- The people therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of his grave, and raised him from the dead, bare record. 18- For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle. 19- The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, "Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him."
The celebration of the reception can be reviewed with (Mt 21:1-11; Mk 11:1-11).

"The next day": it is the day of Sunday, and the coming of Christ had become known to the crowds, who were the Jews of Jerusalem, Galilee and beyond the Jordan, without doubt, and it was information whose source was everyone who attended or passed on the news at Simon's feast in the house at Bethany.

"Branches of palm trees": it was the custom for the common people to receive leaders victorious in wars with palm branches, as an expression of their joy and exultation at salvation and victory. And this great festal procession had the effect of hastening the events of the cross, because of the pain it caused to the chief priests and Pharisees.

"Hosanna" means "save us." But this does not necessarily mean the crowd's faith that the Lord Jesus is the Redeemer Christ, but perhaps some saw in Him a teacher and prophet worthy of honor, and others believed He was a political savior who would free the Jewish nation from the Romans.

St. John did not concentrate on the details of obtaining the colt as the other Evangelists mentioned it, but was content with the general depiction of the scene of Christ's entry into Jerusalem. He also refers in (v. 15) to the prophecy concerning Christ's riding the colt in (Zech 9:9) without detailing it, unlike St. Matthew in (21:5), because St. John concentrates more on the saving, theological side of the events, and not the historical. As for St. Matthew, his Gospel was directed to the Jewish nation, so he had to elaborate, and link more with the prophecies of the Old Testament that prophesy about the person of Christ, to prove His identity.

The meaning is that at the time of Christ's entry into Jerusalem and His riding the colt, it was not in the disciples' minds that this was the same scene that Zechariah had seen and prophesied 500 years before. But when Jesus was glorified, they understood its meaning after His resurrection and ascension, and it also means after the descent of the Holy Spirit on the disciples, by whose descent the eyes of their hearts were opened, so they discovered and linked all the prophecies of the Old Testament with the events of Christ's life on earth, and His saving work.

St. John makes clear the strongest reason for the joy of the crowds and their thronging to receive the Lord Jesus, which was the crowds' testimony and affirmation that He had raised Lazarus from the tomb. And on the other hand, he brings us to what was going on in the hearts and minds of the Pharisees of hatred, as they provoked one another to the necessity of acting to confront that One whom everyone had gone after. And instead of making sure and following the truth, their fear of losing their standing as teachers with a position among the people was their greatest concern.

What is meant here by the Greeks is not the Gentile idol worshippers, but they were either Gentile proselytes to Judaism, or Jews who had lived for a long time in the land of Greece, and had gone up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices in the Temple, and to celebrate the Passover. And we understand that what they had heard about the person of the Lord Jesus and His miracles and teachings was the reason for their seeking Him until they found one of His disciples, who was Philip, who in turn informed Andrew, and both went to Christ to inform Him of the Greeks' desire.

Christ's answer here was to the two disciples, and also to the Greeks and the listening crowd, and was the beginning of the prediction of the nearness of the salvation that Christ offers. And since their thoughts were confined to the kingdom and earthly glory, Christ began His discourse with what was in their minds, in order to raise them to spiritual understanding. And the expression "that the Son of man should be glorified" means the declaration of His first heavenly glory, which was hidden by the Incarnation. And the way this glory is declared is the cross, then the Resurrection, then the Ascension.

This verse is a clarification of the way the Son of Man is glorified, so the Lord Christ used here the parable of the grain of wheat, which points to Him in His Incarnation, for all the glory and value of this grain is in its being buried in the soil and being enveloped by the death of the earth, so what people see as the death of the grain of wheat is the source of life itself, since it will rise and live from its death. And when it rises, it is a source of satisfaction and life for all who feed on it. And this is what Christ wanted to make clear to the crowds, by the efficacy of His death and His granting salvation to everyone who accepts His redemption on the cross, and eats His Body in Communion.

After Christ spoke about Himself, He directs a general spiritual teaching, which is considered one of the laws of the Christian life, for every rise to a higher spiritual level requires a loss in material things, which are the lesser, for eternal life with all its glory and splendor requires sacrificing everything that hinders reaching it. So if the body, or the various lusts of the soul, bind a person to the world and make him lose heaven, then the person must resist, and even sacrifice anything, even his life itself, for the permanent and eternal inheritance; and this is what the Lord Christ meant by the word "loseth it." And this faith is what made our fathers the holy martyrs go forward to death with utmost courage and indifference to the might of rulers; for whoever places eternal life before his eyes fears nothing.

That is, whoever wants to be a true Christian, and a disciple and servant of Christ's commandment, must follow his Lord and Teacher in all that He did. So if the Lord gave Himself and put Himself to death for the redemption of others, then the faithful servant must imitate Him. And Christ also linked that to the reward, which is the permanent presence of the faithful Christian in the bosom of his Lord, and the honoring of him by the heavenly Father. And we do not think there is any language or conception that brings near to us the meaning of this eternal honor, unlimited by time or size, except trust in all that the Lord Christ says, that whatever a man leaves here, or bears for the sake of Christ, has this reward and this honor. (4) Christ speaks about His death and its effects (vv. 27-36):

27- Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour. 28- Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again." 29- The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it thundered: others said, "An angel spake to him." 30- Jesus answered and said, "This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes. 31- Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out. 32- And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." 33- This he said, signifying what death he should die. 34- The people answered him, "We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou, The Son of man must be lifted up? who is this Son of man?" 35- Then Jesus said unto them, "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth. 36- While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light." These things spake Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.

What is meant by the soul here is the center of emotional feelings. Christ knows the hour of His crucifixion and death and its nearness, but as a perfect man, He expresses His human feelings by being troubled, for He is between two important matters: a matter that the ordinary human soul rejects, which is the death to which He will submit in order to accomplish our redemption, and then conquer it by His resurrection to accomplish our salvation, and what the righteous spirit, subject to the heavenly Father in His plan, wills. Therefore, the second part of the verse was "What shall I say... save me from this hour?" as though the spirit knows, and answers and strengthens the soul against its emotion, affirming that for the sake of this hour, on which all mankind depends, Christ came.

St. Chrysostom and Augustine say that the will of the Son is the glorification of the name of the Father, and the way is death and suffering and the redemption of perishing mankind, and leading them to heaven, so that they glorify the name of the Father on earth, and then in heaven, with eternal glorification, and the Father replies to the Son: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again," and its meaning is that through the life of Christ and His repeated witness about the Father, and His teachings about the mysterious relationship between them, and His performing miracles, the Son glorified the Father in this way, and the Father glorified His only-begotten Son by bearing witness to Him also. For the Father declared the glory of the Son:
First: at the Baptism (Mt 3:17).
Second: at the Transfiguration (Mt 17:5).
Third: in this verse, "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again."
For the glory between the Father and the Son is one and mutual glory (ch. 13:31, 32; 14:13).
"And will glorify it again": it means Christ's ascension into heaven.

As for the crowd, when they heard this voice, some believed, because of the surprise and the unexpectedness, that it was the sound of thunder; while others, who distinguished the words, thought it was the voice of an angel from heaven.

Christ answered those who thought that an angel was speaking to Him, saying that this voice is for you, that you may believe, for I have no need of it, and I do not doubt the glory of my Father's name or my glory, but it is to remove your doubts toward me.

"The judgment of this world": it is not the last judgment, but the judgment of the rejection of Christ, and the judgment of the pagan world, and the judgment of the kingdom of Satan, who held the reins of affairs in the world, so it is the judgment of declaring the iniquity of the whole world.

"Cast out": that is, as a result of the first judgment, Satan is bound in his authority over the world, by the crucifixion of Christ, and cast out; and this is what St. Paul explained about Christ's work on the cross toward Satan: "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:15).
So Satan has no authority over the children of God who believe in His name and act upon His commandments.
"If I be lifted up from the earth": by the cross, hung upon it, I draw all to myself and to the heights.

For man without Christ is shackled with the chains of sin and the material life, but with Christ, and in the cross alone, this Crucified One draws all the victims of the evil prince of the world, to take us into His bosom and to His chest upward, that we may be freed from everything that is from below, and enjoy the life with Him that begins here and does not end there.

So would that all of us, with firm desire, stretched out our hands to our Christ, our sacrifice, and met with Him at His altar, to take our strength from Him. And then we shall be able to tread the world and Satan under our feet.

The crowd faced a difficulty, which was Christ's reference to His death, hung on the cross, on the one hand, and what they had learned from the Law, that the kingdom of Christ is an eternal earthly kingdom (Dan 7:14; Ps 110:4; Isa 9:7), on the other, and the problem is in the mistaken understanding. All the prophecies speak of the eternal spiritual Kingdom of Christ, and not the temporal one. And this is the reason for His saying to Pilate afterward: "My kingdom is not of this world" (ch. 18:36). "Who is this Son of man?": a question of astonishment! For Christ used this expression of Himself repeatedly, and it is the same expression that Daniel used in his prophecy to describe Christ (Dan 7:13). So what do you mean by this usage?! Are you the eternal Christ, or are you an ordinary man liable to death?

Christ answered with an indirect answer, pointing to the nearness of His death, describing Himself as the light, which He had said before in (ch. 8:12). And He also urges them to seize the opportunity in holding fast to this light, lest the darkness overtake them through their rejection of this light.

And the one who walks in darkness is a lost man who has lost the way and the goal, and this is the case even now for everyone who is far from Christ and His Church. For outside the Church, which is the ship of salvation, there is nothing but the material and intellectual whirlpools of the world, which swallow a person far from the voice of Christ, so he drowns and his spirit is suffocated, while he supposes that he knows the right way and is walking in it. And the result, sadly, is the loss of the salvation of his soul.

Christ still urges them to believe in Him, and to make use of the opportunity of His being with them, even if it is short. And He adds also that whoever follows Him in His way, and obeys His commandments, becomes a child of light, that is, bearing the characteristics of the true light, reflecting this light to all around him.

So people see in the Christian man righteousness, purity, faithfulness and the rest of the virtues. Are we so? "And departed, and did hide himself from them": it indicates the end of the discourse, and His withdrawing by Himself away from the crowds, as came in (ch. 8:59). And the Lord Jesus was accustomed, during His life on earth, to these spiritual retreats.

entries.section: (5) The reasons for the Jews' unbelief

paragraphs.text: "So many": St. John makes clear the abundance, multiplicity and variety of the miracles that the Lord Jesus performed. And yet most of the Jews did not believe, to make clear the hardness of their hearts. And this expression also indicates astonishment and amazement at the reaction of the Jews to all that the Lord had done.

entries.section: (5) The reasons for the Jews' unbelief

paragraphs.text: St. John removes from us the astonishment and amazement at the Jews' stance toward Christ, and says to us: had not Isaiah said before that they refused to believe his prophecies, and refused also the arm of the Lord stretched out for salvation? Their present stance in rejecting Christ is no different from their stance in the time of Isaiah in rejecting God and His redemption of His people (Isa 53:1). And St. John also presents in (v. 40) a new prophecy that Isaiah prophesied, which also makes clear the cause of their rejection of Christ.

entries.section: (5) The reasons for the Jews' unbelief

paragraphs.text: This prophecy is taken from (Isa 6:9, 10), and the Gospels transmitted it with some adaptation (Mt 13:13-15; Mk 4:12; Lk 8:10), and what is meant is not that God is the cause of the hardness of their hearts, but their many murmurings and their rejection of God and not hearing Him are what blinded their eyes and hearts to the works of God in the time of Isaiah, and the miracles and teachings of Christ in His time. Therefore, the responsibility for the rejection falls on the Jews, stiffnecked and hard of heart, after God had exhausted every attempt with them.

entries.section: (5) The reasons for the Jews' unbelief

paragraphs.text: "Saw his glory": what is meant is the glory of Christ, and the talk returns to the vision of Isaiah (6), in which he saw the glory of God and around Him the cherubim and seraphim crying: "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory" (v. 3). And since the Holy Bible testifies that no one has seen the Father (ch. 1:18), therefore the One whom Isaiah saw is God the Son, that is, Christ.

entries.section: (5) The reasons for the Jews' unbelief

paragraphs.text: St. John returns and makes clear that every rule has an exception. For if most of the Jews did not believe in Christ, there were also those who believed in Him from among the council of seventy, which is the highest Jewish council, and its members were called the rulers, and examples of those who believed are Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, whose faith appeared after the events of the crucifixion. But because of fear of the Pharisees and their religious and social power, no one was able to declare his faith (see ch. 7:3; 9:22; 19:38; 20:19).

And St. John also makes clear a reason that makes many deny their faith, or at least not declare it, which is their desire to preserve people's love and praise for them, even if this be at the expense of God. So do not descend, my brother, to these relationships or bargains, out of love for a position or honor, and remember the saying of Peter and the Apostles that "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), whatever the temptation, or whatever the threat.

entries.section: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: "Jesus cried": that was in another place, but on the same day. And what the Lord would say in these verses came as a summary of what He had said in previous verses, especially (ch. 5; 7; 8; 10), and its summary is His oneness with the Father who sent Him, for faith in the Son is faith in the Father, and denial of one is denial of the other. And Christ adds that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, because the two are one in divinity (ch. 14:9), and this is strong evidence of equality; for who of mankind, or of the greatest prophets of the Jews, or of the archangels, dares to declare that he is the visible image of the Father, other than Christ, to Him be glory? Because He is: the imprint of the Father's essence, as St. Paul describes Him in the Epistle to the Hebrews (3).

entries.section: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: This is what Christ had already declared in (ch. 8:12) (see the commentary). We can also summarize the saying in that Christ is the only light of the world, and apart from Him there is nothing but destructive darkness and the ignorance of error. And the light of Christ is a light of experience in the life of all His holy children, for talking about the light of Christ is one thing and living within it is another.

entries.section: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: "I came not to judge the world": (see ch. 8:15) the purpose of my Incarnation now is not punishment or judgment, but the salvation of the world, on condition of faith in me and acting upon my commandments; for the judgment of mankind is connected with the Second Coming of the Lord Christ.

entries.section: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: But those who reject my words, or faith in me, will have a great judgment. And every word and teaching and work that I performed and they did not accept will be a witness against them in their condemnation.

And this makes clear to all of us that divine judgment is not by partiality or for chosen ones to the exclusion of others, but has a standard, which is faith in the words of Christ and acting upon them as far as possible, in a life of spiritual striving that knows no weariness.

entries.section: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: (See the explanation of 5:30; 7:16-18) For the Father is the source of everything, and the Son is the means of His declaration and communication, and the two are one in essence and equal.

entries.section: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

paragraphs.text: "And I know": and Christ's knowledge here surpasses all human knowledge. Therefore, what He declares is all the truth, that is, the way to reach eternity is acting upon the commandment and living by it. For theoretical faith does not save its possessor, and what is its use if it is not turned into a life lived.

And these words are for all of us, for Christianity is not a set of obligations, but the obedience of the love of God in His commandment, and whoever endures the toil of carrying out the commandment, Christ gives him the experience of the pledge of eternal life, here on earth, according to the riches of the work of His grace in us.
The washing of the feet; the foretelling of Judas' betrayal; Peter's denial

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: This refers to Thursday evening, when the Lord knew, by His divinity, that the time of His betrayal had come. Note the contrast with what St. John mentioned earlier, and repeatedly: every time the Jews tried to seize Jesus they did not succeed, although He was in their midst, because His hour had not yet come. Here, however, he declares to us that Christ knew the appointed time, and prepares us for the last stage of Christ's life on earth. He also used the word "departure" instead of the word "death," as a new theological expression that clarifies the nature of bodily death in the understanding of the children of God: it is a passing from one life to another life. This is what the Church uses in her prayers, when she says: "There is no death for Your servants, but a departure." St. John concludes his words by revealing the secret behind what Christ was about to undertake of suffering, torment and crucifixion: His eternal and boundless love for His creation, which He was about to redeem.

We may note that St. John is the one who spoke most about divine love, as though he were the disciple who knew the heart of Christ best. This is true, for his gentle nature made him cling more closely to the Lord Jesus, so he was more aware of His love and better able to express it.
The invitation is to all of us, to enjoy this overflowing love, which is available to each one of us if he wishes.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: That is, at the time of the Jewish Passover supper, and before it was completed.

"The devil having now put": this shows us the role of Satan in provoking and inciting the carrying out of evil; but he chose the weak soul that would respond to his counsel. He tries with everyone, but the human will is responsible for falling or for resisting. Perhaps St. John pictures for us that one table held both the heart of God, who loves to the end, and the heart of the wicked man who was about to betray Him.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: St. John repeats the word "knowing" as clear and strong indications of the divinity of Christ. The expression "the Father had given all things into His hands" has two meanings:
The first: the complete authority of Christ, which is entirely heavenly, the authority of the Father.
The second: a preparation for what the God was about to do.
For with these very two hands, into which all the authority of the Father was given, the Lord was going to bend down and wash the feet of the disciples.
"He was come from God": that is, by His incarnation, in which He emptied Himself and hid His glory. But His coming forth does not mean that He left Him, for He is united with Him in divinity.

"And went to God": that is, the return to His glory in the bosom of the Father. But He will not leave us either, because of His work and care for us, even though He will be hidden from our eyes in His body.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: He rose after supper was prepared and before beginning to eat it, took the form of a servant ready for a lowly task, humbly laid aside His garments and girded Himself with a towel, in order to undertake a work that no man could understand or mind comprehend ... that is, to begin to wash the feet of His disciples, a work that the ordinary human soul rejects. The dust on the feet is a symbol of sins, and washing them with water points to Baptism and repentance, and this by the hand of Christ, which was to be crucified on the Cross and redeem man.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: Christ may have begun to wash the feet of the disciples, who were seized with amazement and made no comment, until He came to Peter; or He may have begun with Peter, as St. Augustine thought, and Peter expressed his astonishment and his rejection of the idea, voicing it in a question of protest: Do You, my righteous Lord, wash the feet of a sinner like me?! This reminds us of the attitude of the Baptist, when he held back from baptizing the Savior when He came to him. But Christ's answer, in both cases, contained insistence and decisiveness, not without gentleness, in order to accomplish His purpose. For what Christ wanted by the washing of the feet Peter did not understand at that time ... But what was it that he did not understand?

The first lesson: humility. If the Lord of the whole world, its Teacher, Creator and Redeemer, bent down to wash the filth of others in true humility, correcting the concept of authority in the minds of all people, how much more ought we to do likewise with others.

The second lesson: not condemning. Removing the filth means helping a person to be rid of sin, by our having a positive work with him, and not being content with pointing at his uncleanness, as the Jews did with the woman caught in adultery (ch. 8:1-11).

Because of the greatness of what the Lord Christ did with all humanity in the person of His disciples, the Church arranged in her prayers the rite of the Lakkan of Holy Thursday, by which she recalls all these lessons to our minds. The priest, or the bishop, or the Patriarch stands and girds himself with a towel, in imitation of his Lord, and begins to wash the feet of the deacons and the people, and the rest of the priests help him in the same work. So we remember what the Lord did for us, and we also understand that God appointed bishops and priests as shepherds and servants, first of all for the service of His people and their repentance.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: Although the virtue of Peter's humility and his shyness appeared in this refusal, it was misplaced, because he did not grasp the spiritual meaning. Therefore Christ made clear to Peter that what He was doing was not an optional work in which Peter had the right to accept or refuse, but that everything depended on it. For this washing is a symbol of the cleansing that comes by the blood of Christ, and whoever refuses has no part with Christ Himself; that is, there is no salvation outside the blood of Christ.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: Peter was taken aback by Christ's answer, and could only ask for even more, that the washing include his whole body, declaring that he did not want a single thing to separate him from Christ.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: "He that is washed": this means the washing of Baptism, built on faith in the power of the blood of Christ to cleanse from all sins. Whoever has been washed does not need to be washed again, that is, to repeat Baptism, but needs only to wash his feet ... This is also what the Church teaches her children: the sacrament of Baptism is not repeated, even if a person leaves the faith and returns to it again ... But the washing of the feet, that is, the sacrament of repentance and confession, a person needs always, for the feet are a symbol of the soul that lives in the world and moves about in it, and so becomes soiled with many sins, and is always in need of the washing of repentance.
The Lord Christ, by His foreknowledge, adds a hidden allusion to Judas, who would betray Him, since He declared all the disciples clean except one.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: "Know ye": without doubt, what the Lord had done was far beyond the disciples' imagining? And had it not been for the Lord's decisive word to Peter, they would not have allowed Him to wash their feet. So Christ used the form of a question as an introduction to a teaching discourse.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: This completes that introduction in establishing the truth that He is the true Lord and Teacher, who must be respected and honored.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: Here comes the essence of the teaching about what the Lord Jesus did. If the Lord and Teacher did this, how much more should the servant do for his brother ... If the servant does this for his brother, it is not counted to him as a boast, but is only an imitation of the greatest Teacher. And whoever among us considers himself a lord and teacher and not a servant, let him also bend down, overcome by Christ's love for him and His wonderful humility in washing the feet of all. The washing here is not literal, but carries in its meaning all the Christian virtues: endurance, self-giving and self-denial. And when Christ says: "ye also ought," this became an obligation for us and not a choice or a favor from us; that is, it is a commandment that must be carried out, but it requires of all of us self-emptying and true contrition.

entries.section: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

paragraphs.text: The Lord affirms once more that, since the servant is not greater than his lord, he must not be ashamed or disdain to do what the Lord did. The Lord Christ also declares the distinction between the one who sends and the one sent, in a clear reference to the work of ministry in His Church: He is the Sender who calls the servant to His service, so the servant must imitate the humility of Him who sent him in his ministry, bearing with those he serves and being patient with them.

Christ concludes His teaching here by clarifying the difference between a person's understanding and grasping something and his carrying it out in his life. For the reward and the crown here are counted, not to the one who knows the commandment from his youth (Mt 19:20), but to the one who strives against himself in order to live by it.

There is no exception for Judas from the sending, nor from the application to him of all the preceding words (v. 10). He adds that although the Lord chose Judas, for the call is to all, Judas chose betrayal by his own will. Christ points to a scriptural witness, which is what came in Psalm 41:9: "Mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me," in that what David said about the betrayal of Ahithophel is also a prophecy about Judas' betrayal of Christ. The meaning is that the one who shared with me in my eating and drinking was preparing to deal treacherously with me and entrap me ... and the direct meaning of "hath lifted up his heel against me" is: kicked me with his foot.

"Now I tell you": that is, so that you may not be offended in Me when the sufferings of the Cross begin with Judas' betraying Me, when I shall appear as a man with no strength and no power. Rather, then you will remember what I told you before, that on the one hand I am the Christ ... and on the other, that I prophesied that this would happen.

The talk here is about the sending of the disciples. Here Christ made the honor of the servant a part of His own honor, so that whoever receives the servant of Christ is as though he received the Father and the Son together. And whoever rejects the servant who is sent rejects the One who sent him, who is God Himself (see Mt 10:14; Mk 6:11; Lk 9:5).

"Troubled": this clearly indicates signs of unease on the face of Christ, as a result of His contemplating the betrayal of one of His loved ones, Judas, and the enormity of the hideousness of this sin, which made the holy nature of Christ shudder at its mere mention and at telling the disciples of it ... Christ confirmed His prophecy by saying: "Verily, verily," because He knew very well how hard it would be for the disciples to believe what He foretold, that one of them would betray Him.

Perhaps we may reflect here on what our daily sins do to the person of the Lord Jesus, or to the Holy Spirit who dwells in us ... How many times do we grieve Him every day?! And how many times do we please Him in all our life by true repentance and abandoning sin?

Astonishment, wonder and bewilderment seized all the disciples; indeed, the words of the Lord Christ were almost like a thunderbolt too incredible to believe, for even if betrayal were to come, it was far from their minds to imagine that one of them would be its source. This shows us the extent of Judas' cunning and hypocrisy, by which he deceived everyone. And when the bewilderment grew with no answer, Peter motioned to John, who was close to the bosom of Christ, to ask who it was!

"Whom Jesus loved": an expression St. John used to refer to himself, hiding his name out of humility, trusting that the reader would understand his intent. We must make clear that Christ's love had no partiality or distinction of one disciple from another; rather, according to how much a person strives to receive, Christ gives of His love. John was closer to Christ than the others, so he also enjoyed this love more than the others.
Truly, among the miracles of Christ's love for man is that everyone who loves Christ with true love feels that the Lord Christ is wholly his own possession ... Truly, how beautiful You are, O Lord.

St. John responded to the sign of Peter the Apostle and asked Christ, who instead of answering with the name of Judas used a sign, careful not to embarrass him among the disciples. And more wonderful still, the sign that Christ used, which was dipping a morsel in a dish containing a mixture of fruit juices blended with wine or vinegar and giving it to Judas, was used only as a symbol of honoring a dear guest, or the eldest son who is close to his father ... as though Christ were giving Judas a last opportunity, as one dear to Him and close to Him, as though He were saying to him: If only you would not commit this great error. But without interfering with his will.

"Satan entered into him": the conspiracy and the agreement with the chief priests had already been made (see v. 2), but the meaning of "Satan entered into him" is that Satan took firm hold of Judas' will, and he no longer had any hesitation in betraying the person of the Lord. The Lord, who searches the hearts and determines the times, knew this, and gave permission for Himself to be betrayed through the traitor, to confirm that He alone has the authority to lay down His life and to take it again.

Since Judas held the money box, the furthest the disciples' understanding of Christ's words to him reached at that time was that He was commissioning him to hasten to buy what was needed for the feast before the crowding, or to give something of the money for the service of the poor.

This teaches us not to forget the service of the poor and their needs out of our money, which is a gift of God, deposited with us in trust. So do not close your heart, beloved, to the needs of a brother of yours in Christ, in whose place you might well have been.
"Having received the sop": it was a morsel from the Passover supper, and not from the Lord's Supper and the Eucharist.

This is what our Church teaches: Judas, in whose heart evil had been kindled, rose in haste to carry out his conspiracy, and did not attend the table of the Lord's Supper with the rest of the disciples. Therefore the liturgical icon of the Lord's Supper in the Church depicts eleven disciples, and not twelve.
Here Christ begins a long discourse, which extends to the end of chapter seventeen.

"Now": that is, from the going out of Judas, the story of the glorification of the Son began. The glory meant here is the glory of His humility and of His love for mankind, in which He gave Himself even to death. It is the glory of the Son's obedience to the Father in the complete emptying of Himself. It is also the glory of the Cross, which the world does not understand, and it is a glory that precedes the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension, and the return to His true glory by sitting on His heavenly throne, which is temporarily hidden by His incarnation.

"God is glorified in Him": this means that the glory of the Son is bound to the glory of the Father. The Father is glorified by the Son, because the purpose and will of the Father are fulfilled in the redemption by the Son. And since the glory of the Father was accomplished through the Son, who continued to reveal the glory of the Father throughout His incarnation, and revealed it all the more at the time of His redemption, the Father also will reveal all the glory of the Son that belongs to Him and is hidden from the eyes of all; and this revelation begins quickly with the events of the Cross:
First: by the fulfillment in Him of all the prophecies, of which He was the subject and the hope.

Second: by the miraculous events, such as the darkness of the sky at the time of the crucifixion, the tearing of the veil of the Temple, and the coming out of many of the dead from their tombs. All of these are declarations of the glory of the Son, more than they are mere miraculous events.

"Little children": since the difficult time had come upon the disciples, Christ reveals His tender fatherly heart toward His disciples, and addresses them as "children," because of the sense in this address of the Son's reassurance at the presence and care of his father. Then He begins to refer to what is coming, and to the nearness of His separation from them, and that what He was about to go through He must pass through alone, and no one can share it with Him or follow Him in it.

Christ made love the mark that distinguishes His disciples, and everyone who follows Him among His flock, before the whole world, even without asking for a name or identity. People see the love of Christians, and so they know who they are and to whom they belong. But what is meant by calling it a new commandment, although God also commanded love in the Old Testament? What is new in the commandment of love is its dimension and depth, for it is no longer a commandment or an obligation, but a life that all Christians receive from a God who loved even unto death and gave Himself, who once bent down and washed feet, and had no rest in His body for the sake of the rest of those around Him. It is a new and unique model, which surpassed the level of love for the neighbor to the level of love for the enemy and the one who hates (Mt 5:44). It is a love that the ordinary natural man cannot reach, but only the Christian who abides in his God, and who has a living ecclesial communion through the sacraments of the Church, and especially partaking of the most honored Body and Blood of the Lord.

Peter's question about where Christ was going is an inquiry about what Christ Himself said in (v. 33), about His going to a place where no one can come. So Christ affirmed the same statement once more, showing that the first part, which concerns redemption and the way of suffering, Christ would pass through alone, and Peter, in spite of his love, could not share it or follow Christ in it. But after the Resurrection and the descent of the Holy Spirit, Peter and the rest of the disciples would follow Christ on a long road of preaching, evangelizing, endurance, and sufferings even to martyrdom. And finally, following Christ to heaven and all its glories.
Emotion and human zeal overcame Peter, so he spoke of what he did not understand, and claimed what he could not do and offer.

He did not understand that redemption, in the eternal purpose of God, could be accomplished by no one but Christ alone, and also that he could not live up to the courage that he expected in himself, and which he proclaimed with some pride: "Although all shall be offended, yet will not I" (Mk 14:29).

This teaches us not to claim for ourselves what we do not possess, and to present ourselves to the Lord Christ in humility, without boasting or false confidence in ourselves. For Christ works through the weak and the small, and resists those who are proud and great in their own eyes. And may we, my beloved brother, keep before our eyes the word of divine inspiration on the tongue of Paul the Apostle: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2 Cor 12:9).

Christ began His answer to Peter with a question of protest: "Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake?" as though He were asking him: Do you know what you are saying?! And to show him the great difference between what he spoke and what would come from him. Christ continues His discourse with the prophecy of Peter's denial of Him, and the setting of a sign by which Peter would remember his denial of Christ, which is the crowing of the cock.

Perhaps we learn, my friend, that without God we cannot do or offer anything. But by relying on Him, and on the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, we can become Peter, who afterward offered his life with joy for the sake of Christ.
Christ comforts His disciples and promises them the Holy Spirit

"Let not your heart be troubled": the discourse in the previous chapter was disturbing and frightening to the disciples, for it spoke of betrayal, death and denial, and because of all this their state of mind worsened.

Therefore Christ began to comfort and encourage them with kind words to remove their distress from them, and to offer them a remedy: faith in Him and in all that He had said, and that their faith in Him should be no less than their faith in God Himself. "Ye believe in God": here the Lord Christ gives the first beneficial remedy for anxiety and distress, which is offered to all of us and not only to the disciples. It is faith in God, that is, in Him, and in all His true promises that He promised us in the person of His disciples.
Faith in God, the powerful Ruler of all things who loves His children, is the first and most important remedy for anxiety; may we take refuge in Him in times of affliction and temptation.

Christ presents a bright side to His disciples: if He is parted from them for a while, it is for their sake and for ours, to prepare a place in heaven, where the glory is unseen. The words "many mansions" mean the infinite vastness of heaven, and also mean that there is one rank higher than another, as St. Paul indicated in (1 Cor 15:41). For if God, in His love, receives His believing children into His Kingdom, He also, in His justice, rewards each person according to his labor and striving.

My separation from you is not eternal, but I will come again, in My glory, and receive you unto Myself, and you will enjoy being with Me forever, after which there is no separation: "that where I am, there ye may be also."

This promise made the saints, in every generation, take no interest in this earthly life; rather, all their hearts were fixed on the bosom of Christ, for there is no feeling in the whole world that equals this spiritual feeling in its happiness.
"And whither I go ye know": what is meant is going to heaven, but passing through the way of the Cross.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: It seems that what the Lord Christ said in the preceding verses did not satisfy Thomas, the rational disciple, but perhaps increased his perplexity, so we find him in a state of inquiry. He admitted that he did not know the place, and consequently did not know the way to it, and he phrased his question in a form in which he included the disciples with him.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: As usual, the Lord Christ answers a limited question about time and place with a deep spiritual answer. He is the Way for everyone who is lost in the estrangement of the world and stumbling in his sins; and He is the Truth, that is, everything other than Him and outside faith in Him is falsehood; and He is the Life, so that whoever lives with Him on earth enjoys Him and is not troubled by the changes of the world, until he reaches Him in heaven, for He is eternal life, and "neither is there salvation in any other" (Acts 4:12). May we learn from Thomas to ask God and our guides in the Lord about everything we do not know, and God will reveal to us what is farther and deeper than our minds would have reached.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: Here Christ links the disciples' knowledge of Him with the knowledge of the Father Himself, for the two are one in essence, and seeing the Son in His authority, His miracles and His commandment is seeing the essence of God Himself. Because the discourse was difficult, Philip did not understand Christ's intent, especially the word "ye have seen him," so he asked to see the Father plainly, if that was within Christ's power, forgetting what Christ had declared earlier: "I and my Father are one" (ch. 10:30). So the answer of the Lord Christ comes as a reproach ... After all these years and miracles and works and parables, have you still not known Me, Philip? For "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father."
This verse is considered a direct and clear declaration, added to the earlier declarations about the divinity of Christ, and St. John was careful to record it.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ continues His talk with Philip with a question, in which He invites him to examine himself as to the extent of his faith in Him, after having reproached him in (v. 9); then He turns His words to the rest of the disciples, declaring clearly that He is in the Father and the Father in Him. Here Christ affirms His equality with the Father, and that all the works He does have the Father as their source. To bring this truth nearer to our minds, we say that the relationship between the Father and the Son is like the relationship between the mind and thought: thought has its source in the mind, and the essence of the mind is thought, so there is no mind without thought and no thought without mind.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: The discourse is still directed to the disciples, that they must believe that Christ is God, just as the Father is God. Because Christ knows that the time of the disciples' perfect faith had not yet come, He gives them proof of His oneness with the Father, which is the multitude of miracles and works that He did, which no one can do but God.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: A precious, valuable and very encouraging promise to the holy disciples, and after them to everyone who has sincere faith in the Lord Christ, that he will do the very works of Christ, but through Christ Himself; for we have no power in ourselves, but it is His power given to us by the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:8).

"Greater works than these shall he do": it is impossible for a creature to do works greater than his Creator. But what Christ means here is that spiritual miracles, such as satisfying souls with the word of God, are greater than satisfying them with bread and fish, and giving life to souls dead in their sins by calling them to repentance is better than raising the dead bodily. Therefore, beloved, do not belittle what Christ can do through us, His Church, for He has deposited in her all His power, not for boasting, but for the salvation of others and the glorification of His holy name.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: Here the Lord Christ presents the honor of His holy name, and the effectiveness and intercession of using this name in answering all who ask with faith ... The word "whatsoever" means the breadth of the circle of requests from the believing disciples, and the infinite power of using the name of Christ in answering. This is what made our Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, use the name of the Lord in all her prayers: she concludes the Lord's Prayer with the name of Christ Jesus our Lord, and repeats His holy name in all her praises and prayers.
3) The promise of the Holy Spirit (vv. 15-26):

15- If ye love me, keep my commandments. 16- And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; 17- Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. 18- I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.

19- Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also. 20- At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you. 21- He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him. 22- Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot, Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world? 23- Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him. 24- He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings: and the word which ye hear is not mine, but the Father's which sent me. 25- These things have I spoken unto you, being yet present with you.
26- But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: True love for Christ is not an emotional feeling, but obedience, commitment and action according to His commandments; perfect obedience and faith are the sign of love and its proof.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: "I will pray the Father": that is, after the completion of redemption and My ascension, as though the hypostasis of the Son hands over to the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit the care of the Church in her new covenant, which the Son began with His blood.

"Comforter": in Greek it means "comforter, helper, intercessor and advocate," and the Arabic translation has lost its meanings. These meanings give a quick glimpse of the work of the Holy Spirit in our lives, and in the Church in general.

"That he may abide with you for ever": that is, the words are not limited to the Church in the age of the Apostles only, but He is at work in her and in the life of her children until the end of the ages ... This verse is one of those in which the Holy Trinity meets: the Son asks, the Father answers, and the Holy Spirit is sent, because the will in the divine essence is one.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: "The Spirit of truth": God is absolute truth. Therefore, whoever has not been born of this Spirit in Baptism cannot receive Him, for the world is material and sensual and sunk in falsehood; therefore it does not receive God, who is Spirit and Truth, and does not know Him. But whoever knows the Holy Spirit and makes Him dwell in his heart is the one who enjoys the true knowledge of God. "With you ... in you": the Holy Spirit no longer merely surrounds the children of God, but dwells within them, and this is a gift that each one of us received in the anointing with the Holy Myron; and this is what St. Paul reminds us of when he says: "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" (1 Cor 6:19).

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: Since the hour of separation by death was near, Christ wanted to reassure His disciples that He would not leave them orphans after His death, but would come to them and they would see Him; this is, on the one hand, a direct reference to His appearing to His disciples for forty days after the Resurrection, and on the other hand, He speaks of the sending of the Holy Spirit and His permanent presence in them and with them, by which the person of Christ would always be revealed in them, by reminding them of all that He taught them and all that He commanded them. Consequently, they would not be orphans, so long as the Holy Spirit dwelt within them and with them.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: "At that day": it carries two meanings: either after the declaration of His Resurrection, or the day of the descent of the Holy Spirit. And the word "ye shall know" here means you will be certain without any doubt. For despite the many earlier declarations of His oneness with the Father, the speech was obscure and not understood. But the day would come of complete certainty and the completion of the incomplete knowledge, either through His talks with them during the 40 days after His resurrection from the dead, or through the Holy Spirit, who would teach them mysteries that cannot be uttered.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: This verse adds to what came in (v. 15) that there is a divine reward, which the hearts of the children of God who love Him and act by His commandments take hold of and enjoy, which is God's revealing Himself in their lives, so that they enjoy His presence and friendship more than others do; for God loves all people by calling them, but whoever acts by His commandments has another standing, for he sees God every day in his life.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: "Judas": he is Thaddeus, the brother of James the son of Alphaeus, and the writer of the Epistle of Jude. He did not understand the Lord's intent here, for he thought that Christ would manifest Himself to the disciples only, without others seeing Him. This is what made him ask in wonder ... So Christ answered him again with what He had said before about the connection of our love for God with our acting by His commandments, and added and made clearer the recompense for that: that He and His Father would have presence and permanent dwelling, by the Holy Spirit, in the hearts of His children who act by His commandments, and this is a gift that surpasses all the gifts the spiritual man could wish for; it is not hosting for a temporary visit, but residence, companionship, friendship and permanent presence. Does this not encourage us, my friend, to put aside our excuses and laziness, and to strive to bring the commandment of Christ into the field of practice and struggle in it, so that we may enjoy seeing the hand of God working in our lives with a power that is tangible and perceived? And Christ attributes the words He spoke to the Father, to make clear the divine authority in these words, and also to affirm that He is the only Son who has declared Him (ch. 1:18).

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: That is, as though He were depositing His words in trust in their hearts before His departure from the world.

entries.section: (2) I am the way ... I am in the Father

paragraphs.text: This is a return to what the Lord Christ began and spoke about concerning the Holy Spirit in (v. 16), and He makes clear His role with the disciples and the Church in all her generations ... He teaches us and guides us to the way of our salvation, and He is the One who always reminds us and brings to our minds all the words and teachings of the Lord Christ, and even urges us to carry them out and live by them in the midst of the world, and gives us the power needed for that.

Although the discourse here is directed to the disciples, it goes beyond them to the whole Church in every time and place. The inheritance of fathers to their children may be money or standing, but the inheritance of Christ and His gift is a peace that passes understanding and that the world does not understand, for the whole world cannot give any of this peace; and Christ's granting this peace as a gift from Him is a clear indication of His divinity, as Isaiah prophesied about Him: "And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (Isa 9:6).

The natural result of this peace is steadfastness of the heart and its fearlessness, whatever the terrors. Perhaps the most brilliant proof of this is the state of our fathers the martyrs at the time of their torments, for their peace and calm were bewildering and incomprehensible to those who were tormenting them.

"If ye loved me": ... that is, spiritual love and not emotional love, for emotion grieves at parting, but spiritual love goes beyond it, because it understands and is aware of the results of what happens after Christ's bodily separation from the disciples, such as: the preparation of the place (v. 2), the sending of the Holy Spirit (v. 16), and the permanent enjoyment with the Father and the Son, whether on earth (v. 23) or afterward in heaven (v. 3). Perhaps we also feel and understand this in our lives when one of our beloved saints departs to heaven: we miss him with human emotion, but in the Spirit we rejoice, since he has become an intercessor for us, asking on our behalf before the throne of grace, until we meet him there too.

"My Father is greater than I": ... not in nature, for the two are equal in essence. But He speaks of the glory of His divinity that was hidden during the journey of suffering and crucifixion, while the glory of the Father is not hidden, for the visible image of the Son in the coming days would be empty of all greatness in the human sense. Here St. Paul says of Christ: "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7), that is, He left aside showing His divine glory, in order to redeem mankind by His body. Since this verse is one of those that many heretics (dissenters and innovators) used to diminish the equality of the Son with the Father, here, beloved, is what Christ also said in the same Gospel on this matter:
1) "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (ch. 5:17).
2) "That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father" (ch. 5:23).
3) "I and my Father are one" (ch. 10:30).
4) "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (v. 9).
5) "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (v. 10).
6) "And all mine are thine, and thine are mine" (ch. 17:10).
7) "Thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee" (ch. 17:21).

That is, everything connected with the sufferings, the journey of the Cross and the hard times; so when they come, you will remember that I prophesied all this to you, and your faith will not faint but will be steadfast and increase.

Beloved, how much we need to remember the promises and words of the Lord Christ about His comforts, and His care for us in hard times. The more we have faith and hold fast to His presence, the more steadfastness and peace we receive in the midst of tribulations.

"Hereafter I will not talk much with you": that is, only a few hours remained for the disciples with Christ, the time of talking and teaching had passed, and only the time of redemption and the Cross remained.

"The prince of this world": this is the last war that Satan was about to wage ... the stirring up of the priests and the people, the carrying out of Judas' betrayal, and all the accompanying trials and conspiracies, and this is what Christ declared in (Lk 22:53): "this is your hour, and the power of darkness."
"And hath nothing in me": that is, Satan, with all his power, has no authority before the righteousness, greatness and authority of Christ.

And also, my beloved ... this same authority was given to the children of God. Satan is skilled at conspiracies and causes many outward wars, but he cannot triumph over any of the children of God, who alone have the authority to crush him, if they do not surrender to their passions and the evil desires of the world around them.

This verse is connected to the one before it: that although the prince of this world has nothing in Me, yet because I love the Father, I lay down My life according to His will for the salvation of the world.
Chapter fifteen: Christ likens Himself to the vine, and commands His disciples to love, and not to be disturbed by the world's opposition to Him and to them

Christ likens Himself to the vine that bears us, who are its branches, the members of His body, and He also makes clear the responsibility of God the Father in caring for the branches of this vine. Every person in Christ who has no good works is a dead branch, which the Father takes away. But the person who is alive in Christ, the Father tends and prunes and purifies from sins by teaching and embrace, and by rebuke and trials at times, so that he may ripen further in the fruit of his virtues and grow in holiness.
The words here are to the disciples as good branches, and Christ makes clear the reason for their cleanness, which is their hearing and receiving His word.
This applies to all of us, for reading the Holy Bible, and hearing the word of God and acting on it, give a person purity, peace and understanding.

God's role in caring for the branches does not cancel the role of the branch (the person) in the salvation of his soul, for the person is required to bear fruit, and he has no means for that except abiding in Christ, the Vine. Is it conceivable for a branch cut off from the vine to grow?! Christ is the root of our growth and progress, and without Him we can do nothing. The abiding that Christ speaks of here reminds us of what He said before in (ch. 6:56): "He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him." That is, true abiding in Christ is through His Body and Blood.
But whoever makes light of the grace of God and does not abide in it, his end, his punishment when the just judgment of God is revealed, is:
(1) Being taken away, that is, having no part in Christ.
(2) Being gathered with the rest of the wicked like the gathering of firewood.
(3) Being cast into the fire.

"If ye abide in me": through My Body and Blood, and all My commandments are fixed in your hearts and appear in your works, then your special gift is My immediate answer to everything you pray for. This is also what James the Apostle affirms, when he said: "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much" (Jas 5:16). And a natural result of abiding in Christ, and of God's answering the requests of His children, is that the fruit of the branches increases in service and in the salvation of the souls of those far away, so that all the glory, praise and laud return to the Father. As for the pride of the fruitful branches, it is in the title that Christ gives them, "My disciples."

Christ found no comparison to describe the degree of His love for His disciples, and for all of us, stronger than the degree of the Father's love for the Son, a love that no man can describe. In the face of this boundless love, Christ requires us to abide in His love for us. The only means to that is keeping the commandments and obeying them, as He also obeyed the will of the Father, accomplishing redemption for all mankind (see ch. 15:10, 14; 14:15, 21-23).

"These things have I spoken unto you": that is, My talk about abiding in Me and keeping My commandments, so that you may have lasting joy. Just as Christ gave us a peace that the world does not understand, so everyone who strives to keep the commandment receives a divine joy that none of the joys of the world equals in its perfection and fullness.

Here the Lord Christ repeats what He mentioned in (ch. 13:34), that the level of love among His children should be on the pattern of His love for us. For Christ, in His love, humbled Himself and washed our feet, bore our sins and died for us on the wood of the Cross; indeed, He also forgave His enemies.
And none of us can offer an example of this love unless:
(1) He humbles himself with contrition before the One crucified for us.
(2) He continually contemplates God's love and forgiveness toward us, so that we can love and forgive others. (3) He keeps the commandments and acts on them.

In (ch. 13:16; 12:26) the Lord Christ gave His disciples the title "servants and slaves." And this is true, for before Christ, to whom be glory, there is no one who may be called "lord." But here, after the talk about abiding in His person and obeying His commandment, Christ moves His disciples from the state of slaves, who do not know their master's purposes, to the status of beloved ones and sons, who know their master's intent. And this is not a right of ours, but a proof of God's boundless love for His own.
Here the Lord Christ makes clear that, by His grace, He is the one who takes the initiative in the salvation of man by choosing him, and by appointing His disciples to bring forth lasting fruit.

As for the Father's answering all that we ask in the name of Christ, and in the face of the work of Christ's grace, there is a responsibility on all of us: to bring forth fruit at the level of striving for the virtues on the one hand, and the fruit of calling others to share in the love of Christ and faith in Him on the other.

The Lord Christ concludes this part of His discourse, affirming what He said before in vv. 9, 12 and 15, about the love between Him and His disciples, and among one another; for love is the protective shield for what He will speak of in the following verses.
The Lord Christ moves the disciples, and the Church after them, to what they are expected to find in the world of rejection and persecution.

And He gives all of us comfort and encouragement, which is that the world rejected Christ Himself. If we always remember this truth, it gives us patience and endurance, and we regard it as something natural.

And Christ makes clear the reason for the world's hatred of the children of God: they are different from it in their thoughts, opinions and spirituality, and therefore the people of the world, with their materialism and lusts, hate them; it is natural for darkness to hate the light that dispels it. And just as they did not receive Christ or His word, it is no wonder that the same is the case with the disciples and the Church.

Here Christ gives a new comfort, with which the disciples are to be comforted in the face of the persecution and rejection they would meet. This comfort is that He Himself is the reason for the world's rejection of them, for the world in its darkness did not know the Father, and therefore did not receive the Son. Christ here does not seek an excuse for the world, but condemns it for not believing in Him, especially after He had come ... and told ... and done wonders and miracles. So the sin of not believing in Christ remains; indeed, Christ adds also that the world's rejection of Him is its hatred of the Father Himself, for the honor of the Father and the Son is one and indivisible.

"They hated me without a cause": this verse came in its very words in (Ps 35:19), as though the Holy Spirit was foretelling, through David, the state and persecution of the Jews toward Christ without cause, so that Pilate the Roman declared that there was not a single reason for the death of Christ (ch. 18:38; see also Lk 23:4, 14, 22); rather, it was the malice of the rulers and priests that blinded them.
And those who today reject the call of Christ and His Church to them, are they not also considered haters of Christ without a cause?

Since the Lord's word to the disciples about the world's rejection of them was hard on them, Christ concludes His words by encouraging them with talk about the Holy Spirit, of whom He had spoken before (ch. 14:26; 7:39). For it is the Holy Spirit who will bear witness to Christ, through His disciples, before the whole world, by what they will say or the miracles they will do, whose source is the Holy Spirit. These are matters that gladden and strengthen the servants in every age, when they touch the power of the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church of God.

"I will send ... proceedeth": this shows the harmony and concord of the work of the three hypostases with one another. The word "I will send" highlights the divinity of Christ and His heavenly authority together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and also highlights that the future sending of the Holy Spirit depends first on the redemption that Christ would accomplish on the wood of the Cross. The word "proceedeth" means continual coming forth from within without separation, as when we say: heat proceeds from fire, yet it has not left it ... So the Son, in His incarnation, did not leave the Father; and the Holy Spirit, in His procession, has left neither the Father nor the Son.
Chapter sixteen: Christ foretells His death to His disciples, the world's persecution of them, and the help of the Holy Spirit

entries.section: (1) Christ foretells to His disciples His death and the persecution coming upon them

paragraphs.text: "These things have I spoken unto you": that is, all the preceding talk about the world's rejection and persecution of you. And the reason I have spoken to you is that your faith may not weaken, but that you may be strengthened by the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (1) Christ foretells to His disciples His death and the persecution coming upon them

paragraphs.text: Being put out of the synagogue is the severest penalty that can come upon a Jew, and it represents a moral disgrace; indeed, they would also be exposed to being killed. The motive of the Jews in that would be their mistaken zeal for God and the Law, as they did with Stephen (Acts 7:54-60). But the real reason for this persecution and killing is their rejection of Christ and the Father.

entries.section: (1) Christ foretells to His disciples His death and the persecution coming upon them
