paragraphs.text: The same meaning as in the first verse. And He adds that He did not tell them from the beginning, for two reasons: first, their lack of moral readiness to hear this hard word.
Second, there was no need to refer to the work of the Holy Spirit the Comforter, so long as Christ was among them teaching them and strengthening them, and He was the source of their comfort.

entries.section: (1) Christ foretells to His disciples His death and the persecution coming upon them

paragraphs.text: "But now": that is, the events and dispensations of redemption began after the eating of the Passover, and Judas' going to the chief priests to agree on the arrest of Christ.

"I go my way to him that sent me": this means the ascension to the Father, passing through the Cross, then the Resurrection and its proclamation. "None of you asketh me": this is not a command from Christ, but a form of expressing wonder, as it came in the Greek: no one asked Him where He was going. The explanation of this is that grief filled the hearts of the disciples, because of Christ's talk about persecution and His separation from them, so they were occupied with what awaited them after Him rather than with the destiny of Christ!!!

I beseech You, my God ... we too often sink into our worries and grieve and are anxious, not looking to the dispensations of Your salvation and what You prepare for us ... Lift up our hearts and our eyes toward You, that our hearts may be strengthened and our resolve made firm, and that we may complete our lives with faith in Your promises.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: Since the Lord Jesus felt the effect of His words on the disciples, and how they grieved, He wanted to move them to a place that carried comfort, and to lift them above grief. So He returned to reveal to them a secret of the dispensation and of the work of the Holy Spirit, making His departure a source of joy, carrying them over from sensory, bodily sight to heavenly sight. They might lose Him in visible sight, but Christ offers the Spirit, the Comforter who gives joy, as a better situation for the disciples and the Church, for the incarnation of the Son has a specific temporal mission that ends with the completion of redemption. But the Holy Spirit tends and cares for the preaching and the Church to the end of the age. Christ used here the attribute of Comforter as one of the attributes of the Holy Spirit, because the disciples were in the greatest need of comfort.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: This verse is a summary before the detail: Christ presents the work of the Holy Spirit, then details it in the following three verses, which makes clear the importance of the sending of the Holy Spirit, and His varied work necessary for the salvation of mankind.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: "He will reprove the world of sin": one of the works of the Holy Spirit is rebuke with the aim of pushing to repentance. However many the sins, the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of the children of God is to reveal the sin within them, then urge them to repent. The greatest sin is the sin of not believing in Christ, and without the Holy Spirit it is impossible to believe in Christ. See the prophecy of Zechariah: "And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him ..." (Zech 12:10); that is, had it not been for the descent of the Holy Spirit and His work on the day of Pentecost, many of the Jews would not have been "pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, what shall we do?" (Acts 2:37).

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: "Of righteousness": the direct and intended meaning here is that the Holy Spirit reproves the Jews concerning the Righteous One whom they rejected, who is Christ Himself. For when Christ came, who was their only hope of salvation and acquittal from death, they crucified Him!!! And the indirect meaning, from which all believers benefit, is that the Holy Spirit who works in them does not reprove them only for the sin they committed, but also reproves them for falling short in growing in the virtues, and in the righteousness with which they should be adorned and by which they should overcome their pride.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: "Of judgment": that is, the Holy Spirit bears witness and condemns the world and its prince (Satan) for the trial of Christ. What appeared outwardly to be a victory for Satan and his helpers in getting rid of Christ became a judgment on Satan and the wicked world.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: Because of the distress of soul the disciples were going through at that time, Christ did not tell them everything, but gave them as much as they could bear. But in the near future, after the descent of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, their eyes would be opened when they were filled with the Holy Spirit, and their knowledge of spiritual matters would increase, and the Holy Spirit would take over leading, guiding and completing the teaching. The Lord Christ points to the hypostatic nature of the Holy Spirit and His relation to the Father: He is the Spirit of God who takes from Him and tells the disciples the things to come, that is, everything that concerns the Kingdom of God.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: "He shall glorify me": that is, showing the glory of the name of Christ in the Church and in the hearts of the disciples and all believers, after Christ hid His glory by His incarnation and His submission to and endurance of humiliation.
"He shall receive of mine": that is, even after My ascension and My bodily disappearance from you, He is the means of conveying to you My purpose, My thought, My teaching and My guidance.

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: "All things that the Father hath are mine": the word "all" here means complete equality between the Father and the Son. And because the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one essence, the Holy Spirit will take what Christ wants to convey to us, and He Himself will deliver it to His Church.
Here we note several functions that the Holy Spirit performs, which this chapter highlights:
(1) He reproves the world (v. 8).
(2) He guides into all truth (v. 13).
(3) He glorifies the Son (v. 14).
(4) He conveys to the Church the purpose of the Father and the Son (v. 14).

entries.section: (2) The work of the Holy Spirit

paragraphs.text: That is, a reference to His death and burial, then seeing Him plainly at His Resurrection, then His ascension to the Father.

entries.section: (3) The grief and joy of the disciples

paragraphs.text: It was hard for the disciples to understand what the Lord Christ said, so they whispered together, declaring that they did not understand His meaning. The Lord knew what perplexed them, and repeated what He had said before about their not seeing Him and then seeing Him, as a preparation for what He would declare and explain afterward.

entries.section: (3) The grief and joy of the disciples

paragraphs.text: "Ye shall weep and lament": that is, with the beginning of My sufferings, My crucifixion and My death; and "the world," that is, the Jews and their rulers, will rejoice, because they believe they have rid themselves of Christ forever. But be assured that after a little while, with the declaration of the Resurrection, your sorrows will turn into joys and glories that the world does not understand. Vv. 21-22: Christ gives a comparison that affirms what He said before, and uses, to bring it near, the example of the woman in labor, and the pains of her travail that she must pass through before these pains turn to joy at the coming of new life, for the mother's joy in her child makes her forget all the former pains. So will be the spiritual joy of the disciples, which is distinguished from all the temporary joys of the world in that no one can take it from the children of God. We have seen this very picture, not only in the life of the pure disciples, but in the life of all the martyrs, who offered themselves to death in a joy the world does not understand.

entries.section: (3) The grief and joy of the disciples

paragraphs.text: "In that day": that is, at the descent of the Holy Spirit, there will be no need for you to ask Me as you do now, for the knowledge that the Holy Spirit gives is complete knowledge, and it will be enough for you at that time to ask and request of the Father in My name, and the Holy Spirit will give you all you need.

entries.section: (3) The grief and joy of the disciples

paragraphs.text: All the pride of the Jewish man was that he would add intercession to his prayer with the names of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; but it became ours, in the glory of the New Covenant, to offer our prayers in the name of Christ Himself, as He taught us here. For this is the good pleasure of the Father, that all requests be offered through His Son who redeemed all mankind; and when asking in the name of Christ, there is an answer, and from it, full joy.

entries.section: (4) The perfection of the disciples' faith

paragraphs.text: "I have spoken unto you in proverbs": I have been accustomed to speak with you in parables, to bring hard meanings near to your minds. But when the Holy Spirit comes and makes known to you the truths of the crucifixion, redemption and resurrection, there will be no need for parables, but the teaching of the Holy Spirit will be direct and understandable. And Christ regarded what the Holy Spirit will tell and declare to the disciples and the Church as the declaration of Christ Himself to them, because the Holy Spirit and Christ are one essence.

entries.section: (4) The perfection of the disciples' faith

paragraphs.text: "At that day": that is, after the descent of the Holy Spirit and the birth of the Church, you will ask in My name as I told you (v. 23), and there will be a direct answer from the Father, because everyone who loved the Son and believed in Him entered, through the Son, into the presence of the Father Himself, and the Father gives him everything.

entries.section: (4) The perfection of the disciples' faith

paragraphs.text: A completion of the preceding verse, and a full and concise theological explanation of the stage of the Incarnation and redemption, then the Resurrection, the Ascension and the sitting at the right hand of His Father.

entries.section: (4) The perfection of the disciples' faith

paragraphs.text: In (vv. 17, 18) the disciples declared their perplexity about what Christ was speaking of. And after the explanation that Christ gave in (vv. 19-26), Christ summed up the theological truth in (v. 28) simply and in few words: that He came forth from the Father and became incarnate, then leaves the world and returns to the Father ... So the disciples expressed the clarity and plainness of the matter and their certainty of faith in all that Christ said, and also acknowledged their understanding that He came forth from the Father and came into the world.

entries.section: (4) The perfection of the disciples' faith

paragraphs.text: "Do ye now believe?": the Lord Christ indicates that the faith of the disciples existed, but was so weak that it could not face the coming hours, which begin with His arrest and trial, then the events of the crucifixion. Therefore Christ prophesied to them what their state would be of fear, which would make them scatter, every man to his own, and leave Him to go through the winepress alone. Christ concludes His prophecy to them by saying that even if they leave Him, He is not alone, because the Father is with Him. And what Christ declared here is considered a translation of the Father's love for His incarnate Son on the one hand, and for all His children on the other.

My beloved brother ... if every form of persecution befalls us, and people leave us, and even our nearest ones neglect us, we have comfort, hope and faith in God, who never leaves us; and this faith is that from which all the holy martyr fathers drew their strength at the time of their torments.

entries.section: (4) The perfection of the disciples' faith

paragraphs.text: "These things I have spoken unto you": this returns to the discourse in the previous three chapters, and the Lord Christ makes clear here the secret of His words in all that went before, which is that the world, which is in the grip of Satan, will be a source of pain, tribulation and persecution ... but I am the source of peace, so whatever you may meet, you must always have faith and confidence that "I have overcome the world," and I have given you also to overcome through Me ... Just as Christ crushed Satan on the Cross, and abolished the power of death and triumphed over it, so He also gave the disciples, and everyone who truly believes in His name, this victory over the world and the whole kingdom of darkness.
Chapter seventeen: Christ's intercessory prayer for us

entries.section: (1) The glory of the Father and the glory of the Son

paragraphs.text: After Christ finished His long previous talk with His disciples, He began a talk with the Father, and lifted up His eyes toward heaven to teach us, when we pray, to look to heaven, so that our thoughts may rise above earthly things. He declared the nearness of the hour of accomplishing redemption on the Cross, for He knows it beforehand, and became incarnate for it. "Glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee": the glory of the Son is the accomplishment of redemption on the Cross, and the glorifying of the Father is the accomplishment of His will, which is the salvation of mankind by redemption.

entries.section: (1) The glory of the Father and the glory of the Son

paragraphs.text: The glory of the Son in His incarnation was hidden, and so Christ begins here to declare some of the secrets of this glory: He is the only One who has authority over all creation, and He is the Giver of eternal life by redemption to everyone who believes in Him.

entries.section: (1) The glory of the Father and the glory of the Son

paragraphs.text: Eternal life is the knowledge of God and permanent existence with Him, and reaching it is through faith in Christ the Savior, who redeemed us on the Cross and taught us how to live with God on earth by His life.

entries.section: (1) The glory of the Father and the glory of the Son

paragraphs.text: Christ completed His mission and glorified the Father by fulfilling all the righteousness of the Law, and called people to the Kingdom of Heaven by continual talk about God the Father and how to live with Him. And finally by obeying the Father in offering Himself as a sacrifice on the wood of the Cross for the redemption of all mankind.

entries.section: (1) The glory of the Father and the glory of the Son

paragraphs.text: The glory of divinity belonged to the Son from eternity, was hidden by the Incarnation, and appeared in the Resurrection and Ascension.
May we fulfill the commandments of God, so that we taste the pledge of eternity on earth, and God may glorify us and make us rejoice in the Kingdom.
"I have manifested thy name": that is, by My speaking of You as Father. The Jews' knowledge of God was limited, and did not grasp the Trinity.
And through the incarnation of Christ they knew God more, and many of them followed Christ, holding fast to His commandments.

"All things whatsoever thou hast given me": that is, perfect wisdom, the teaching of the commandments, and all the miracles they saw, by which they became certain that Christ was sent from the Father and His word is the word of God, so their faith became firmer.

This does not mean that Christ does not pray for the world, for in (vv. 20, 21) He prays for the world that will believe in Him. Likewise on the wood of the Cross, He prays for those who crucified Him (see Lk 23:34). But He singled out His disciples here for prayer, because of the persecution and troubles to which they alone would be exposed as a result of the responsibility of preaching falling on them, and their need of a higher level of support.

He declares the equality of the Son with the Father in the ownership of all creation, that is, that Christ is God. Christ is glorified in His disciples by their keeping His commandments, then by their preaching in His name.

My beloved brother, the glorifying of the name of Christ and its proclamation did not become the responsibility of the disciples alone, but the responsibility of all the children of God. So a great task lies on us, which is to glorify the name of Christ before all those around us. And this will not come about except by our acting on His commandment, our constant repentance, and our striving against our lusts, so that our old man disappears (see Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22; Col 3:9), and in its place our Christ who dwells in us appears.

That is, the time and season of My mission and My work on earth has ended, but they are still remaining, and will meet much, and they also must show forth and glorify My name, and complete the preaching I began. Therefore I ask also for them that You keep them from evil, and from the world that they will face, and from all that awaits them. "Through thine own name": a metonym for the power and care of God, as the wise man says: "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Prov 18:10).

"That they may be one": that is, union at the level of heartfelt love, thought and purpose, without quarrel or division. How much the shepherds and servants need this petition now, for the peace of the Church and of those served is founded on the love of the servants and the unity of their thought. And how much the Church needs to pray for her shepherds, that God may keep them from the wars of division and partisanship.
"As we are": Christ's desire that the perfection of union among the disciples be as it is between the Father and the Son.
"While I was with them ... and now come I to thee": the two verses are connected and complete one meaning.

That is, during My presence, the disciples were in My keeping, and so My teaching, My guidance and My following up on them preserved them. But now that the time has come when I will leave the world, I return the responsibility of preserving them to Your name, O Father. And here I pray this before them, that they may have joy and confidence in the continuation of divine care for them, in the face of the distress and persecution that the world will bring upon them.

"The son of perdition": a clear reference to Judas. The Lord called him by this name to show Judas' evil will, that he is the one who deserved perdition, and did not benefit from the keeping care of Christ that kept the rest of the disciples.
"That the scripture might be fulfilled": as the prophecies in the Holy Bible (Ps 109:8; 41:9) mentioned about the betrayal of Judas and God's rejection of him.

Christ taught His disciples and His Church the word of God, which is exalted above the thoughts of the world and reveals its errors. Therefore the world hates all the children of God who hold fast to the pure and clean life, as it hated Christ also before them.
And what comforts us here is what St. Paul mentioned: "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 3:12).

Since the world hates the children of God, the solution is not that Christ lift them up with Him to heaven, but that He keep them and strengthen them in facing evil and the evil one. And Christ gives encouragement to the children of God, since He affirms their spiritual lineage to God, and not to the world.

Christ asks in His prayer that the disciples be established in all His words, the truth, which they heard from Him. And just as Christ set Himself apart, sanctified Himself, for teaching them and redeeming them, the turn comes to them also to be set apart, like their Lord, for being sent to the world and preaching redemption and the Kingdom of Heaven.
In His prayer here, the Lord Christ goes beyond the disciples to the whole Church in all her ages.

"That they all may be one": is the blood of redemption not one? Is the Teacher not one? Is the water of Baptism not one? So it is natural that we be one, not in form or outward appearance, but in thought and heartfelt love, on the pattern of the oneness between the Son and the Father, not in essence, but in love as far as we can according to our human nature.

"The glory which thou gavest me I have given them": the glory here is explained by St. John Chrysostom as authority and gifts, and sharing with Christ in the work of salvation by preaching. And the aim of giving this glory is also oneness. Just as the glory of the Father and the Son is one because they are one, Christ gave us this glory for the same purpose, that is, the oneness of the members and structure of the Church.

Christ rises to the highest levels of oneness, presenting a wonderful spiritual theological truth, explaining it thus: I am in them by My humanity, My incarnation and My sacrifice for them, and You are in Me with the fullness of Your divinity, and I am in You. For Christ joined and reconciled the Father with mankind in His blessed person; in Christ, humanity was united with God, and heaven with earth, and Christ became an intercessor and propitiatory mediator, which made the Father's love for mankind an extension of His love for His only Son.
By submitting to the commandments of God we become one in Him.
Comment:

Verses 20-23 show God's concern for oneness in His Church. But the devil was able to divide the Church by means of pride. The solution is humility to reach oneness, while holding fast to the faith delivered by Christ and the Apostles.

The first petition was for their sanctification, and the second for their unity together and their union with Him. This third petition is for continual presence with Him, and it is the highest of the longings of Christ's love that He declares. Therefore the Lord used here the word "I will," and not "I ask"; for asking is a request, but "I will" adds the dimension of feelings, attachment and true care in having all His children with Him in His bosom. And as they shared in bearing the cross of persecution and the toil of preaching, they will also have fellowship in the glory of the Son (1 Cor 12:26).
"Before the foundation of the world": this shows the eternity of the Son (see ch. 1:1).

"The world hath not known thee": in the whole world, idolatry was dominant. And in Israel, the knowledge was theoretical and literal, without entering into the depth of the knowledge of God. But Christ's knowledge of the Father is eternal and of His very being. And the knowledge of the Father became available to all of us through His only Son. Christ pointed here to the faith of the disciples, by their receiving the Son, which is the first step in the knowledge of the Father that has begun, and which Christ will complete after the Resurrection, by explaining the things concerning the Kingdom. And the Holy Spirit completes our knowledge of the infinite Father, so our love for Him grows; and by this Christ abides in our hearts.
I thank You, my God, for Your great love, of which I have grasped only a little; grant me to respond to Your love, so that it is reflected as love for all those around me.
The arrest and trial of Jesus

The closing Passover discourse, which occupied chapters 14, 15 and 16, and likewise the prayer of the Lord Jesus to the Father in (ch. 17), ended, and the events of the last scene in the life of the Lord Jesus on earth began, with His going out to the garden of Gethsemane in the Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem toward the Mount of Olives, and He took His disciples with Him.

We note that St. John did not mention the details of Judas' agreement with the priests, or the price of the betrayal of the Lord, being content with what came in the other three Gospels, pointing to Judas' knowledge of the place where Christ gathered with the disciples in many retreats, and he also pictures the scene of the crowd coming out to arrest the Lord Jesus.

"Went forth ... knowing": ... that is, He went to death by Himself to meet it, and they did not enter to Him. St. John pointed to Christ's knowledge with a new sign to affirm His divinity, and He asked them what they wanted, which He knew well, and the answer of the Lord Christ, "I am he," shows us the reaction of the whole kingdom of darkness before God and His Word: they were soldiers and servants and crowds, and Christ was alone, and yet they drew back and fell to the ground, as though Christ were saying: You have no right to seize Me, unless I give Myself over to you to death.

Christ repeated the question, and they repeated the same answer, so this time He offered Himself for that for which He came, and did not fail to redeem His disciples, but asked that they be let go. St. John refers to what the Lord Christ had said before in (ch. 17:12) in His prayer to the Father, that none of them be lost.
See (Mt 26:51; Mk 14:47; Lk 22:50), but note that St. John mentioned the name of Peter and the name of the servant, which are not mentioned in the other three Gospels.

See (Mt 26:52, 54), and note that the Lord Christ rejected the human, emotional manner of what Peter did, making clear that there was a greater work that Christ had to accomplish, which was to accept the cup of suffering, that is, to accomplish redemption on the Cross.

"The band and the captain": that is, the Romans. Although they, with the servants of the Jews, formed a company, and Christ was alone, they bound Him, perhaps for fear of His escaping in the darkness, or in order to further put Him in the form of a guilty accused man, for malice had taken its share of them. And in the binding of Christ there is also a correspondence with the story of Isaac, whom Abraham bound to offer him as a sacrifice.

O Fashioner of all creation, its Redeemer and Liberator, they bound You willingly, though You are able to command legions of angels ... What love is this, that the guilty is set free and the innocent is taken bound ... Understand, O my soul, and if only you would understand.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

paragraphs.text: Caiaphas was the high priest, and his father-in-law Annas was also an earlier high priest, and every high priest keeps his title after the period of his high priesthood. The meeting with Annas was mentioned by John alone, while the other Gospels were content to mention the meeting with Caiaphas. Some hold that the meeting with Annas was a passing meeting on the way to Caiaphas, but the servants were careful for this quick meeting with Annas because of his old age, and his advanced honor as a former high priest. As for Caiaphas, his son-in-law, St. John wanted to remind us of him, for he was the one who gave the counsel that one man should die for the people (ch. 11:49, 50), and this reference has its importance in making clear that the Jewish trial was a sham, and that the decision for the death of the Lord Jesus had been premeditated.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

paragraphs.text: John did not mention the flight of the disciples as Matthew did (Mt 26:56), but was content to mention that, with Peter, he followed Jesus. And because of John's connection with the priestly circle, he was able to enter inside the house. But Peter stood outside until he brought him in. However, before bringing him in, when Peter stood with the servants and guards warming themselves outside, St. John mentions the first incident of Peter's denial before the maid who questioned him, and he denied out of his fear before the crowd.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

paragraphs.text: The questioner here is Annas, and the purpose of the question was that he might find a complaint against Christ to present to Caiaphas and the council after him. The subject of the question was Christ's teachings to the crowds, and His private teachings to His disciples. But the answer of Jesus came as a complete dispelling of Annas' hopes, for He had taught nothing in secret or in hiding, for all His teachings were heard by everyone, whether in the Temple, the synagogues or other places. Therefore also Christ answers with a question: "Why askest thou me?!" Ask rather all the crowds who heard Me!

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

paragraphs.text: One of the servants flared up, considering it an improper answer, and the hand of the wicked struck the face of the Righteous One, and this blow carried flattery to the high priest at the expense of truth and justice. Therefore the Lord Christ commented, rebuking the one who struck Him, for Christ had not sinned against the high priest according to the Law of Moses (Ex 22:28): "why smitest thou me?" That is, you, wicked servant, have become a breaker of the law, which I did not break...
In this text there are lessons to be learned:
The first: what did Christ endure for my salvation? Behold, God has become a spectacle to every gloater, struck by the hand of a servant. Shall I then endure people's insults to me?!

The second: there is no objection to the wronged person's making clear to the wrongdoer the wrong he has done him, so as to show him what he has fallen into, so long as that is with gentleness and love.

In this regard, St. Augustine wrote a wonderful reflection on this blow, saying: "Christ did not only turn His other cheek to be struck, but gave His whole body to be crucified, thereby fulfilling more than He taught in (Mt 5:39)."

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

paragraphs.text: The trial before Caiaphas was the official Jewish trial of Christ. Yet John did not focus on it, being content with what Matthew and Mark recorded of its details. But he mentioned what the two did not about the first meeting with Annas, then referred to Caiaphas and passed beyond him, taking Christ across to the official Roman trial before Pilate.

entries.section: (2) The meeting with Annas and Peter's denial

paragraphs.text: St. John mentions here the second and third denials of Peter, and the incident of the crowing of the cock, and his account was more detailed, for he brought out the first denial at Annas' house, and the second and third at Caiaphas' house. As for Matthew (26:69-73), Mark (14:66-71) and Luke (22:55-62), they summarized the three denials after the trial, so as not to interrupt the narrative, and so that the dialogue of the trial remained continuous.
It is also noted that St. John did not mention here Peter's oaths in denying, or Christ's looking at him, or his bitter weeping and repentance as came in the other three Gospels.
Many wonder how Peter denied You after these years, and what he saw and heard in them...?!

But perhaps Peter had an excuse in his fear, and in Your divinity's not yet being revealed by Your Resurrection, or the Holy Spirit's not yet having come upon him. What excuse have the many today, who declare with their tongues their faith and their following, but with their hearts and works deny You, and become a cause of others' blaspheming Your name?! Yes, my God ... forgive us and have mercy on us; how much we need the bitter tears of Peter.

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: As we said, St. John did not mention the details of Christ's trial before Caiaphas, in which He declared clearly that He is the Christ, the Son of God, which the Jews considered blasphemy (Mt 26:65; Mk 14:64; Lk 22:71). Nor did he mention the gathering of the rulers in the morning, the council of the Jews, and the taking of the decision, but moved us directly to the trial before Pilate.

"The judgment hall": a building built by Herod the Great, set aside for the lodging and residence of the Roman governor during his visits to Jerusalem. It was considered unclean by the Jews, because it belonged to the dwellings of the Gentiles, and therefore they did not enter it, but Pilate went out to them in the courtyard before the building, and asked them the reason for their gathering, and the reason for their complaint against the Lord Jesus. "That they might eat the passover": that is, the continuation of the Passover celebrations. But what truly amazes us is the leaders of the Jews' holding fast to formal bodily cleanness, while their hearts were plotting the betrayal of pure, innocent blood?!

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: The rulers of the Jews did not present an accusation against the Lord Jesus, but only wanted a decision for His death, and therefore they said to Pilate: "If he were not a malefactor."

That is, we have investigated and made sure that He must die, and all that remains for you is the decision, that is, the order for His crucifixion, over which we as Jews have no authority, but it is from your authority alone (crucifixion was under the authority of the Roman governor). But note Pilate's deliberateness, and his not rushing after their opinion.

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: "That ... might be fulfilled": that is, what Christ, to whom be glory, prophesied, that His death would be by the Cross, as came explicitly in (Mt 20:19), and implicitly in (Mk 10:21; Lk 9:23; 14:27), because if the Jews had judged Christ without Pilate, His death would have been by stoning. But everything that Christ prophesied had to be fulfilled to the letter. Therefore the Jews, in their malice, went to Pilate to have Him crucified, not knowing that by this they were fulfilling the highest divine will.

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: Pilate was alone with Christ, and asked Him about what had been raised by the priests and their servants, concerning Christ's claim about Himself that He is the king of the Jews, knowing that such an accusation alone is enough for the crucifixion of Christ, for kingship belongs to Caesar alone, and any attempt to attribute kingship to another is considered rebellion and a coup. But Christ did not answer, but replied with a new question, which is considered a warning and an awakening of Pilate's conscience. The meaning of Christ's question: Is this your own opinion, or are you repeating the accusations these men have reported to you about Me, so that you may find a reason to try Me?

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: "Am I a Jew?": a question of protest, in which Pilate makes clear his position, that he does not consider Christ a king, for he is not a Jew; as though he were saying: I have nothing to do with all this, for these are the words of the Jews. Some see that the saying "Am I a Jew?" means a protest and a stirring up of Roman pride against the nation of the Jews, over their having a king other than Caesar, king of the whole ancient world. Pilate continues his inquiry of Christ with his experience as an investigator: "What hast thou done?", especially since the whole Jewish nation, that is, the great crowds outside the judgment hall, had delivered You up, complaining against You?!

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: Christ defends Himself against the accusation the chief priests attached to Him.

But this defense is not intended to avert the Cross for which He came and became incarnate, but to teach us all a spiritual rule and constitution. If Christ our King declares to us that He does not belong to this world, but has another, heavenly, eternal kingdom, then what should the state of His subjects be but that they too rise above this world with all its lusts, and say, as Christ said before: "We are from above; we are not of this world" (see ch. 8:23), and that the world not rule over us in anything, but that we seek the heavenly Kingdom of our God.

And Christ adds a proof to His words, that if He were an earthly king, He would have cared to have servants and guards to defend Him, so that the Jews would not seize Him, but on the contrary, He asked to give Himself over gently in exchange for the release of the disciples.

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: "Art thou a king then?": a question that expresses bewilderment and wonder. For Christ declares that He is a king, and denies the earthly kingdom that Pilate understands. His answer came affirming the spiritual meaning of His kingdom, for He did not deny being a king, but adds that He became incarnate to redeem mankind and to reign over its heart.

"Every one that is of the truth": that is, everyone who received My word and the work of the Holy Spirit within him, or everyone who is subject to God, who is the Truth, and knew Christ as the sheep know the voice of the shepherd and follow him (ch. 10:4).

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: "What is truth?": Pilate did not understand the words that Christ spoke. Therefore he asked a question and did not wait to hear its answer, as though he were in truth not concerned to understand ... but it was merely a question. Without doubt, Pilate found no cause in Christ that deserved death. Therefore he went out again to the Jews who were waiting outside, declaring the first verdict of innocence, that he found in Him no fault at all. Perhaps God made Pilate utter this very sentence to show one thing: Christ is the true Passover, who is without a single blemish, and He is the sacrifice for sin, which also required that it be without blemish ... So what Pilate uttered is nothing but a confirmation of the perfection of the sacrifice of Christ that was offered.

entries.section: (3) The beginning of the trial before Pilate

paragraphs.text: Pilate erred when he abandoned the duties of his office, as a judge of truth, in releasing the one he saw to be innocent, but gave up his authority in judgment, and gave the right of choice to the people, which was unheard of, and thought that his declaring Christ's innocence relieved him of the responsibility that he left to the people. Perhaps he thought that by opening the door of choice, they would ask for the release of the one in whom there was no fault, but the surprise was in their asking for the release of one known to be a robber and an insurrectionist.
How strange a people that released a robber and crucified a righteous man!!

Pilate's gross error gives all of us a lesson in witnessing to the truth. Politicians may bargain or strike deals, and the limits of truth become very wide. But the children of God are not so; rather, truth is truth, for "he that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD" (Prov 17:15).
The crucifixion, death and burial of Christ

Pilate wavered between the voice of truth (conscience) and the weakness of the Jews and the ferocity of their cry for Christ's crucifixion, so he first handed Him over to scourging, hoping to calm the Jews' uproar; and St. Luke affirms this in (Lk 23:16): "I will therefore chastise him, and release him." Matthew and Mark both mention the scourging and crucifixion together (Mt 27:26; Mk 15:15), but St. John separated them, as well as Pilate's feeble attempts to acquit Christ. And St. John moves to the scene of the Roman soldiers' mockery of Christ during the scourging: they ridiculed Him and put on Him a robe whose color represented the garments of kings, and they also plaited a crown of thorns and crowned Him with it (see Isa 53:5).
"And they smote him with their hands": and Matthew adds (Mt 27:30) that they struck Him on the head, and we do not think there is a tongue or a writer who can describe or express this wicked scene...
But we are content to ask the Lord of glory: Why, my God, did You endure the hands of wicked sinners being stretched out against Your righteous, holy face, and how can this happen?!
And His answer comes: For your salvation, my child!!!
In an attempt to clear his conscience, Pilate goes out and declares a second time the innocence of Christ, but it is a declaration without a verdict to that effect.

Pilate brought Jesus out after the scourging, wearing the purple and with the thorns on His head, in a last attempt to win the sympathy of the Jews so that he might release Christ. But they grew more hardened and demanded His crucifixion, so Pilate gave his third testimony to the innocence of Jesus (see ch. 18:38; 19:4-6). And in an attempt to warn the Jews, Pilate wanted to rid his hands of responsibility, so he said to them: "Take ye him, and crucify him," without involving me in your crime.

The Jews presented their first accusation, that Christ was an evildoer (ch. 18:30), and when they failed, they presented the second accusation, that He was a traitor to Caesar, and Christ repelled this accusation from Himself when He answered that His kingdom is not of this world (ch. 8:36). And here the Jews came with a third accusation, that He was a blasphemer of the Law, that is, their religion, and according to it He must die, and by this they nullify Pilate's defense of Christ, that he finds no fault in Him.

Pilate was frightened when the Jews mentioned that Christ is "the Son of God," and we may understand why: he was afraid of passing sentence on an innocent man whom he did not condemn in anything, but he sensed the Jews' plot and cruelty that were leading him in the current toward sentencing Him, and he was also afraid of the words "Son of God," since the Romans and Greeks believed in the possibility of the gods appearing and becoming incarnate or begetting offspring ... Perhaps Christ was one of the sons of the gods, so would Pilate bring himself into enmity with the gods? We add to that another reason for his fright, which was the dream his wife dreamed and told him of, saying to him: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man" (Mt 27:19).

In an attempt to overcome his fright and fear, Pilate took Jesus inside to inquire of Him: "Whence art thou?" Is it from heaven?! Are you a son of the gods as I have heard? And Christ's not answering is the conviction of His blessed person that what He says would not change the situation at all, and what Pilate had heard from Him was enough for him to acquit Him. And to push Christ to speak, Pilate threatened Him with his authority to kill Him or release Him.

So there came Christ's strong answer, which frightened Pilate: "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above." The crucifixion, then, is the will of the Father and the consent and submission of the Son, and no earthly or temporal authority has power to control it, and at the same time, Pilate was not relieved of responsibility because he was hesitant and passive, and did not declare His innocence. "But he that delivered me unto thee," that is, Judas and the Jews, out of envy, "hath the greater sin" than yours; and perhaps the reason for the lessening of Pilate's sin is that he was a Gentile who did not know the Scriptures and the promises as these men knew them.

We do not know how Pilate sought to release Christ, whether by talks with the crowd or some of the chief priests. But it is certain that his fright and perplexity increased before his conscience and his examination of Jesus on the one hand, and before the shouting of the Jews and their threatening on the other, so they threatened him with what he had not counted on, which is that if he released one who claims to be a king of the Jews, he would implicitly agree to the existence of a king other than Caesar, and this we do not accept, and it would also make you a traitor to Caesar. The Jews thereby succeeded in bringing a new kind of fear into his heart, which was the fear for his political position and being an enemy of Caesar himself.

Pilate brought the Lord Jesus out of the judgment hall to the courtyard where the Jews were waiting, and sat on his seat that the Roman governors used when issuing their judgments. And St. John adds, to involve us in the scene, the place and position of the seat, for it was on a raised hill (Gabbatha) relative to the courtyard where the Jews had gathered, and it is also called (the Pavement) because it was paved with marble and alabaster.

And as it approached the sixth hour, and only three hours remained until the offering of the Passover (at the ninth), Pilate had to take a decision about Christ, so he tried for the last time to rid himself of the decision and leave the Jews to judge Him, saying: "Behold your King!"

Pilate's saying "Behold your King!" provoked the Jews and their agitation increased, and they answered him: "Take him, why do you give him to us? Take him and crucify him." And when he asked them: "Shall I crucify your King?" they cried out: "We have no king but Caesar." This is a denial and a renunciation ... for the Jews know that they have no king but God, and that the Romans occupy them, and they were waiting for deliverance from them.

But now to declare that their king is Caesar, they are thereby an example of the person who changes all his principles in a moment because of malice in his heart, and thereby they applied the principle "the end justifies the means." And the end of the feeble trial scene came with the submission of one who feared for his position because of the riot: let one die even if innocent so that I may save myself; and what a principle!!!

Beloved reader, it is easy for us here to criticize Pilate for misusing his authority, and for his fear and cowardice. But in other situations in our daily life, may we not lie to escape from an act for which we deserve rebuke, or evade the responsibility of declaring the truth, trying to wash our hands and throw the responsibility on others as Pilate did, or do like the Jews: find a justification for our evils with which we numb our consciences?! Have mercy on us, O Lord.

That is, from the judgment hall first, then from Jerusalem second, to be crucified outside the camp (Golgotha). And St. Paul speaks of this: "Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate. Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach" (Heb 13:12-13).

And note, dear reader, that our Church, in bringing out this spiritual meaning, took care in the rite of Holy Week to leave the sanctuary and the choir of the deacons and pray in the nave of the church, to go out with Christ outside Jerusalem.

"Skull, Golgotha": the tradition inherited among the Jews said that it was the place where the skull of Adam was buried. But scholars describe it as a hill of moderate height, whose rocky form resembles a skull in its structure, and this place was used for stoning and was near the city.

St. John referred to the crucifixion briefly, and mentioned the two robbers without mentioning the dialogue with Christ. Therefore, to review the events of the crucifixion, see the texts (Mt 27; Mk 15; Lk 23) in the parts concerning the events of the crucifixion to complete the whole picture.

There used to be written on the cross the name of the crucified and the reason for his crucifixion. St. John mentions here that what was written was first by the order of Pilate personally, and second in the Hebrew language of the Jews, the Greek language of thought and learning, and the Latin language of the official state. Because the place was elevated, and many of the people read it, the chief priests objected to the declaration that Christ was their king, because in this was a condemnation of them for killing their king. But this objection was met coldly by Pilate, and he insisted on his word that Christ is the King of the Jews. We do not know whether this was out of spite toward the chief priests, or out of reverence for a person in whom he saw no evil.

St. John was the one who made the story of the dividing of the garments clearest to us, so we understand that they were four soldiers, each of whom took a part. But the coat was woven and could not be divided, so they cast lots among themselves for whose it should be. And St. John reminds us, as Matthew also did (Mt 27:35), of what David said in his prophecies about the sufferings of the Cross: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture" (Ps 22:18).

entries.section: (3) The words of the crucifixion and death

paragraphs.text: Who were the women whom the Holy Bible mentions at the Cross?! By reviewing the texts of all the Gospels we conclude that they were the Virgin Mary first, and "Salome," her cousin, second, as Mark mentioned her in his Gospel (Mk 15:40; 16:1), and as Matthew referred to her (Mt 20:20) as the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who is the mother of St. John; and the third of the women is Mary the wife of Clopas, the mother of James the Less and Joses; and the last of them is Mary Magdalene, whom Matthew mentioned in his Gospel first because of her piety after her repentance (Mt 27:56). And note that St. John did not mention the name of his mother, so as not to depart from his habitual practice of not mentioning his own name.

entries.section: (3) The words of the crucifixion and death

paragraphs.text: In the midst of His sufferings and crucifixion, and at His hardest moments, He did not forget His mother according to the flesh, the holy Virgin Mary. Since she had no sons according to the flesh but Him, Christ gave John to her as a son, and Christ charged John with the responsibility of caring for His mother; and the evangelist makes clear the response of both parties to Christ's commandment, since the beloved disciple took her to his own home.
But why was John the one who received this honor? Was he not, dear friend, the only one remaining in the midst of all the sufferings while others fled?!

My friend, St. John received the honor of hosting the Mother of God in his house because he did not leave the cross of the Lord of glory, for there is a special gift for everyone who does not flee from his cross, but receives it from God with joy.

entries.section: (3) The words of the crucifixion and death

paragraphs.text: "After this": it carries more than one meaning:
The first: that is, after the three hours of darkness.
The second: that is, after all the dialogues or words that took place on the Cross, whether John mentioned them or did not.
The third: that is, after He was assured of the handing over of St. Mary to John.
St. John pointed out that there were two final prophecies about the sufferings of Christ: "My tongue cleaveth to my jaws" (Ps 22:15), "and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" (Ps 69:21).

These two prophecies had to be fulfilled, so the Quencher of all humanity's thirst, in the blood of His love, cried out: "I thirst." Only John mentioned this vessel of vinegar, and this vinegar is wine that has begun to spoil, which is why it is called vinegar. The guards used to drink it because of its low price, or instead of throwing it away, so that it counted as free wine, and the guards took a stalk of the hyssop plant (its branches were used for sprinkling holy water according to Jewish rites) to bring the sponge soaked with vinegar to the mouth of Christ. This vinegar was different from the first vinegar, mixed with myrrh, which was used to dull the senses of those about to undergo the sufferings of crucifixion; and this first one Christ refused to drink, that He might pass through the sufferings in full without alleviation.

"It is finished": that is, He accomplished what He came for, offering Himself as a sacrifice for sin and an atonement for our sins, and the word "It is finished" is the sixth word in the order of the words that Christ said on the Cross, which are in the following order:
1) "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:24).
2) "Woman, behold thy son! ... Behold thy mother!" (vv. 26, 27).
3) "I thirst" (v. 28).
4) "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Lk 23:43).
5) "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani" (Mt 27:46).
6) "It is finished" (v. 30).
7) "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit" (Lk 23:46).

entries.section: (3) The words of the crucifixion and death

paragraphs.text: "Because it was the preparation": that is, the state of utmost concern for the Passover celebrations. And the first Sabbath of Passover week was the holiest Sabbath of the year among the Jews, and this did not suit the presence of bodies hanging on the crosses. So the Jews asked Pilate's permission to break the legs, a tradition known for quickly finishing off the crucified, by increasing the loss of blood after the shattering of the legs, so that the Sabbath would not be defiled by the crucified remaining on their ground. And the soldiers carried out the task on the first and the last, but as for Jesus, no one approached Him, and they marveled that He had given up the spirit so quickly (see Mk 15:44), and to be more certain, one of the soldiers pierced His side and there came out blood and water.

The coming out of the blood and water: all the ancient Fathers of the Church paused before the "phenomenon" of the blood and water coming out of the pierced side of the Savior, a pause containing many reflections, of which we cite the following few: Chrysostom sees: "We were born of the water and fed from the blood. Therefore, when we approach the cup of the Eucharist, we drink from the very pierced side."

And St. Tertullian comes close to Chrysostom in his reflection, saying: "We are baptized by water and glorified by blood; we are called by water and chosen by blood; this is why His side was wounded; for whoever is washed with water is prepared to drink the blood." As for St. Ambrose and the scholar Origen, they agreed almost on one meaning: "After death blood is glorified and no water comes out of a body, but this had to happen, so that we may know that from the dead body of Christ all life came forth."

entries.section: (3) The words of the crucifixion and death

paragraphs.text: St. John refers to himself, as usual, with a veiled reference, and makes clear the reason for the legs of the Lord Jesus not being broken, and His side being pierced with the spear and the blood and water coming out, that we may believe in Christ, in whom the following prophecies were fulfilled:

(1) A bone of Him shall not be broken: this commandment was concerning the Passover lamb, which directly symbolizes the person of Christ, and it came in (Ex 12:46), and St. Paul also referred to it in (1 Cor 5:7) when he said: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us," and also the prophecy that David mentioned in (Ps 34:20): "He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken."

(2) "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced" (Zech 12:10): "And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem ... and they shall look upon me (Christ) whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn." That is, as John said before, that death had taken place, but it was the hand of God that moved the hand of the soldier to pierce the side of Christ, so that what the Father had declared before by the Holy Spirit concerning His Christ might be fulfilled.

And here we pause, beloved, for the pierced side of Christ is not only a proof of prophecy, but a sign of love that Christ bears in His body, besides the nails, so the pierced side became a source of hope and protection within it from all the wars of the wicked adversary. So if you ever doubt that you have no place in the bosom of Christ, remember the water of Baptism with which you were washed, and the flowing blood that comes forth, awaiting you on the altar, and your hopes will be renewed, and your heart will be kindled with hope in the love of Him who loved you.
Why did Christ choose Joseph of Arimathea from among His followers (disciples) to bury His body?
(1) He was rich and owned a new tomb in the same place as the crucifixion, according to the prophecy: "And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death" (Isa 53:9; Mt 27:57-60).
(2) He was an honourable counsellor of high standing, so he was able to go in to Pilate (Mk 15:43).

"And there came also Nicodemus ... and took the body of Jesus": the events and their sequence indicate a distribution of tasks, then their meeting together for the shrouding. Joseph went to Pilate and Nicodemus brought the requirements for the shrouding, and the two took the body together. St. John refers to Nicodemus as the one who first came to Jesus (see ch. 3), and he is the same one who tried to defend Jesus before the council of the rulers of the Jews in (ch. 7:50). What Nicodemus carried was myrrh, which is the sap of one of the well-known trees, used for cleansing or lessening pain, and was one of the embalming materials the Pharaohs used and the Jews took from them. As for the aloes, it is a powder made from a fragrant tree and has a sweet smell ... and the amount Nicodemus brought was a hundred minas, and the mina is a Roman measure of volume and weight taken from the Greeks, amounting in volume to about half a liter, and in weight equal to 340 grams.
"Wound it in linen clothes": they mixed a blend of perfumes and fragrant oils and put it on the body, then wrapped it in linen.
"As the manner of the Jews is": this means what they took from the Egyptians of the customs of embalming.

The tomb in which Christ was buried was new and hewn in a rock inside a garden owned by Joseph of Arimathea near the place of the crucifixion, which helped to complete the procedures of shrouding and burial quickly before the twelfth hour, which is six in the evening by our reckoning, so that they would not enter the great Sabbath. Perhaps the surrender of the Savior's body into the hands of those who shrouded Him is the last of the scenes of the humility of God, whom we shall see afterward in the glories of His Resurrection.
The visit to the empty tomb; the appearances of Christ after His resurrection

entries.section: (1) The visit of Magdalene, Peter and John to the empty tomb

paragraphs.text: "The first day of the week": that is Sunday, the day of proclaiming victory and the breaking of the power of death. It became the Lord's Day in place of the Sabbath for all Christians from the first Church, in the apostolic age.

"When it was yet dark": how wonderful was Magdalene's love for the Lord! At the first threads of dawn, when the gates of Jerusalem were opened, she went out of the city to visit the tomb, while darkness still covered the western side completely... and she did not care that she was a woman... All she hoped for was to catch a glimpse of the tomb from the outside, but she saw the tomb empty, for the angel had rolled away the stone, as is mentioned in (Mt 28:2).

entries.section: (1) The visit of Magdalene, Peter and John to the empty tomb

paragraphs.text: She hurried out as the first herald of the Resurrection, and her eagerness led her first to the house of Peter, the eldest and most renowned, and then to the house of John, where the Virgin Mary was staying. Since she did not yet grasp the dimensions of the Resurrection, she told them, according to what she had seen, that they had taken the Lord to an unknown place. The eagerness of Peter and John also appeared in their running toward the tomb, and John outran Peter because of his young age.

entries.section: (1) The visit of Magdalene, Peter and John to the empty tomb

paragraphs.text: The body of the dead man was wrapped entirely in linen cloths, while his head was covered by a larger napkin that enclosed all of it, and it was a separate piece. The purpose of mentioning these details is to prove one thing, namely that the body was not stolen, because whoever wanted to steal the body would not have had time to unwind all these wrapped cloths, but would have taken the whole body and then thrown away the cloths somewhere far off.

St. John does not fail to mention some details in order to make us share the scene with him. His stooping down shows how low the door of the tomb was, and his not entering, after looking at the linen cloths, shows the awe of the moment. As for Peter's entering, it confirms his bold nature and readiness to act, which we have grown accustomed to.

entries.section: (1) The visit of Magdalene, Peter and John to the empty tomb

paragraphs.text: Then John's courage came after Peter, and he entered too, and wonder turned into faith: faith in what Magdalene had told them, which he had doubted. It was a faith before which mind and tongue are powerless, faith that Christ had risen and come out by Himself from this dark tomb.

entries.section: (1) The visit of Magdalene, Peter and John to the empty tomb

paragraphs.text: The death of Christ was a shock to the disciples because they had not understood the prophecies of the Old Testament about His resurrection... And this scene ends with the two disciples returning to Jerusalem, where their homes were.

entries.section: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

paragraphs.text: The two disciples went back, but Mary's love bound her to the tomb, and she could not leave it. Instead she stooped down, because of the low door of the tomb, and looked inside, and saw two angels who appeared in the form of men. Mark described them as "a young man" (Mk 16:5), and Luke as "two men" (Lk 24:4), and St. John also makes clear the position in which they sat.

entries.section: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

paragraphs.text: It is remarkable that Mary was not afraid of the presence of these two angels, who had not been there before.

"Woman, why weepest thou?": this question did not mean that they did not know the reason for her weeping, but rather that they disapproved of it, since one ought to rejoice at the resurrection of the Lord from the dead. Her answer came to express her lack of conviction, or let us say her lack of grasp of this Resurrection, for she still believed that the body had been taken away and did not know where it was.

And when she had finished her answer, "she turned herself back, and saw Jesus standing". And because she was in bewilderment and grief, she did not know who He was, for it was far from her imagination and expectation that this should be the person of the Lord Jesus.

entries.section: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

paragraphs.text: The tomb was hewn in a rock within a garden, and so the quickest possibility that leapt to Magdalene's mind was that the one speaking, who was awake at this early hour of the morning, must be the gardener. She did not turn or look closely at His appearance or His voice, because the event of the Resurrection was not within our reckoning. As for Christ's question to her, it was of course not by way of inquiry, since He knows the thoughts of hearts, but to rouse her and to present Himself to her.

entries.section: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

paragraphs.text: The Lord called her by her name, and her response was like that of the lamb that knows the voice of its shepherd, and she seemed to be waking from a dream and heedlessness to the wakefulness of the Resurrection, unable to believe, and she answered: "Rabboni", that is, Master, which was the expression and title by which Christ was addressed. Therefore, by this answer she declares to us her recognition of the person of Him who rose from the dead.

entries.section: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

paragraphs.text: "Touch me not": in (Mt 28:9) we learn that Mary Magdalene and the other Mary held Him by the feet, so why did the Lord say here, "Touch me not"?

Some explain this situation by saying that Mary, the first time, did in fact touch Christ, but some doubts about the Resurrection returned to her, and for this reason Christ forbade her to touch Him, as a kind of spiritual discipline for her doubt of the Resurrection.

St. John Chrysostom, however, says that the Lord wanted to move Magdalene from a state of emotional attachment to His person to the truth of the Resurrection and the glory of His new divinity, as though He were leading her gradually to maturity, weaning her from fleshly feelings to higher spiritual ones.

There is also a third opinion, which holds that what Christ meant was: do not hinder Me or delay the proclamation of the Resurrection, for there is the work of informing the disciples that you must do, and then "for I am not yet ascended to my Father", that is, I am not ascending soon, but I will remain forty days, so this is not the only opportunity in which you will see Me. "My Father, and your Father": My Father in particular and your Father in general, that is, My hypostatic Father, whose Son I am, the Word, and your Father, that is, the general Fatherhood of God to all His believing children.
"My God, and your God": My God because the Father in His glory is greater than the Son incarnate on earth, whose glory is hidden, although the two are one; and your God because you are His creation.

entries.section: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

paragraphs.text: So Magdalene hurried to tell the disciples that she had seen the risen Christ, and of all the conversation that took place between them, and that He would ascend to heaven after a period during which He would appear to them.

entries.section: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: On the evening of Resurrection Sunday, St. John depicts the state of the ten disciples (since Judas had disappeared and Thomas was absent), their fear, and how the doors were tightly shut on them from the inside; yet this proves the doctrine of the glorified resurrection body, which is not subject to material laws.
The disciples were startled to find the Lord Christ in their midst, bestowing on them His divine peace to reassure their hearts and free them from the fear in which they had shut themselves.

So are we all... we have closed doors and high walls of fears or anxiety... and we all ask for Your peace and the shining of Your divine light upon us, that our hearts may be reassured and we may cast fear outside.

entries.section: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: Christ gave proof of the resurrection of His body: He is therefore not a spirit or an apparition, but a risen body bearing the wounds of the Cross... And for this reason the disciples' joy was wonderful when they saw the Lord and were assured of His resurrection... and there is nothing in existence that equals the joy of seeing the Lord.

God has granted us to see Him with the eyes of faith in our daily life, a gift from which everyone who does not confess Him, or who lives outside His Church, has deprived himself. And this gift is a pledge for whoever abides in the love of God, that we shall see Him there in heaven and our joy in Him will be complete, a joy without care, grief, sighing or anxiety, as the Church prays in the Litany of the Departed.

entries.section: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: Christ repeated the greeting of His peace, granted to them a second time, to increase their sense of reassurance, and then moved on to something else, namely the disciples' coming work. "As my Father hath sent me" for the work of redemption, which no one other than I can offer, "even so send I you" as preachers and witnesses of this redemption that has been accomplished.

entries.section: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: "He breathed on them... the Holy Spirit": the Lord Christ had said earlier of the Holy Spirit that the Father would send Him in His name. And here He grants the disciples the gift of the Holy Spirit by breathing into their faces, because His authority is the authority of the Father Himself. We point out two things here:
That this breathing was the foundation of the sacrament of the priesthood in the New Testament.

That this breathing, in the apostolic tradition, became like the leaven which the Apostles received from the Lord Christ and deposited within the sacraments of the Church. The priest, in the sacrament of Baptism, also breathes into the face of the one baptized, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit." Likewise, in the sacrament of the priesthood the bishop breathes into the face of the priest and repeats the same words... and many priests also use it in the sacrament of confession as a breathing for the forgiveness of sins... and so on...

entries.section: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: A verse that makes clear, without any ambiguity or doubt, the authority of the Holy Spirit present in the sacrament of the priesthood, which the Lord Christ granted in the preceding verse to His Apostles, who deposited it in the Church.

We content ourselves here with what St. Cyril the Great cited in explaining it: "Forgiveness belongs to the nature of God alone, but those to whom He has given His Holy Spirit He has granted to possess the power of forgiveness, because however they act, it is the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, through the sacrament of the priesthood, who forgives or retains sins. The work, however, is carried out by means of a man, the priest, and this authority derives from the Holy Spirit and not from the holiness of the man (see the incident of Peter with Sapphira and Ananias, Acts 5:1-10), and Peter's saying: 'Why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost?' (v. 3), and he did not say: to lie to me? As for the sacrament of the forgiveness of sins, repentance and confession, it is the acknowledgment before the Holy Spirit, who uses the hand of the priest to transfer the sins of the penitent to the account of the atoning blood of Christ. The Holy Spirit also declares, through the priest, God's forgiveness of this sin. For this reason the sacrament of confession is one of the most joyful and comforting sacraments for man, especially for the one who practices it with understanding and awareness.

entries.section: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: Thomas represented the rationalist character that hinders simple faith of the heart, so that he refused to believe the rest of the pure Apostles and the testimony of the women of the Resurrection, and he also had a precedent (see ch. 14:5). Indeed he declared, in an unconcealed challenge, that he would not believe unless he saw and felt the wounds of the Cross materially. St. John mentions the attitude of the Apostle Thomas here because he considers it a prelude to the events of the coming appearance of Christ among His disciples.

entries.section: (4) The second appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: On the following Sunday the appearance was repeated with the same circumstances, the only difference being the presence of Thomas, who had been absent before. After the Lord gave His peace to the disciples, He addressed His words directly to Thomas, and the aim of all of Christ's words is: "and be not faithless, but believing".

Christ's manner with Thomas gives us an example of largeness of heart, kindness and long-suffering, even toward one who doubted and made it a condition for God to answer his requests before he would believe in His resurrection, to teach us thereby the true meaning of humility, condescension and compassion for people in their spiritual weaknesses.
Some also hold that Christ's words were not without gentle reproach.

entries.section: (4) The second appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: "My Lord and my God": Thomas's answer came as "a declaration and an apology": a strong declaration of faith, and also an apology for his shame at Christ's gentle reproach for his blatant unbelief. Thomas did not say only "My Lord", but also "and my God", a strong expression by which he conveys his understanding of the mystery of the Resurrection, and that he was before the incarnate God, who by His divinity broke the sting and power of death.

entries.section: (4) The second appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: Here the Lord Christ also gently reproaches Thomas for his doubt, for it was not fitting for a disciple who had lived with Christ more than three years, in which he saw the miracles and heard the teachings, to take such a position, demanding a material sight of the risen Christ. And for this reason the Lord Christ also declares the blessedness, that is, the blessings, which everyone who believes in Him receives in every age, without letting his mind stand as an obstacle to his faith.

entries.section: (4) The second appearance to the disciples

paragraphs.text: St. John makes clear here the purpose of writing his whole Gospel: that it was not a book to enumerate the miracles and wonders, which all the books of the world could not contain (ch. 21:25), but it had one purpose only, which is the faith that Jesus the man is the Christ, God, and is the hypostasis of the Word, the eternal and heavenly Son of God. It is as though John, as he concludes his Gospel, reminds us of what he had already declared about the person of the Lord Christ in his first chapter, that the Word is the Son of God and that the Word was God, and he gives all readers the summary of his whole Gospel and its purpose, namely that there is no life and no eternity outside the name of Christ; for those who received Him are the only ones who became children of God.

Our beloved God, grant us this living and active faith which is the secret of overcoming the world, as St. John said in his first epistle: "Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God?" (1 Jn 5:5).
The appearance of Christ to the disciples a second time and His last commission to Peter to shepherd the flock

The Sea of Tiberias is the same as the Sea of Galilee, but St. John attributes it to the modern city of Tiberias, which was built by Herod, who was tetrarch of Galilee. The number of the disciples was seven, among them John and his brother James, and two of the disciples who were not of the Apostles.

"After these things Jesus shewed himself again": a phrase that points to the multiplicity of the appearances of the Resurrection after the previous appearances, to prove the divinity of the Lord Christ, as will become clear from the kind of this miracle.

Some thought that what Peter did was a turning back to the world, while others thought there was nothing in this, for Christianity did not forbid work; rather this was a course proclaimed by St. Paul in (Acts 20:34; 1 Thess 3:8).

The most moderate of these opinions is what St. Gregory the Great said: "Peter returned to fishing, but not to collecting taxes, because there are occupations to which one cannot return after renewal." It can also be said that what is held against Peter is his return to his first occupation without accompanying it with any work of preaching.

After they had toiled and failed to catch anything, the appearance of the Lord occurred, obscure at its beginning, and the dawn with its faint light removed its obscurity. The Lord Christ addressed them with His question: "Have ye any meat?" that is, anything to eat with bread, and the intended meaning of course is fish. Their negative reply expressed their condition. And of course the Lord's question here was only a preparation for the coming miracle.

The Lord offers advice to the fishermen, the servants, who were exhausted and had labored all night, reminding us of the first advice by which Peter recognized the Lord Christ in (Lk 5:4). It can be said that this miracle is a lesson for what happens in our life every day, and in the life of servants in particular, for we often depend on our hearts, our understanding and our experiences without God, whereas dependence on God and His word is behind true success; there is no value in any effort separated from God who works in His Church... and no value in any work that Christ does not bless, as if Christ were giving the disciples and the Church this lesson so that we may act on it in every aspect of our life. Peter, who followed Christ, denied Him when he depended on himself, despite his love for Him. But when the Holy Spirit worked in him, on the day of Pentecost he caught with his sermon 3,000 souls (Acts 2:41). Was that not a great deal of fish...?!

"He was naked": because they were fishing, Peter had taken off everything that hindered him in his work, and John, with his loving heart and greater alertness, was quick in faith to grasp what was happening and to connect the events with one another. For this reason his declaration was strong, firm and joyful: "It is the Lord."

Although it would have been natural for Peter to throw himself in as he was, he did something unnatural: he put on what he had taken off before throwing himself into the water. And we may understand that what Peter did:
First: befits the honor of God, before whom the angels cover their feet and their faces.

Second: relates to Peter himself, for he still felt shame because of the sin of his denial, as though he were covering not only his body but his naked soul, which, although it had wept bitterly, had not yet heard from the Lord His forgiveness of it.

The distance between the boat and the shore was about 95 meters, and what matters more is the spiritual, contemplative meaning here: the boat is the Church, the disciples are its priests and servants, and the fish are the souls that the Church has drawn from drowning in the world to the shore of spiritual deliverance...

And when everyone who has labored in service and drawn souls to God comes out, he finds that the almighty Christ has prepared for him food and a heavenly portion, as though He were rewarding with a special reward everyone who has toiled and kept vigil in catching souls for Him.
"Bring... which ye have now caught": ... we notice two things:
First: that what the disciples caught was fundamentally a miracle worked by the Lord, yet God, in His humility, attributes His work to His children...
Second: that He wants them to bring from their nets, in addition to what He Himself had prepared for them, in order to share the table with them and in their joy.

And this teaches us something important, which is that God is the One who works. But man too must offer to God what he has of energy, effort and money, so that the limited and weak is united with the work of God of infinite power.

The fish were very large and abundant (153), a number beyond imagination to come out in a single haul. It means that despite the darkness of the world and the multitude of spiritual battles, the Church of Christ, by the power of His work, is able to draw many and great souls, because she comes with all her abilities and gifts to the Kingdom, however long and pitch-dark the night (the darkness of the world) may be.

"Come and dine": God is the source of all nourishment. Did He not feed the people before in the wilderness, and likewise in the miracle of feeding the multitudes? He is the source of satisfaction for all who follow Him, satisfying them in every respect... spiritually and materially.

"None of the disciples durst ask": ... this points to the awe of the Person and the awe of the situation itself.
