And St. John gives another reason for their not asking Him, namely their knowledge and certainty that He was the Lord Jesus, as though the situation did not call for a question. Perhaps their caution and awe at this situation kept them standing, despite the Lord's invitation to them to eat, so the Lord Christ Himself came forward and took the bread and the fish, completing the course of His humility. For He, God and Lord, offers and performs the duty of hospitality for His disciples... And of course, when St. John said "This is now the third time", he did not mean by this that it was the last time, but it is a sequential record of what he had reported in the previous appearances.

After the meal Christ directed His words to Peter, but He called him by his human name and not the name He had given him as an apostle, since by his denial he had come down to the level of an ordinary man: "lovest thou me more than these?"

And here Peter recalls what he had said earlier in pride, setting himself apart from the rest of the Apostles (see Mt 26:33; Mk 14:29), and he answered: "Thou knowest that I love thee." Christ's comment was a charge to Peter that the proof of true love is the shepherding of the sheep, that is, souls or the Church, for the love of the faithful servant for his master is the shepherding of his children with all faithfulness, devotion and self-giving, and not by words or by claiming this love, which may fail before trials because of our false claim, as happened first with Peter.

The Lord Christ repeats the question twice after the first, to answer Peter's three denials. And each time He commands him that the true apology which He accepts from him is the shepherding of His people. However, the third time St. John shows us Peter's grief at the repetition of the question, so he wanted to defend himself against the charge of not loving Christ, and said to Him: "Thou knowest", that is, You do not need my answer to the question, for You are the searcher of hearts and know what is within them... and You also know that, if I denied You, it was out of human weakness.

What Christ said here to Peter directly applies to all of us indirectly in its spiritual meaning. For man in his spiritual youth, with little experience of faith, depends on himself and on his own human arms in service and in his life in general. But when he grows and increases in experience in the spiritual life, he becomes more humble and obedient to the work of the Holy Spirit, so the human self disappears and in its place comes a life of complete surrender to the divine will and purpose. As for the direct meaning for Peter, which St. John made clear in (v. 18): you, Peter, in the youth of your faith were impetuous, and promised what you could not do. But when you grow, you will go forward, by the power of the Holy Spirit working in you, to the death that frightened you before, and you will accept crucifixion head downward, and the end of your life and your martyrdom will be the greatest glorification you offer to My holy name.

And we all, how greatly we need, O God, to rely on the work of Your Holy Spirit in our life, emptying ourselves and stretching out our arms, that You alone may take the lead by Your good will; as for our own thinking, it is utterly deficient.

The last word Christ said to Peter was: "Follow me." After Peter was reassured of his return to his apostolic standing, and of Christ's forgiveness of the sin of his denial of Him, he turned to St. John, whom he saw also following Christ, and turned to Christ asking about John's future fate, which was a question out of place, since Peter gave himself a right that was not his, to ask about the standing or future of another, which is a matter belonging to the very work and will of God. For this reason the answer of the Lord Christ to Peter was decisive: "what is that to thee?" It means that this is none of your concern... attend to the matter that I direct to you alone, which is that you follow Me, without looking to anyone else, even if I wish him to remain alive until My second coming.

Perhaps the answer of the Lord Christ to Peter is an answer directed to all of us, for our thoughts often slip into comparisons or inquiries that are none of our business, such as asking whether others will be saved or not, and Christ's answer to us is: "Follow thou me... and you have no concern with others." May we take in these words, and not be occupied with anything but the salvation of our own souls...
He clarifies the confusion that arose in the disciples' understanding of Christ's last saying, and St. John explained it.
Here, as St. John has come to the end of his Gospel, it was important to him to emphasize two things:
First: the truth of his testimony, because he saw and wrote with his own hand what he witnessed, and not by report from another.

Second: that what he mentioned in his Gospel and his testimony is not everything, for he mentioned some things for the sake of faith in the person of the Lord Christ, and not an enumeration of all His miracles, discourses or parables, as the other Gospels attempted, though they mentioned only a little, as much as they could. And he shows the greatness of what the Lord did, and the impossibility of recording everything, in a beautiful turn of phrase, saying that all the books of the world are not enough to write down everything about the Lord Jesus; indeed, the world itself, in all its breadth, could not contain these books. And to our God be glory forever... Amen.
